items.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
items.text: It’s a pleasure to rise and take a call on a third reading of the Regulatory
Systems (Primary Industries) Amendment Bill. Just noting that this was a Labour Party bill that was
introduced in 2023, and it has now, eventually—three years later, and through a select committee
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 296 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
process—made its way back to the House for its final reading. So it’s great to see that things are
happening quickly in this place.
This is a sensible bill that is an omnibus bill. It covers across a number of different Acts and it’s a
wide-ranging piece of legislation. It strengthens and modernises the regulatory systems that underpin
some of New Zealand’s most critical sectors: our farming and food production systems, forestry,
fisheries, biosecurity, and animal welfare settings. This bill in total amends 17 Acts of Parliament and
repeals five outdated Acts. It contains more than 300 clauses and over 250 substantive amendments.
So there has been a significant amount of work put into what is a detailed piece of legislation. It was
introduced in 2023, it had its first reading in 2024, and now it’s come back to the House.
I’m going to talk through some of the changes that have come through as a result of both the bill and
the select committee process. The Acts being repealed reflect early eras of industry, structure, and
policies. These include the Animal Products (Ancillary and Transitional Provisions) Act 1999, the
Food Safety Law Reform Act of 2018, the Forests (West Coast Accord) Act of 2000, the Hop Industry
Restructuring Act 2003, and the Wool Industry Restructuring Act 2003—who knew all these Acts
existed? These frameworks are either no longer in use or have been fully superseded by more
modern legislation. There are an extensive number of Acts being amended. They span the breadth
of the primary industry system, from biosecurity and fisheries to food safety, forestry, animal welfare,
and export systems. A few other Acts were added to this bill through the select committee process,
including the Forests (Legal Harvest Assurance) Amendment Act 2023, the New Zealand Horticulture
Export Authority Act 1987, and the Organic Products and Production Act of 2023.
This bill can be grouped into four clear objectives in terms of its intent. The first is around reducing
administrative burden. It reduces the unnecessary administrative burden on industry and regulators.
For example, under the Agricultural Compounds and Veterinary Medicines Act, companies
previously faced full re-registration of trade name products when approvals expired. That process is
costly, repetitive, and discouraged companies from maintaining products in the New Zealand market.
This bill introduces a renewal pathway that removes unnecessary duplication and helps maintain
access to safe agricultural tools for farmers and veterinarians.
Similarly, under the Fisheries Act, commercial fishers currently must apply individually for approval
to use alternative disposal methods for unwanted catch. This creates delays and inefficiencies for
both industry and officials. The bill allows for standardised regulatory settings, reducing hundreds of
individual applications and improving operational efficiency.
There’s a further change to the Fisheries Act which was quite important, given that the Government
has chosen to delay the Fisheries Amendment Bill, as that bill would’ve dealt with a legislative cliff
that would’ve been occurring in September of this year. Under the Fisheries Act, there are rules that
require commercial operators to land all of their catch. There are some fish species that are currently
subject to some transitional landing exceptions, and those are listed in Schedule 1AA of the Act.
Those transitional landing exceptions were due to expire in September of 2026, and that would have
been dealt with, as I’ve said, through the Fisheries Amendment Bill. The Minister in charge of the bill,
the Hon Shane Jones, has therefore proposed extending those transitional dates for landing
exceptions through until 30 September 2028, and so that’s a further two years to give that time for
the full impact of Labour’s on-board camera roll-out to occur, because those two parts actually
operate together, the landing rules and the cameras on board boats. So this is a pragmatic decision
to continue with that exemption for a further two years while more work is done in that space.
The second objective of this bill is around clarifying and updating legislation. This bill updates
outdated provisions to better reflect how systems operate today. For example, under the Animal
Welfare Act, decision makers will now be able to consider an exporter’s compliance history when
issuing animal welfare export certificates. This is a topical issue at the moment and an important one
in this Act. It closes a gap in the current law and will strengthen animal welfare oversight through a
more practical and risk-based approach.
The Walking Access Act is also renamed the Outdoor Access Act, reflecting the broader scope of
the commission’s work beyond walking alone. This provides clarity for landowners, councils, and the
public about the true nature of its functions.
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 297
Thirdly, this bill fixes errors, gaps, and inconsistencies, and that’s probably why it’s quite a long,
omnibus bill that we’ve got in front of us today. Under the Biosecurity Act, for example, authorised
persons will be able to seize unauthorised goods without requiring the presence of a constable in
certain situations. This strengthens front-line responsiveness and removes unnecessary procedural
delays that can hinder the effectiveness of our biosecurity system.
Finally, the bill ensures our regulatory frameworks remain modern and adaptable. Under the Organic
Products and Production Act, for example, the bill introduces the ability to make minor or technical
amendments, where the statutory test for minor or technical change is met, to delegated legislation
without requiring a full statutory process. This reflects the fast-moving nature of the organics sector,
where small technical updates must be made efficiently while maintaining appropriate safeguards.
Another example is the Commodity Levies Act, where levy orders have been extended from five to
six years. This reduces administrative burden on industry bodies and supports stability in levy-funded
programmes.
Finally, I want to talk to some other updates in this bill, namely amendments around the Horticulture
Export Authority and Cyclone Gabrielle. Not only does the bill reduce administrative burden, clarify
and update legislation, fix errors, gaps, and inconsistencies, and ensure our regulatory systems
remain up to date, it is also the product of responsive policy making driven by recent events.
One of the most important changes in this bill relates to the New Zealand Horticulture Export
Authority. The devastation caused by Cyclone Gabrielle is still fresh in the minds of many New
Zealanders, especially farmers and growers who are still recovering from that devastating event.
Orchards were buried in silt, infrastructure was destroyed, and families who had spent generations
building their livelihoods saw that work swept away in a matter of hours.
Section 62 of the New Zealand Horticulture Export Authority Act empowers regulations relating to
the fees the authority can charge licensed exporters. However, it did not clearly empower regulations
to provide for exemptions, waivers, or refunds of fees. There were policy proposals in 2023 to allow
fee relief for exporters affected by the North Island weather events, but under the existing legislative
settings those proposals could not be implemented. So growers may have had nothing to export, but
under New Zealand’s current legal settings, they still faced fees or obligations, even where they had
been unable to benefit from the authority’s services. That isn’t fair, and it raised concerns around
fairness and flexibility.
This bill addresses that by enabling the authority to grant exceptions, waivers, or refunds where
climatic or other events result in loss of export produce, and ensures the system can respond
appropriately in times of severe hardship. With the increasing frequency of extreme weather events
across the country, including in my area of Nelson-Tasman, it is important that the legislation does
not become a barrier to what is fair.
The select committee gave a lot of detailed consideration to this bill. One of the changes that came
back was on the National Animal Identification and Tracing information-sharing system (NAIT).
Submitters raised concerns that wider sharing of data with police could weaken privacy protections.
The committee agreed, and the proposed amendment was removed, ensuring farmers retain
confidence in the protection of their personal and commercial information.
On agricultural compounds and inhibitors, submitters highlighted concerns about delays in approvals
and regulatory uncertainty. New Zealand farmers operate in a highly innovative and competitive
environment. It is essential that they have timely access to new technologies.
In conclusion, the bill isn’t about radical change. This one is not a world-changing, front-page
headline - driving bill. But it is about ensuring that the systems that govern our primary industries are
efficient, coherent, and fit for purpose. It is important for the sector.
Importantly, it ensures that New Zealand’s primary industries—our farmers, growers, fishers,
foresters, and exporters are supported by a system that is responsive, practical, and future-focused.
Labour was proud to introduce this bill to the House, and we’re pleased to see it reach its conclusion,
today, three years later. On that note, I commend this bill to the House.

First Reading
Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction) ( 15:35): Thank you, Mr
Speaker. I move, That the Building Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the
Transport and Infrastructure Committee to consider the bill.
Building in New Zealand has become more complex with risk averse practices, limited accountability,
and slow, costly consenting processes holding the sector back. This bill supports the Government’s
objective to promote and enable a more efficient and productive building system—one where it is
more quick and affordable for Kiwis to build. It delivers major systems reform, including a fundamental
change to liability settings, removing barriers to building consent authority (BCA) consolidation and
modernising the building research funding system. It also includes two targeted measures: a fast-
track consent pathway for homes with solar generation and other sustainable features, and an
amendment to support the uptake of offsite buildings for consent-exempt small, stand-alone
dwellings, popularly known as granny flats.
A central feature of the bill is the shift for building and construction from joint and several liability,
which prioritises full recovery of the claimant, to proportionate liability—a fairer system where each
party can only be held responsible for their contribution to defective building work. Of course, the
purpose is to prevent work from being defective in the first place.
The joint and several setting has held back the sector’s performance for decades. It creates an
imbalance where parties with deeper pockets, such as building consent authorities—typically
councils, and therefore their ratepayers—can be held responsible for the full cost of defects, even
where their contribution is relatively minor, at least in some situations, exposing ratepayers to those
costs and making BCAs disproportionately risk averse. This has slowed building progress across
New Zealand.
This is not a new issue. The Law Commission carried out reviews of joint and several in 1998 and
2014 and the inefficiencies it causes and considered whether it’s the right system for New Zealand.
This has been raised in the office of various Ministers of building and construction since long before
my time, yet nothing has changed, and the issues persist. In that sense, it’s been a team effort, and
I’m glad that we are in the process of being able to bring it to a conclusion together.
Australian states, by contrast, have been operating proportionate liability models for some 30 years.
We’ve taken lessons from our counterparts across the Tasman and engaged directly with them as
well as local stakeholders, of course, and legal experts in the development of the bill. In April 2025,
I attended a roundtable hosted by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. I give a
particular shout out to Dr Michael Warren. The roundtable brought together leading Australian liability
experts and key stakeholders from New Zealand’s building, legal, and insurance sectors. Their
message was loud and clear: it’s time to move from joint and several liability to a proportionate model,
with appropriate measures in place to protect consumers.
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 299
While fairer at a system level, some building owners risk being left out of pocket when building work
goes wrong and liable parties are absent or insolvent. To mitigate this, and to help protect the so-
called mum and dad homeowners in particular, we are introducing mandatory home warranties for
most residential building work and higher value renovations. This requirement will also make it harder
for cowboys to operate—yee-ha. Without a track record of quality and accountability, it will be difficult
to obtain warranty backing, and that’s a good thing because these measures are about better
protecting homeowners taking on significant risk.
We’re also making professional indemnity insurance compulsory for design professionals, such as
engineers, architects, designers, and surveyors. These changes formalise existing good practice and
have been welcomed by industry. As a precaution, to avoid disruption in the construction sector, we
have enabled targeted, temporary suspension of home warranty and insurance requirements should
this become necessary in the future. It’s not a signal of concern but a forward-looking safeguard
developed alongside the sector. These requirements can be paused in the event of significant
disruptions and global market shifts, with home warranties and insurance remaining available on a
voluntary basis, if that should come to pass, just as they are now. Taken together, these reforms
rebalance the system, moving to fairer allocation of liability while ensuring that homeowners are
supported by stronger, more reliable consumer protections.
Another change introduced by the bill, which is again being welcomed by councils and industry alike,
is the removal of legislative barriers that have hampered the consolidation and collaboration of
building consent authorities. When the current framework was introduced in 2004, it was expected
that smaller building consent authorities would consolidate over time to achieve greater scale,
resilience, and consistency.
In practice, though, this has been limited. Some building consent authorities process up to 3,000
building consents per year, while the smallest handle only a handful.  Many lower-volume building
consent authorities rely on rates to subsidise their consenting functions. There are also
inconsistencies in how consenting requirements under the Building Code are interpreted and applied,
contributing to delays in efficiencies, including across different council borders. The bill enables
greater flexibility in how building consent functions are delivered. It removes requirements that
currently constrain how territorial authorities arrange their consenting services, including enabling
functions to be transferred to another council or a stand-alone BCA, improving competition and giving
councils more options.
Alongside these changes, statutory processing times for councils to provide project information
memoranda, or PIMs, are being reduced from 20 working days to 10 working days. This will support
more timely delivery of consent-related services by stand-alone BCAs. BCA consolidation is
voluntary, I emphasise to fellow members of the House; the changes do not force building consent
authorities to change how they operate, but they remove unnecessary barriers for those that wish to
do so, supporting a more consistent, efficient, and competitive consenting system. At the same time,
the bill modernises the way that building research is funded, improving parliamentary oversight and
accountability and alignment with sector priorities.
The current Building Research Levy - funded system, established back in 1969, is no longer fit for
purpose. To better support housing and infrastructure development heading into the future, we need
to enable greater innovation, promote value for money, and open opportunities beyond the single
current provider. The bill repeals the Building Research Levy Act and gives the Ministry for Business,
Innovation and Employment (MBIE) chief executive a new role in funding building research, with
funding ring-fenced and collected through a single building levy. The research levy has historically
been paid only to BRANZ, the Building Research Association of New Zealand, which has received
more than $260 million in levy revenue over the last 12 years. Amalgamating the two levies creates
a more coherent and streamlined funding framework, improves oversight and accountability, and
introduces new mechanisms to support contestable funding processes and a clearer link between
research, investment, and sector needs. A more coherent system and a more coherent Minister for
Building and Construction would also be helpful, Mr Speaker!
In addition to the system-level reforms, the bill includes two more targeted changes to support faster,
more efficient, and sustainable building. It introduces a fast-track building consent pathway for new
residential buildings with solar generation and sustainable attributes, requiring eligible building

consents to be processed by BCAs within 10 working days, compared with the standard current 20
working days. To access this fast track, buildings must meet specified performance criteria relating
to solar generation or sustainability, such as energy efficiency, water efficiency, low-embodied
carbon, and/or climate resilience. These criteria will be set through a notice issued by the chief
executive of MBIE to ensure that they can adapt over time as building practices and technologies
evolve. This reform is intended to encourage greater uptake of solar generation and sustainable
building design, while speeding up the consenting process and supporting more efficient delivery of
new homes.
Finally, the bill also supports more efficient construction methods by permitting the offsite
construction of consent-exempt granny flats to take place in advance of receiving a project
information memorandum, or, again, a PIM—that’s for the site a home will, ultimately, be located
upon. Since the exemption came into effect in January 2026, some 225 PIMs have been issued in
the first quarter of this year, representing $34 million worth of potential building work. This is real
progress, but I’ve still heard, none the less, that there can be challenges for some offsite construction
models where homes are built in advance of receiving a PIM. So, again, we’re doing something about
that. The bill allows offsite construction to take place before a PIM is issued, while still requiring a
PIM before any onsite building work can take place. This change will support faster delivery of homes
under the exemption and allow potential buyers to inspect completed dwellings before purchase,
while maintaining the existing safeguards and protections for homeowners provided under the
exemption.
In the closing minute of my speech, acknowledging there’s a lot that we’ve put into the bill, as well
as into this 10 minutes, I note that the bill makes a deliberate shift in how the system works, from
one that concentrates risk and holds back performance to one that shares responsibility more fairly
and supports better outcomes across the sector. It pairs changes to liability settings with stronger
consumer protections so that while responsibility is more fairly shared, homeowners remain well
protected. Alongside this, the bill removes unnecessary barriers to support a more efficient
consenting system, it modernises how levies are collected and allocated, and it makes targeted
changes that will have real impacts for Kiwis looking to get on and build.
This is a practical package of reforms that improves system performance and gives New Zealanders
greater confidence in the homes they build and buy. For all those reasons, I commend this bill to the
House.

CLIMATE CHANGE RESPONSE (TORT LIABILITY) AMENDMENT BILL
Legislative Statement

items.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: I present a legislative statement on
the Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill.

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: That legislative statement is published under the
authority of the House and can be found on the parliamentary website.
First Reading

items.speaker: Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH
items.text: I move, That the Climate Change
Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Justice
Committee to consider the bill. At the appropriate time I intend to move that the bill be reported to
the House by 30 July 2026 and that the committee have authority to meet at any time while the House
is sitting (except during oral questions), during any evening on a day on which there has been a
sitting of the House, on a Friday in a week in which there has been a sitting in the House, and outside
the Wellington area, despite Standing Orders 193,195, and 196.
This bill clarifies climate change laws to provide businesses and New Zealanders with certainty
around their obligations. Ongoing litigation in the High Court, where civil claims have been made, is
creating uncertainty in business confidence and investment. It risks the development of a new regime
that runs in parallel and it may contradict the framework that Parliament has already enacted to
respond to climate change. Ultimately, if there is legal uncertainty, there is less investment over time,
and that affects us all by making our country less competitive. Therefore, the Government will amend
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 307
the Climate Change Response Act 2002 to prevent findings of tort liability for activities that cause or
contribute to the emissions of greenhouse gas and, through those emissions, may cause or
contribute to climate change harm.
A tort is a civil claim brought in private law in situations where the conduct of one person causes
harm or invades the interests of another person. Tort law has primarily been developed through the
common law, which arises from decisions made by judges in court, rather than by legislation that has
developed in Parliament.
In the Smith v Fonterra case, the defendant is asking the court to develop a regime to control and
reduce the emissions of six of this country’s largest businesses. This would be potentially contrary
to the regulatory response set by Parliament under the Climate Change Response Act 2002, which
sets out our legal framework for New Zealand’s regulatory response to climate change. This
framework includes a 2050 target for emissions reduction and a regime for setting and meeting
successive emissions budgets with a view to achieving that target.
The Government’s view is that greenhouse gas emissions and climate change harm are best
regulated by Parliament and the executive, who take a whole-of-economy approach that carefully
considers environmental, economic, and social implications, rather than having that done on a case
by case basis through litigation in the courts. A statutory bar prevents courts from issuing a certain
type of finding or considering a particular issue. In this case, the bill will prevent a person or entity
from being liable in tort law for climate change or harm caused by greenhouse gas emissions. This
will apply to all activities contributing to greenhouse gas emissions directly and indirectly, regardless
of when or where they occur.
However, the bill is targeted and will only affect tort claims relating to climate change damage or
harm arising from greenhouse gas emissions. It will not affect traditional environmental torts—for
example, where a factory burning fossil fuels causes harm through odour or ash residue. This may
still be covered under the tort of nuisance.
The bill will also apply to the proceedings of Smith v Fonterra. I acknowledge that care is needed
when deciding whether legislation should apply to existing court proceedings. However, these
proceedings are still at the procedural stage, and the substantive proceedings have yet to start.
Currently, there is no tort liability for climate change damage caused by greenhouse gas emissions,
but this is what Mr Smith is asking to be developed. I therefore consider that the application of the
bar to existing proceedings that have not been finally determined is necessary. This will ensure that
there’s no risk of a parallel regulatory regime being developed in future which applies to some of
emitters and is inconsistent with the Government’s regulatory response. As no rights have yet been
identified in the existing case, this legislation will not deprive the litigants of the fruit of litigation.
The bill clarifies the regulatory framework in which we are operating as a country with regard to
climate change. The bill doesn’t change New Zealand’s climate targets or the approach that the
Government has taken. Businesses with obligations under the emissions trading scheme will still be
required to meet them. We have a good regime in the Climate Change Response Act and the
emissions trading scheme, and we’re seeking to make sure this regime is clearly in place without
confusion.
The bill makes it clear that the response to climate change sits squarely with the elected Parliament
and the executive. The bill clarifies the law to ensure that there is certainty around climate change
obligations of New Zealand businesses. It also ensures our response to climate change is managed
by Parliament and the executive at a national level, rather than on a case by case basis through the
courts. On that basis, I commend this bill to the House.

Decarbonising Industry (GIDI), the fund for helping industries transition away from fossil fuels; they’ve

New Zealanders, that ordinary people should rely on the executive and the Parliament to manage
our climate change response and that is why he is engaged in putting a statutory bar on any tort

rely on them to do that, so one of the only courses of action that has to be available to us is through
the courts, and they are cancelling that course of action too. What a wretched thing to do. They are
cancelling it on the spurious grounds, not backed up by the Minister’s own officials, that it will cause
business uncertainty; and they are cancelling it on the grounds that the executive is the entity best

My suggestion to the House is that it would be appropriate for the select committee to open a briefing
that heard submitters for a period of six months, while also considering the bill that would be reported
back in the shorter period. This is a suggestion that has been made by the Rt Hon Geoffrey Palmer
in relation to bills that proceed through urgency—all stages—that another sort of bill would be
introduced to a subject matter select committee instead of the Regulations Review Committee, so
that even though it was presented back to the House in time for the executive to advance its
legislative agenda, the select committee would still then be able to consider submissions, to be able
to consider advice, and then to come to a reasoned view not only in its departmental report, advised
on by the Minister’s advisers, but in its report to the House. As we know, often a select committee
will come to a different view than the departmental report provided by the advisers. That is an
appropriate part of the select committee process.
This novel method of opening an inquiry at the same time as hearing a bill would provide for that. It
would also allow for a select committee to test what has been a suggestion by one of our preeminent
scholars of our constitutional arrangements in New Zealand, the Rt Hon Sir Geoffrey Palmer, and
whether this would work in an ongoing way, whether the House would be aided by select committees
being able to review legislation in the normal way even when urgency is afforded. You can imagine
that members on this side of the House would also be in a situation where, in Government, they
might be able to use urgency for certain things—there are incentives for both major parties to be able
to use it—but, in a new sort of arrangement where select committees could proceed at an ordinary
pace, to be able to consider the submissions of submitters and also the advice from the department,
you might then pick up things along the way, where a Minister can then consider those things. That
is already the arrangement whereby these periodic checks by different parts of the legislature and
the executive will check the legislation and will notify Ministers of changes they need to make.
Just today, we saw a Minister of primary industries in the chair in a committee stage, where he was
presenting to the House a number of updates to primary industries legislation—23 pieces of
legislation were being updated in that way. We already have a mechanism for Ministers to hear
feedback, not only from the industries they are representing but also from the legal experts who come
along and make these representations. This is the perfect way to make this a part of our ordinary
constitutional framework whereby those things are formalised: people aren’t accessing the members
of the executive via a back door or a fast track to access to a Minister but they are coming in through
the front door, through a select committee process and making the representations to a select
committee of nominally independent MPs from the executive who can consider those submissions
separately.
That is an important part of the scrutiny process that New Zealand Parliament has. Many of us really
enjoy that feature of the New Zealand Parliament, where someone can rock along to a select
committee and make a suggestion and the law will reflect that. This is an appropriate way of building
that into the system and still allowing an executive Government to, at times, require the House to
move at pace and on its terms. There will always be a need for that in this system, and the tension
here between speed and between proper scrutiny does not need to be arranged in the way that it is.
We can have proper scrutiny of this bill, and we can have proper scrutiny of later bills. The process
for a select committee to be able to do this can be enabled now via the inquiry or briefing process.
Opening a briefing on a piece of legislation that is before a committee is well within its power. It does
not need to be directed by the House to do so—although that is what the Minister should have
included in his referral motion, and that is why I am making a speech on his original referral motion.
It is important that we consider here what the role of select committees is, because this Parliament
has had some uniquely good select committees that have been great at grappling with, particularly,
legislative detail. This is a Parliament where you can see, in the mix and the make-up of it, with minor
parties being chairs of select committees and with engaged Opposition members being right in the
detail of their portfolios, that we are capable of this and we always should arrange our select
committees in a way where Ministers can look at a select committee and see a chair who they trust
not only to scrutinise the legislation that they have before them but, also, to make changes to it.

This Government is one that has been in the habit of introducing legislation at the first reading before
it is finished, and that is a process that our legislature is not designed for. If we want to continue to
use it in that way, where legislation comes to the House at first reading in a way where the policy will
be changed at the committee stage, then we have to have select committee chairs who can deal with
that. We have to have a system that is robust enough to be able to hear from experts; for committee
chairs to be able to seek guidance from the departments who are advising them, not the executive.
That has to be clear, too, because a number of times in this Parliament, it has been unclear whether
the department officials are advising the Minister or are taking instructions from the Minister, or are
actually there to serve the committee, which is what the constitutional arrangement requires of them.
This is something that non-executive MPs must constantly defend, but this is a way which practically
enables it. And so, I hope—it is my genuine hope—that the Justice Committee will open a briefing
alongside this piece of legislation to be able to give the submitters their full due in terms of presenting
their submissions on this issue. I don’t think it is an overlap; I think it is the appropriate thing to do in
the circumstance. People are sophisticated enough to know that they are not only submitting on a
bill but they also need to submit to a briefing that is a wider inquiry about the policy statements in the
bill and what is written. That kind of process should be genuinely cross-partisan, because that is the
only way that this will continue to work—that executive Government will be able to get away with
using the legislative system in this way, where undeveloped policy positions come to the House in
the form of legislation at the first reading and they are finished by the end.
We have seen, a number of times, that Ministers have amended things at the last minute. There are
also changes that should be made by the Standing Orders review about that. Those should be fully
debated with no time limitation on them, and that was reflected in the Speaker’s comments on
Tuesday about that kind of debate. This is similar to that, where you have an unfinished policy
statement that is introduced to the legislature by a Minister open to feedback and criticism, and so,
we should give it the appropriate time at the select committee stage, as well as allowing a department
and the other organisations within Government that want to contribute to it to be able to submit to

items.speaker: ANDY FOSTER
items.text: Look, I’m delighted to get to this point of finally being able
to speak on this bill, because it’s the third time I’ve actually been the next speaker up on this particular
bill. It’s taken a long time to get to this point, but it’s great that we got here.
The Government’s got quite a number of initiatives in respect of local government going on at the
moment. We’ve got this bill, we’ve got regional deals, we’ve got the rates cap proposal—which we’ve

talked about, but no legislation yet—and then we’ve got all the structural reform announcements
which have been made.
It’s interesting: I’ve spoken to probably most councils’ mayors, and often chief executives as well,
over the term of this Government. Sometimes it’s the ones before the last local body election;
sometimes it’s the ones after; sometimes both. I’ve never seen as much interest and as much
enthusiasm as I have seen now, in terms of exploring amalgamation. So the Head Start
announcement is potentially a good nudge. But I have talked to a lot of mayors also since the
structural reform announcements a few weeks ago, and while there’s wide agreement about getting
rid of regional councils, there is real concern about the time frame which is being announced there—
real concern about those time frames—and also that feeling of: is this the last chance for councils to
be able to put a Head Start proposal before some sort of backstop stick is applied?
There’s also concern about the place of community consultation, which is absent from those
documents: the protection of local voice, the ability to be able to do the numbers, the effect on rates,
debts, and so on. Those numbers really matter; they matter in terms of the choices that councils and
communities should be able to make. There is this idea that every council must have a dance
partner—the rural-urban split: most of the rural areas don’t particularly want to be taken over by their
neighbouring urban areas—and the ability for bigger-population councils to, effectively, apparently
take over small ones.
There’s also a lot of desire to see a greater clarity about the rationale, particularly around the idea—
and I think there’s a lot of scepticism about this idea—that bigger will be better and bigger will be
more efficient. That has also come from the likes of the New Zealand Initiative and the Infrastructure
Commission. So my appeal in all of this is that central government needs to work much closer with
local government, and in a respectful way, as we go through any reform proposal.
All of that said, this bill, and all of these other initiatives, have a big, clear focus on rates—on
affordability. That is absolutely right and absolutely understandable. Across New Zealand, between
2022 and 2025, that triennium of councils, we saw and we paid unprecedented increases in rates
across the country. I understand the cumulative average was something like 34.4 percent, which is
absolutely unaffordable and unsustainable. Inflation during that time—admittedly, that was
Consumers Price Index, not Local Government Cost Index—was 13.7; way, way, way above
inflation.
Consequently, rates have become a very significant component of the inflation rate. It’s interesting:
in the debate that was going on a few weeks ago on this particular reading, Labour and the Greens
seemed to want to continue with that trajectory. That is unsustainable, and I suggest they think again
about that.
In my 30 years in local government in Wellington, generally I saw people saying, “I want more and
more services.”—more and more services. That’s really frustrating for a fiscal conservative like me.
They never ask for water services, incidentally, but now what I’m hearing is that that’s changed. In
some places, I’m hearing real fear that people will be forced out of their homes and will certainly have
to make decisions about what basic services they, in their lives, and have to forgo to pay the rates
and the water bills. So I reject completely the assertions which are made, particularly by the Green
Party, that this bill is not thinking about people; it is.

items.speaker: The question I would ask local government is
items.text: has it shown the same discipline that Government has
shown in terms of its expenditure—right-sizing and ensuring value for money? Some councils are
much better at this than others. Often it’s the smaller ones who are better at doing it. So if we are
going to make councils bigger, then I wonder whether some of that discipline of being close to
community will be lost.
This bill’s encouragement to focus on core service intends to bring rates down. I understand that the
intention is that a rates cap would also apply to core services. It is a point there that councils are
really concerned about, because they’re concerned that there’s a real tension between rates capping
and asset management, and I think that argument is a real one, and we need to think about that very,
very carefully. Local government would often say they just need more money; I don’t accept that
without seeing, first, a serious improvement in delivery efficiency and better prioritisation, because
rates and water charges are unaffordable for property owners.

I would ask the question of what we can do as central government to reduce costs that local
government faces, and therefore the rates bills—for example, the seismic costs, with the earthquake-
prone building legislation which we will consider, hopefully, later today; traffic management costs;
health and safety costs; audit costs; and representation reviews, which, hopefully, they won’t have

The other issue, which I know there are amendments about—and they will come up in the committee

Second Reading
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) ( 20:57): I move, That the Crimes
Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
One of the core pledges of this Government when we came into office 2½ years ago was to restore
law and order. That is the work of generations and is certainly the work of all New Zealanders—to fix
the basics and build a future where people feel safe in their communities. That has been an unerring
focus of this Government for the last 2½, years, and this bill, the Crimes Amendment Bill, is about
putting victims at the heart of our justice system, and it strengthens consequences for crime. It builds
on work that we’ve done bringing back real consequences for crime through changes to the
Sentencing Act and three strikes, but it also moves its focus to dealing with matters around retail
crime.
I want to thank the Justice Committee for its careful consideration of the bill—very hard-working
committee—and extend my hand across the aisle to work and contributions on the other side. The
committee received 233 submissions on the bill, and I want to thank all the submitters and the time
that they put into it.
So what does it cover? Coward punch—what it does there is it recognises the horrendous nature of
these so-called coward punches, where people come and attack somebody from behind, with no
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 349
warning, to the head and can turn a life upside down. The bill targets perpetrators of these attacks
by adding three coward punch offences to the mandatory sentencing framework of three strikes and
maximum penalties for coward punches causing grievous bodily harm increasing to eight and 15
years depending on the intent. The coward punch manslaughter offence defines this category of
violent offending and responds to the need for greater denunciation.
The Act will be another tool for police in their response to violent crime. While I’m sympathetic to
calls for even tougher responses around, say, minimum sentences, that can’t be accommodated
within the confines of this crimes bill, but it’s something that people can give consideration to over
time.
Now, the committee also notes that the Government’s capping of sentence discounts is already
increasing sentences for coward punch offenders and will make it more likely that fewer of such
offenders would be eligible for home detention, for example. I’ll continue to monitor the impact of the
recent sentencing reforms on penalties imposed for coward punch cases. I also intend to put an
Amendment Paper to better address this issue at the committee stage.
The second area is around citizen’s arrest. There has been a lot of discussion around that matter.
We are recognising that we’ve had provisions in place for a long time for things happening at night
after 9 p.m., but during the day it’s been a different regime. We were concerned about instances,
particularly in the retail crime sector, of people walking off with trolleys full of food, not paying, people
seeing that, and undermining public confidence in law and order in our community. We wanted to
make it clear that people, security workers for example, can grab hold of somebody and hang on to
them, with very clear instructions that they need to immediately call the police and follow the
instructions of the police.
There have been a lot of comments about this, and I just want to make the point, of course, that
nobody is compelled to do anything. Everybody will make a judgment based on the circumstances
of the time, and whether they think it’s safe to get involved or not. Businesses can decide whether
they’ll have protocols around this, or not, but we heard a very strong call, particularly from small,
family-owned dairies and retailers who wanted to have another tool available to them to deal with
what continues to be a real problem in the retail crime sector.
Another one is shoplifting. This bill brings in an infringement regime for shoplifting. At the moment, if
you steal a small amount of goods from a shop, the only option is to arrest that person and send
them off to court. That’s quite a high threshold. Our concern was, well, the outcome of that is that a
lot of people tend to, in practice, get away with it and face no real consequences. An infringement
regime provides an opportunity for a police officer to bring an instant consequence such as a fine,
such as a speeding ticket situation, so that there are immediate consequences. It doesn’t replace
our theft offences, but it’s another tool for police to use.
Finally, our human trafficking offences are strengthened by this bill. As one submitter noted, these

If we start with citizen’s arrest—nobody wants this. The only person who wanted this was the scone-
eating ministerial group into retail crime, who were a total waste of money and came up with all of
these crazy ideas, including allowing dairy owners to use mechanical restraints to arrest shoplifters.
Now, the police are well aware of the fact that you have to be carefully trained to detain someone
and that if you’re going to detain someone, you have to know what to do next. If you detain someone
and it turns out you’ve done it wrong, they’re going to be a little upset, but you’re going to have to let
them go. Even if they were shoplifting and the police say, “Look, we’re a bit busy with a much more
serious crime. We can’t attend. You’re going to have to release them.”, what happens at that point is
very complicated and actually quite dangerous.
We certainly don’t want people in retail situations to have some kind of expectation that they will be
not just security guards but police officers and arrest and detain people who they find shoplifting,
because it’s not their job and it’s not safe. The retail association, the police know that, the
supermarkets know that, so it’s no surprise that the overwhelming majority of submissions said,

Then we come to this creation of a new offence, the strike to the head or neck. It’s really problematic,
and, in fact, it’s ironic, and I’m not sure if I regret it or not, but here we had an offence that was so

Look, let’s be clear: when people engage in violent behaviour, this side of the House agrees that the
law should come down on them. There should be an appropriate response which does all of those
things that the criminal law should: denounce, punish, deter—all of those kinds of things. But here

items.speaker: DAN ROSEWARNE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Labour opposes this bill and
remains concerned about the way the legislation has been put together.
This is a bill that covers everything from human trafficking to citizen’s arrest powers, assaults on first
responders, shoplifting, and the proposed coward punch offence. Some of those measures are
sensible, some deserve support, but then others raise some serious concerns. The difficulty is that
instead of bringing these issues to the House in separate pieces of legislation, the Government has
bundled them together into one large bill and then tried to rush it through. When we are dealing with
the public safety, criminal offending, and people’s rights, you know, Parliament should take time to
get this absolutely right.
Let me start with the areas where there is broad agreement: Labour supports the changes relating
to human trafficking and people smuggling. These offences involve some of the most vulnerable
people imaginable. The amendments modernise our law and better reflect the reality of modern
exploitation and slavery. That’s a worthwhile and necessary change.
We also acknowledge the intent behind stronger protections for our first responders and corrections
officers. Nobody should be assaulted while carrying out their duties in the service of the public. But
part of this bill, which has attracted some of the strongest criticism at select committee, was the
proposed coward punch offence. And like every member of this House, I acknowledge the families
who have lost loved ones through these senseless acts of violence. One punch can end a life, and
one punch can leave a family grieving for ever. Those families do deserve to be heard. Coward
punches are probably the one thing that worries me most as a dad. When my son—he’s 15 years
old—does go out with his mates, that does worry me.
A victim, a victim’s family, can have their lives ended or changed forever as a result of a second of
stupidity on the part of an offender. But Parliament also has the responsibility to make good law. The
evidence presented to the committee raised very serious doubts about whether the proposed offence
would actually achieve what the supporters hope it would achieve. Officials advised the committee
that the offence, as drafted, would be harder to prosecute in existing manslaughter provisions. And
why was that? Because prosecutors would have to prove additional elements. They would need to
demonstrate not only that the assault caused death, but also that the victim had little or no opportunity
to defend themselves, and that creates an extra hurdle in prosecution.
Several submitters pointed out that the existing offence of manslaughter already covers this conduct.
Both offences carry the same maximum penalty, as the the Hon Dr Duncan Webb mentioned, of life
imprisonment. So the obvious question becomes: what practical problem is this new offence actually
solving? In fact, officials warned that it could actually create new problems. A jury could be faced
with multiple overlapping options: murder, manslaughter, manslaughter by strike to the head or neck.
And so, rather than simplifying matters, this bill risks making them even more confusing.
Even more concerning is the possibility that the additional elements in the new offence could make
a conviction harder to secure. A prosecutor might choose to proceed under the new offence. If one
of those extra elements cannot be established beyond reasonable doubt, the prosecution could fail.
Officials acknowledged that the legislation does not fit neatly with existing provisions that allow
alternative verdicts. That means that there’s a real risk that the law introduced to secure more
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed

accountability, could actually produce fewer convictions. And this should concern every member of
this House.
Labour’s position on this is straight forward: If there’s a problem with sentencing outcomes for
these offences; yeah, let’s debate sentencing. If there’s a concern about whether the courts are
properly recognising the seriousness of these crimes; then yeah, let’s consider sentencing law. But
creating a parallel manslaughter offence that officials themselves have warned may be confusing,
difficult to prosecute, and potentially counterproductive is not sound law making for. So, for that
reason, we do not support this bill.
DAN BIDOIS (National—Northcote) ( 21:55): The Crimes Amendment Bill is a good bill. It

the law. It’s all a part of this Government’s plan to fix the basics and build the future. I commend this

the fact that it’s a cluster of different changes. And that theme, really, is one that I’ve come to

Now, it doesn’t mean that some of this law that Labour is opposing isn’t going to do damage, and it
doesn’t mean that some of the law, we’ve already said, will do good. I want to focus on that for a
minute, the issue of bluff, because I think it’s a very dangerous game to play with the public. When
we say that we’re going to do things, we’re going to make lives safer for them, but what we’re actually
doing is giving them a piece of paper, a law change, but we’re not putting in the resource that’s
necessary.
Now, years ago, and not that many years ago, I got hit in the back of the head by somebody—just
out of the blue. When that happened, there wasn’t enough response, as far as I was concerned, that
was immediate, from the police force—because they were under-resourced. Actually, what I wanted,
as somebody who had that happened to me, was I wanted somebody to make sure that the person
who did that didn’t do it to anyone who was old or, basically, understood the consequences of what
she had done. That kind of follow up, from our police force, that requires real people. It didn’t really
require a change in the law. it required resourcing. I would have been very happy to have heard that
that young girl, who did that, had been apprehended and had been put into a process of reconciliation
with her actions. That’s nothing to do with punishment, etc. It’s got to do with preventing it happening
to somebody she could have killed. I was just lucky, in some ways, I was older, I was healthy, and I
wasn’t in a situation where I was really hurt by it—but I was pretty shaken up.
Now, I think that’s something I want to take to some of these other changes because that also informs
the way I see the stuff about citizen’s arrest. In my area, we’ve had quite a lot of issues at things like
Countdown with the stealing of food, etc., and we’ve had a terrible tragedy in my area, at somewhere

someone who had stolen something from the shop and they were stabbed and they died. It’s a terrible

What the police have told me about the concern that they have over this, when we’ve talked about
the realities of it, is they can’t get there anyway. If somebody arrests someone in a shop for an action
like shoplifting, the police can’t get there. Just imagine what it’s going to be like when somebody

LAND TRANSPORT (REVENUE) AMENDMENT BILL
Legislative Statement
Hon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport) ( 22:13): on behalf of the

items.speaker: Minister of Transport
items.text: I present a legislative statement on the Land Transport (Revenue)
Amendment Bill.

items.text: That legislative statement is published under the
authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Second Reading
Hon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport) ( 22:13): on behalf of the

items.speaker: Minister of Transport
items.text: I move, That the Land Transport (Revenue) Amendment Bill be now
read a second time.
Mr Speaker, colleagues, this bill is yet another step in the evolution of our land transport funding
system and it meets our changing circumstances and upholds one of the fundamental principles of
how we fund land transport in New Zealand. That principle is that vehicle users should contribute
fairly in proportion to the use that they undertake on our roads. Since we centralised our roading
system in the 1920s—planning came a bit later—this principle has continued to underpin how we
fund and pay for our roading network. However, the system is now under increasing pressure. As
our vehicles have become more fuel efficient, and we start to drive more and more electric vehicles,
the traditional method of collecting revenue from our petrol excise duties and our fuel taxes has
dropped while our transport investment demands have continued to grow.
To better support sustainable transport investment, we must ensure that the tools we collect for
revenue are sustainable, fair, and fit for purpose. To achieve this, the bill advances the Government’s
revenue action plan by proposing amendments that reform the tolling network and modernising the
road user charges system. This bill does two key things: it looks at how we toll in a modern day and
age, and it reforms our road user system.
First, to tolling. We’ve actually got a long history of tolling in New Zealand. We’ve been doing it for
over 100 years. The Auckland Harbour Bridge was built by tolls. The Lyttleton Tunnel was built by
tolls. Tauranga have a few, so there are some people here who are familiar with how they work.
What tolling does is it helps us to bring forward investment and build the roads and infrastructure that
New Zealand needs sooner. It means the users who benefit most from new roads contribute most to
those roads. We currently have toll roads in New Zealand, as I mentioned before, and we now want
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 363
to progress our roading system plan, so we need to make sure we have the revenue to match those
ambitions. It is about fixing the basics of our transport system so we can build a future where New
Zealanders can get around our routing network in a quick and efficient manner.
The bill does a number of things around tolls. It has gone through the select committee process, and
I’ll outline a few of the changes that have come through in a moment. It does allow for the tolling of
existing roads where the users benefit from new roads on the same corridor, so that we can take a
revenue approach across an entire tolling scheme rather than just on new sections of the road. Road
users out there should be aware that the requirement for a feasible, untolled, or free route will remain.
Of course, nothing is free in life. Those so-called free roads are still paid for by our road users.
However, there will be an untolled alternative to all of our tolled roads. The bill will also enable heavy
vehicles to be restricted from using unsuitable alternative routes, but only in specified circumstances.
Finally, we’re also updating the rules to toll concessions to make it easier to partner with the private
sector to deliver the infrastructure we need. Taken together, these changes will ensure tolling is a
more effective tool to help fund new roads, including our roads of national significance, those that
deliver the infrastructure that New Zealand needs.
The second key thing this bill does is it looks at the road user charge system that we deal with in our
modern day State, and it recognises that some changes are needed to be made. We need to
modernise the system. We need to keep the system fair. We must ensure it’s ready to go for a shift
in the future of all light-petrol vehicles onto the road user charge system. Our current system was
designed in the 1970s. It is admittedly a bit clunky. It’s a manual process that relies on us to monitor
our own odometers, pre-purchase road-user charges (RUC) in thousand kilometre blocks, and
display teeny tiny little paper licences on our windows.
I’ve already said many times in this House how annoying those little bits of paper are, particularly
when they fall down the dash, and a zealous parking officer comes along and gives you a nice wee
donation to make to the local council or to the local NZTA because you haven’t put the right sticker
in the right place. This bill does away with those stickers around road user charges. It removes the
requirement to display, carry, or produce a RUC licence. In an electronic age, a paper licence should
not be a strict requirement where people are paying bills, not to put paper in the front of the
windscreens. The bill updates the definition of an electronic distance recorder to address some
current restrictions and allow for more flexible, cost-effective approaches to recording distance.
In a bold modern move, it allows us to have more flexible regular payment systems, so that, instead
of that thrill we get when we’re driving along the road and we realise we might be running out of road
user charges soon, and we’d better pull over to the side of the road, jump on the NZTA website, and
buy another thousand blocks to get us around the countryside a bit more, we’re going to be able to
create some new options for some more regular payments to make it a little bit easier to deal with

I do want to speak about some of the issues around the road-user charges, which is the other major
change which is sitting in this bill. As we all know at the moment, some drivers pay road-user charges
via their fuel excise and some pay road-user charges via the road-user charge. Now, the fuel excise
is becoming less and less effective. We have more electric vehicles, less fuel being consumed—we
hope—and so less fuel excise being collected. It’s a problem that is widespread around the world.
Many, many jurisdictions collect something like a fuel excise and use it to fund their roads. That
particular source of road funding is dropping as people move towards electric vehicles, so we do
need to find a way to ensure that all vehicle users contribute to the cost of the roads.
At the moment, one of the things that doesn’t work so well around road-user charges—around paying
for that—is a heap of us pay for it via petrol, and the amount of petrol we use is taken as a proxy for
the distance we travel and as a proxy for the impact of our vehicle on the roads. Now, it’s an imperfect
proxy. So if we could move away from that, that’s a good thing to do. The particular changes that are
being made for the fuel excise and the road-user charges mean that, in time, we will all be paying
road-user charges instead of, we hope, paying that cost for our roads via the fuel excise. I think that’s
a fairer way of doing things. It’s a more accurate way of doing things. The technologies are starting
to exist so that we can measure very accurately the distances that vehicles travel and therefore ask
for the appropriate amount of road-user charges.
There are a couple of equity issues or issues around payment there. One of them was touched on
by one of the earlier speakers. At the moment, a person who’s paying road-user charges—that’s a
person who’s driving a diesel vehicle usually—those road-user charges are bought in 1,000-kilometre
blocks. That’s a chunk of money. It’s all very well if a person can pay that quite easily, but there are
families for whom that is not possible, so we do need to be able to pay for those road-user charges
in smaller chunks.
The other issue I’m worrying about, though—and this will be one for us as a Parliament to keep an
eye on—is that once we start collecting road-user charges separately from paying for fuel—
remember that portion of funding is currently collected through the fuel excise—once we ask people
to start paying a separate bill, it may well become a deferrable bill. At the moment, a person who
goes to fill up their car automatically pays the amount of fuel excise. I’m sure they notice the cost of
petrol, but they don’t notice the particular amount that is the fuel excise. Once we separate that
amount out and ask for it to be paid separately, it is like any bill that can be paid with a bit of discretion
from people putting off paying their power bill to putting off paying their rent and so on. There are
some bills that can be put off. We need to make sure we have a mechanism so that people pay their
new road-user charges not in big chunks of 1,000 or so, but on an as-you-go basis and that there is
a simple mechanism for collecting that from people as they go; not too much in arrears. Otherwise,
I fear we could add to some of the problems we already have with people ending up in debt and
ending up in desperate circumstances because of their accumulated debt. So that is something else
for our Parliament to keep an eye on.
Having said this, this is a good bill. It takes us further down towards better funding for our road

sections.heading: Infrastructure Funding And Financing Amendment Bill

items.text: Legislative Statement
Hon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport) ( 23:25): on behalf of the

items.speaker: Minister for Infrastructure
items.text: I present a legislative statement on the Infrastructure Funding and
Financing Amendment Bill.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: That legislative statement is published under the authority of the House
and can be found on the Parliament website.
Second Reading
Hon JAMES MEAGER (Associate Minister of Transport) ( 23:25): on behalf of the

items.speaker: Minister for Infrastructure
items.text: I move, That the Infrastructure Funding and Financing
Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
I’d like to start this contribution by thanking all of those involved in getting this bill to the second
reading. To the members of the Finance and Expenditure Committee for their careful consideration
of this bill, to the members of the public who took the time to provide both oral and written
submissions: thank you to you all. Your input has helped to strengthen and improve this bill and it is
greatly appreciated.

items.speaker: The rationale for this bill is as follows
items.text: we need to increase the effectiveness of the Infrastructure
Funding and Financing Act. That is a key component of pillar two of the Government’s Going for
Housing Growth programme, which is focused on making improvements to infrastructure funding—
you might say fixing our infrastructure funding network—and making improvements to the financing
tools to help get more housing and the future of New Zealand’s housing built.
Under the status quo, councils and developers do face significant challenges to fund and finance the
enabling infrastructure for housing. This Government and hopefully this House wants to move to a
future state where funding and financing tools will enable a responsive supply of infrastructure where
it is commercially viable to build new houses. This will shift market expectations of future scarcity,
bring down the cost of land for new housing, and improve incentives to develop land sooner instead
of holding it for land banking. This is a necessary step to help fix our housing crisis.
First, some background. The Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act was first established in 2020
as an alternative means to fund and finance infrastructure needed to support urban growth. It was a
good idea and it had good intentions. However, the Act has fallen short of delivering additional
infrastructure needed to respond to growth. To date, only three levies have been authorised. So this
bill has the purpose of removing unnecessary barriers to using the Act to improve its viability for a
range of infrastructure projects and to make the levy development and approvals process simpler
and more streamlined.
The bill makes changes to streamline that levy approvals process. Currently, there’s an extensive
process required for applicants to have a levy approved, and that can be a barrier when trying to use
the Act. This bill will streamline the process and improve certainty for developers by simplifying
requirements for levy proposals and recommendation reports, simplifying the mandatory
considerations that the Minister of Housing must take into account when assessing the levy and
improving certainty for developer-led proposals.
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 377
The bill also broadens the scope of the Act to improve its flexibility and viability for a range of
infrastructure projects. This will better reflect the developer-led use of the tool and enable the Act to
be used for transport projects delivered by agencies—for example, the New Zealand Transport
Agency and KiwiRail—as part of a funding stack for transport infrastructure investment where it
benefits property owners.
The bill also makes changes to enable the Act to be used for water infrastructure investments
delivered by new water organisations established through the Local Government (Water Services)
Act 2025 and allows for those water organisations to act as the responsible levy authority. In addition,
the bill replaces the definition of community infrastructure so it is not required to be owned or
controlled by a territorial authority. This broadens the potential use of the Act to therefore include
community infrastructure that is owned or controlled by a third party, rather than that vested in a
territorial authority. There are a number of other changes that the bill makes that are very, very
important, but they are the key ones outlined so far.
In December last year, the bill was referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee, so it’s been
a while to get to this stage, and we’re hoping that it’ll progress with pace tonight. The bill received
submissions from 60 interested groups and individuals and the select committee heard oral evidence
from six submitters at hearings in Wellington and some via video conference. The select committee
examined the bill and recommended that it be passed with amendments to a number of clauses,
which the Government supports in full.
To strengthen consideration of affordability, the select committee proposed a change so that when
the relevant Minister is assessing the affordability of a levy, they will also need to consider the
cumulative affordability of the levy when combined with existing levies, rates, and water services
charges. That’s sensible change, and I’m glad the select committee offered it forward.
In respond to feedback from iwi and Māori, an amendment is proposed to require levy proposals to
include details of any consultation undertaken, including with affected landowners, iwi, or hapū. This
will enable the recommender—that’s the person who assesses levy proposals and writes the
recommendation report—and the responsible Minister to consider any consultation that has
occurred, including any impacts for Māori raised during consultation as part of overall decision-
making on the levy proposal.
An additional safeguard has also been added to the accelerated recovery mechanism to require a
special-purpose vehicle to seek a court judgment for Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act (IFF
Act) funding and financing costs before the special-purpose vehicle may apply to the registrar for the
sale of undeveloped land. This new step would introduce an independent assessment of the amount
of IFF Act funding and financing costs the special-purpose vehicle has determined needs to be
repaid, and ensures that there is a judgment issued before sale proceedings may be commenced.
A number of further technical amendments have also been proposed by the committee to improve
the workability of the bill, and, of course, we all agree with them wholeheartedly and look forward to
their passage and acceptance in the second reading.
In conclusion, the changes in the bill and the bill itself will make the Act far more viable and flexible
so that councils, developers, and other infrastructure providers can get on with fixing the basics of
our housing crisis and building the infrastructure that our growing communities need. I commend it
to the House.

SIMON COURT (ACT) ( 23:51): As the co-sponsor, along with Minister Chris Bishop, the
Minister for Infrastructure, this Infrastructure Funding and Financing Amendment Bill has the potential
to fix a real infrastructure blockage. New Zealand needs more homes, but homes need pipes, roads,
stormwater, transport links, and power. Because without that infrastructure, houses are delayed,
they’re made more expensive, or never built at all. That has been New Zealand’s problem for too
long.
Land has been rationed by planning rules, councils have been constrained by debt limits, and funding
tools have been too slow, too costly, and too hard to use. Developers have been ready to build,
buyers have been ready to buy, but the infrastructure system has too often said “no”. This bill helps
turn “no” into a “yes”. It’s part of the Government’s Going for Housing Growth programme: to free up
land, improve infrastructure funding and financing, and to give councils better incentives to support
growth. That’s exactly the principle we need: growth should pay for growth. The people who benefit
from new infrastructure should contribute to its cost over a reasonable time.
Private capital, investors, should be able to respond to demand, but the Act has not worked as
intended. That’s why we’re amending it. Only three levy proposals have been authorised. That’s not
a lack of need; that is a failure of process and, dear I say, a failure of will. New Zealand Initiative’s
report, Finance Freedom, makes the same point. New Zealand’s housing shortage starts with pipes
and roads. Where councils cannot fund growth infrastructure, planning rules, councils end up
rationing growth that forces up the price of housing. Families pay the bill. The answer is a second
finance channel: private investors funding infrastructure and future residents repaying that cost over
time. That is what this bill supports.
In 2022, I visited Texas and Colorado, including Dallas and Denver. I saw how special purpose
vehicles, like those enabled under this Act, support housing growth and development. This year,
where the United States has reached its 250-year milestone, there is much to learn from our state-
side friends as to how to unlock growth and deliver housing at an affordable price. They do not wait
for every pipe, road, and utility connection to be funded through an overloaded council balance sheet.
They define the growth area, finance the network, build ahead of demand, and recover the cost over
a reasonable time from properties that benefit. That is not theory; that is engineering discipline that
is what New Zealand needs right now.
We do not need to copy Texas or Colorado wholesale, but we should learn the lesson. When people
want to build homes, when private capital is willing to finance the infrastructure, Government and
councils should not be the blockage. This bill removes the blockage. It simplifies the mandatory
considerations for approving a levy. It requires levy and infrastructure authorities, including councils,
to provide endorsements where statutory requirements are met. If the legal test is satisfied, a council
should not be able to stall a project simply through enforcing process. It also extends the eligibility
for infrastructure delivered by the New Zealand Transport Agency and KiwiRail and new water
service organisations.
The select committee has improved the bill. I support these technical changes. These changes
protect levy payers, as Arena Williams pointed out—it’s an important consideration—but they keep
the tool workable. This bill is not about Government building everything; it is about Government
setting clear rules so infrastructure can be financed and funded where people need it. We will not fix
housing by signalling intention alone. We will fix it by freeing up land, cutting delays, funding
infrastructure, and letting people who want to pay for it build the stuff we need. I commend it to the
House.

have been delayed because things like the pipes, the roads, and other sorts of essential services
don’t get funded upfront.
Financing infrastructure is never cost-free. The key question in this particular bill is who carries that
cost and where is it transparent, and whether, actually, households can genuinely afford it. I agree
with my colleague Mike Davidson: sometimes, we do have to think about the nature of growth. This
bill does create a model that makes funding easier, but it cannot be used as an excuse to simply shift
costs on to families already dealing with rates increases, mortgages, and everyday expenses in the
cost of living. Ultimately, we can’t solve one affordability problem by simply shifting and creating a
problem somewhere else.
The infrastructure levies, we acknowledge, can help new houses to get built, which is a good thing,
but those levies remain attached to a property, sometimes for 20, 30, 40, 50 years. A developer or a
current owner may support the levy because it makes a project easier to proceed with initially, but
it’s often the future homeowners who are the ones who are going to make those payments. They
almost certainly wouldn’t have been involved in the original decisions, so they might not fully
understand the long-term costs when they purchase that property. Labour’s concern is that removing
the affordability assessments, which has been done in some circumstances, could make a house
appear more affordable upfront, which is alluring, but it does leave the new owner with a substantial
ongoing charge.
The other thing that we are concerned about is the expansion into transport, and that raises some
unresolved questions. One of the most significant changes is allowing this type of financing model to
be used more widely for transport projects, including projects that have traditionally been led by
