Hon MATT DOOCEY (Associate Minister of Health) ( 09:42): on behalf of the Minister
of Health: Thank you very much, Mr Speaker. I move, That the Pae Ora (Healthy Future) (3 Day
Postnatal Stay) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
This bill is about guaranteeing women the choice of a minimum of three days of post-natal in-patient
care after childbirth to ensure all mothers and babies get the support they need during this vitally
important time. This Government believes that every child deserves the best-possible start in life.
That start does not begin weeks or months after birth; it begins immediately, in those first precious
days, when mothers are recovering from childbirth and families are learning to care for a newborn
together. This bill responds directly to what women and families have told us about their post-natal
experiences. They’ve told us that greater certainty and support in the early days following childbirth
is needed. We know that quality early post-natal care can shape positive long-term outcomes well
beyond the hospital stay.
It is for these reasons that this Government is proud to back this bill with significant new funding
delivered in Budget 2026. We are committed to ensuring that this legislation is matched with the
investment needed to deliver it. This new funding of $34.4 million over four years increases maternity
system capacity so mothers can confidently choose up to three days of in-patient post-natal stay
knowing it will be supported by the beds and the workforce required to do this safely.
First-time mothers will be the first to benefit. Starting immediately, up to 2,000 new mothers per year
will be able to access a three-day post-natal stay within the first two years, utilising existing capacity.
As access is expanded to all mothers after three years, we anticipate that up to 18,000 mothers per
year will be able to access a 3-day post-natal stay.
I want to acknowledge the original sponsor of this legislation. How good, Catherine Wedd. This bill
began its life as a member’s bill grounded in a genuine concern for the post-natal experiences of
women and families. This Government made the decision to adopt the bill because we agreed with
the fundamental importance of guaranteeing three days of in-patient post-natal care for all women if
they choose to access it.
I also want to acknowledge and thank the Health Committee, specially chaired by the very hard-
working Sam Uffindell, for its consideration of this bill and for the work it has done through the select
committee process. I also want to thank the many individuals, the midwives, and other health
professionals who took the time to make submissions and share their experiences. There was
widespread support for the intent of the bill and for the principle that post-natal care should be a
stronger and more consistent part of our maternity system. That feedback reflects just how significant
the post-natal period is for families across this country.
Taking this bill forward with the support of my colleague the Hon Casey Costello also delivers on a
clear commitment in the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement to strengthen maternity
services and post-natal support for women. Crucially, it’s a practical and compassionate step that
puts women and their wellbeing at the centre of our health system.
I intend to table an Amendment Paper as part of its adoption as a Government bill. The Amendment
Paper will include transitional arrangements, requiring Health New Zealand to have a plan setting
out how it will progressively build its capability and capacity across New Zealand to deliver this
entitlement to all mothers. It also builds in more time to ensure that the system can safely deliver the
entitlement to all women.
This is about increasing maternity services to mothers and babies in a responsible, well-managed,
and well-funded way. The Budget allocation of $34.4 million over four years will address the
workforce and capacity constraints the system is currently facing. I look forward to consideration of
this Amendment Paper when this bill is debated in the committee of the whole House.

The bill established a clear entitlement that women can access three days of in-patient post-natal
care if they choose, rather than leaving that decision uncertain or inconsistently applied. In doing so,
it supports better outcomes for mothers and babies and reinforces that post-natal care is a valued
and essential part of that maternity journey.
It does not mandate that women stay in in-patient care for three days. Many women will continue to
choose to return home earlier, supported by community-based services and their families, just as
they do now. What this bill does is ensure that women who would benefit from staying longer have
that option available to them without ambiguity or inconsistency.
For some families, particularly first-time parents, the early post-natal period can feel overwhelming.
There is a great deal to learn in a very short space of time. Having the option of additional support,
monitoring, and reassurance within an in-patient setting can make a meaningful difference to
confidence and wellbeing. Some women have told us they would have welcomed more time in in-
patient care—more time to recover physically, more time to establish breastfeeding, more time to
receive advice, and reassurance before returning home. Others have reported leaving hospital within
48 hours, even though they did not feel ready because they were unsure whether staying longer was
an option. This uncertainty adds pressure at a time when families already have a great deal to
manage. The bill removes the uncertainty and replaces it with clarity and confidence. This bill
respects that different families will make different choices about what is right for them, and it ensures
the system is better equipped to support those choices.
This legislation is not the only change. The Government has a broader programme of work to
strengthen the maternity system and ensure it can deliver high-quality post-natal care in a
sustainable way. Health New Zealand is already taking action to build and support the maternity
workforce needed to deliver the strengthened post-natal care set out in this bill. This includes targeted
recruitment initiatives, including international recruitment where appropriate, as well as return-to-
practice support to help experienced midwives and clinicians re-enter the workforce safely and
confidently.
I also understand that retention matters just as much as recruitment, particularly in districts facing
ongoing workforce pressures. Supporting and retaining skilled staff is essential to maintaining safe
services, continuity of care, and good outcomes for mothers and babies. That is why I’m focused on
backing the maternity workforce and ensuring they’re supported to do their jobs well.
The community sector will have an important part to play in the implementation of this bill. Primary
maternity units run by both the public and community providers, including the private sector, will
expand the range of in-patient post-natal care options available to mothers, including care that is
closer to home. Mothers may remain in hospital, where hospital level care is required, or transfer to
a primary maternity unit once that level of care is no longer needed, depending on their preferences
and clinical need. Having a broader range of options, both public and private, reduces pressure on
hospital facilities while continuing to deliver safe and appropriate post-natal care to woman and
babies.
Taken together, this work underpins the delivery of this bill and will support its long-term success. It
reflects my commitment to ensuring women and their babies receive safe, timely, and appropriate
care when they need it. I want to acknowledge the midwives and other health professionals who care
for women and babies every day. Their experience and advice has been central to shaping the
approach set out in this bill. They understand better than anyone the importance of post-natal support
and the need for careful, well planned implementation. I thank them for their professionalism,
dedication, and ongoing commitment to high-quality care. In closing, this bill delivers three important
outcomes: it provides greater certainty for women and families about post-natal care; it supports
choice at a critical moment in family life; and it strengthens our maternity system in a practical and
responsible way. I commend this bill to the House.

To elaborate a little, firstly, the Ministry of Health advised the committee that to implement this
entitlement would cost $100 million in capital expenditure (CAPEX) to make sure that there were
sufficient beds available for this, and then between $31 and $38 million a year in operational
expenditure. The Health Committee also heard that absent that type of investment, there could be
challenges in implementation. So for example, women taking up the right to this entitlement would

challenging unless extra capacity was created.

initiatives. Appropriately, then, this has been taken over as a Government bill, and the
announcements in Budget ’26 included funding for these initiatives. The Minister gave the assurance
that this investment matches the investment needed to deliver these entitlements. It’s worth breaking
down what the Budget ’26 investments were, in that case. Firstly, contrary to the Ministry of Health
presentation at select committee, all of the funding for this is operational expenditure. So there’s no
CAPEX related to this initiative. We look forward to seeing the Amendment Paper, to understand
whether capital expenditure is also expected as part of the implementation plan. Otherwise, we have
to conclude that the entire plan for building new beds would be to use outsourced beds.
We’re told from press statements that the entitlement will apply to new mothers only, for the first two

$1.6 million of operational expenditure each year—so in health terms, a very modest contribution in
the first two years. We had the opportunity to go into the scale of this contribution of this funding at

mothers—those eligible in the first two years—already occupy beds for 2.5 days. I think that was the
number she gave when her statement was corrected in the House by the Minister; 2.5 days is
currently the average length of stay for new mothers. So there’s a minimal need, we’re told, to
increase the funding in the first two years because the increase in entitlement on average will be
slight.
So the substantial implementation of this commitment is really going to follow—well, 18 months after
the election. It is a shame that opportunities to increase capacity in the maternity system weren’t
taken during this term of Government so that the commitment could be implemented in a more
fulsome way. That is to follow in years 3 and 4, so the years covered by Budget ’28 and ’29. In those
years, $13.3 million is appropriated, and $17.9 million, respectively. So returning to the Ministry of
Health modelling that they gave the Health Committee back when the member’s bill was considered,
that’s half. So the assumption is half of women will take up this this entitlement. Look, modelling is
based on assumptions, so we understand that not every health entitlement is taken up by everyone.

ask: how meaningful is it to describe it as it has been, as a right, if it’s only expected that half of

Which takes me back to the stories that we heard from women, NGOs who work with women, and
clinicians who work with women, in the select committee. We heard multiple stories about the wonder

challenge with family finances, challenge with travel around birth, and the juggle of caring for other
children and the partners’ other work commitments. All of these pressures are on families, and there

who are concerned about their other kid and their other children at home and therefore would rather
be at home knowing that everything was OK there—even though if they didn’t have that commitment,
they might well have taken up the opportunity to be in hospital longer.

First Reading
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts) ( 10:55): I move, That the Community
Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Justice
Committee to consider the bill.
Too many New Zealanders are spending too long caught in the court system. For victims, delays
mean waiting a year or more for a case to be resolved. For witnesses, it means uncertainty and
repeated disruption. For defendants, it means cases hanging over their lives. For families, employers,
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 404 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
and communities, it means the justice system is not working as quickly as it should. Timely justice
matters, because justice delayed is justice denied.
This Government is focused on practical changes that make the courts work better. This bill is a
practical reform that improves access to justice, reduces delays, and makes better use of the
resources that we already have. This bill expands the role of community magistrates so that they can
deal with more straightforward matters from start to finish. It will reduce unnecessary adjournments,
free up District Court judges to focus on more serious and complex cases, and will improve the
public’s confidence that the justice system can deliver.
Community magistrates are not new. The role was introduced in the late 1990s to increase judicial
capacity to take pressure off the District Court judges. They were intended to deal with lower-level
criminal matters, represent the communities that they serve, and help the courts to operates more
efficiently. Community magistrates generally sit part time. They preside over certain lower-level
matters in the District Court’s criminal jurisdiction. They are not required to hold a legal qualification,
although many of them do. They bring practical experience, judgment, and community knowledge to
the court system.
But at the moment, they are not being used to their full potential. Too often, if a case reaches a point
where a decision is needed outside of a community magistrate’s jurisdiction, it has to be adjourned
and transferred to a judge. That means another court event, another delay, another day off work,
another round of uncertainty for victims and other court users. It also means some cases are never
scheduled before a community magistrate in the first place, because everyone knows that they might
have to be transferred again later on. That’s not efficient, nor is it fair on court users, and it certainly
is not the best use of judicial time and resource.
This bill changes that. It will enable community magistrates to take guilty pleas for all cases except
those tried in the High Court—that means murder, manslaughter—to preside over trials and
determine guilt for offences with a maximum penalty of a fine, community-based sentence, or up to
three months imprisonment; to order pre-sentencing reports for offences being referred to a District
Court judge for sentencing; to make a greater range of bail decisions, where the defendant has
pleaded guilty before a community magistrate; and make a greater range of administrative decisions,
including transferring proceedings from one District Court to another and hearing unopposed limited
driver licence applications.
These are sensible, practical changes. They do not ask community magistrates to replace judges;
they allow community magistrates to do more of the work that they were created to do so that judges
can spend more time on cases that genuinely require a judge. It is expected that these changes will
free up a net 5.2 District Court judge full-time equivalents. Put simply, this bill is, effectively, five
judges for the price of none. This is good value for taxpayers, good for court timeliness, and good for
victims who have waited too long for justice. The benefits will be felt across the justice system. When
cases move faster victims get answers sooner. Witnesses are not left waiting indefinitely.
Defendants are not held in limbo longer than necessary. Remand pressure can reduce as cases
progress more quickly. Judges can focus on the work only they are able to do.
Expanding the role of community magistrates is sensible, but it must be done carefully. The public
needs confidence that the cases will continue to be dealt with appropriately and consistently. This
bill does not change the sentencing jurisdiction of community magistrates. Community magistrates
will still not be able to impose imprisonment or home detention. Where a community magistrate
considers that either of those sentences may be appropriate, the case must be transferred to a
District Court judge, and that is an important safeguard.
The bill also supports stronger leadership and oversight of community magistrates. Judge Moses
has recently been appointed as the first Chief Community Magistrate, recognising the growing
importance of community magistrates in the court system in providing judicial oversight for the role.
The bill will make it so that there must always be a judge in this role. Budget 2025 also provided
funding for three additional community magistrates and extra training to support them in their work.
This bill is practical, it is targeted, it is common sense, and it makes better use of community
magistrates. It frees up more than five full-time judges’ worth of capacity. It helps cases to move

faster, it supports victims, it reduces pressure on the District Court, and it does all of that while
maintaining appropriate safeguards. I commend this bill to the House.

do support this bill, but there will be some important points to consider at select committee.
Community magistrates are not legally qualified. At their inception, they were instituted as a model
of, essentially, community-based justice—that is to say, people who knew the community, were part
of the community, making decisions about minor offending within that community. I endorse that
view, but we do need to be cautious—so we’re supporting this with some caution—about expanding

Community magistrates are a good thing, but I guess, with the expansion of them, we’ve got to be
careful that we’re not doing this simply because it’s cheap. At the same time, I’m aware that
community magistrates are remunerated on a very modest scale. It’s certainly not anywhere near
what a judge is paid. It’s a bit more than an honorarium. I think it’s around $450 a day, but I’d have

items.speaker: DAN ROSEWARNE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a pleasure to rise and take
a call on the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill at its first reading. We have two
special guests in the House there. We have Andrew Bayly. He’s actually recently departed as chair
of the Justice Committee, so I’d like to acknowledge his service. Then we have the new chair of the
Justice Committee, Tom Rutherford. He was actually appointed yesterday, and he’s off to a good
start. It’s good timing that they’re both there this morning.
Labour will be supporting this bill at its first reading. It’s a practical bill aimed at helping the District
Court work more efficiently. The Government’s own explanation is straightforward. Criminal cases
are taking too long to move through the courts. Community magistrates are not being used at their
full potential right now, and this legislation is designed to make better use of an existing part of the
justice system.
I think most members of this House would agree that delays in the justice system help nobody. They
don’t help victims waiting for a case to be resolved; they don’t help defendants, whose lives are,
effectively, on hold while matters work their ways through the courts; and they don’t help public
confidence in the justice system. If we can safely reduce unnecessary delays and unnecessary court
appearances, that is something Parliament should be willing to consider.
Community magistrates have been part of our court system for many years. They were established
to provide additional judicial capacity to allow District Court judges to focus their time on the more
serious and more complex cases. Yet the legislative statement makes clear that restrictions on their
jurisdiction mean that they are often underused. Cases can end up being passed back and forth
between community magistrate and a judge, creating extra hearings and additional delay.
One example is where somebody wishes to plead guilty. At present, a community magistrate may
have to refer the matter to a judge before that guilty plea can be formally dealt with. The bill allows
community magistrates to take guilty pleas for category 1, 2, and 3 offences, order pre-sentence
reports when needed, and make limited post-guilt bail decisions before the case goes to a judge for
sentencing. The intention is to remove unnecessary steps and avoid multiple court appearances
where one would do.
The bill also expands the ability of community magistrates to manage and hear lower-level criminal
cases. In particular, it allows them to hear those minor offences, as mentioned, and we see merit in
that approach. Importantly, this is not a proposal to give community magistrates more power and to
send more people to prison. The legislation specifically leaves imprisonment and home-detention
decisions with District Court judges. Where a community magistrate considers that a sentence of
imprisonment or home detention may be appropriate, the matter must still go before a judge.
The bill also includes some fairly practical changes that will allow community magistrates to deal with
certain unopposed, limited licence applications and to transfer proceedings between court locations
where all parties agree and jury trials have not been elected. These may not be headline-grabbing
changes, but they reduce paperwork, reduce court events, and save judicial time, so they’re
absolutely worth considering through the select committee process.
Another feature Labour welcomes is the requirement for a District Court judge to be appointed as a
principal community magistrate. If community magistrates are being entrusted with additional
responsibility, judicial leadership and oversight becomes even more important. The bill recognises
that and provides a framework for it.
Now, supporting this bill at first reading does not mean giving it a free pass. The justice system is
one of the most important institutions in our democracy and changes to our judicial powers and court
processes should always be tested carefully. Labour expects the select committee process to
examine whether the right safeguards are in place.
On that note, it’s an important bill, and I look forward to it going through the select committee. I
commend it to the House.

honour to rise in support of the Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill. This bill will
support timely access to justice in the District Court; therefore, I commend it to the House.

items.speaker: Environment
items.text: I move, That the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill be now read a
first time. I nominate the Environment Committee to consider the bill.
New Zealand is undertaking significant transformations regarding how we protect, conserve, and
restore our natural environment, how we sustainably use our resources, and how we mitigate and
adapt to climate change. However, to understand the impacts that our activities have on the
environment and to respond accordingly, we need a comprehensive, reliable, consistent data and
information base.
In 2015, the Environmental Reporting Act was enacted to do exactly that : to establish a trusted,
reliable, and independent environmental reporting regime. Since then, we have completed four
cycles of environmental reports. The Act has made significant improvements to the previously ad
hoc way New Zealand reported on the environment; however, we need to extend its functionality and
flexibility so that trustworthy data and information is at the heart of decision making.
In 2019, the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment released a report raising concerns
about gaps and inconsistencies in environmental data. The commissioner noted a reliance on
passively harvested data and information collected under other pieces of legislation and a lack of a
coordinated environmental monitoring and reporting system. The high frequency of report production
placed the Ministry for the Environment and Stats NZ on a never-ending treadmill of report-making.
These often recycle old, patchy, and inconsistent data collected using a myriad of disparate
monitoring practices. We have a significant opportunity now to address the Parliamentary
Commissioner’s concerns, so in this piece of legislation a number of changes are being put forward.
The Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill before the House represents a commitment by the
Government to quality environmental data and information. The bill will refocus reporting content and
time frames. It aligns roles and responsibilities, and a more active collection of environmental data
and knowledge. The bill ensures improvements to environmental reporting are safeguarded for the
future. These include making data available to the public and decision makers when it is ready, rather
than when a report is merely published. It also means expanding the reporting and setting up an
interim strategic, in-evidence panel.
The bill will require the Secretary for the Environment to publish a State of the Environment report
every six years, independent from political interference. This will achieve a more appropriate balance
between reporting timeliness and the rates of change in our environment. The bill stipulates that the
first State of the Environment report must be published in 2031.
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 410 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
The Pressure-State-Impact framework embedded into the Environmental Reporting Act has been
expanded to include drivers and outlooks. Drivers describe the long-term social, demographic,
economic, and environmental factors that cause pressure on the environment. Outlooks describe
how the environment may change in the future based on projections and trends. Their ongoing
inclusion will render a more complete picture and bring New Zealand more in line with international
best practice.
The report must continue to describe changes to the state of the environment over time and how it
measures against national and international standards. In addition, they can now report on progress
towards Government priorities and limits, goals, and policy outcomes set in other legislation. This
could include, for example, reporting on limits as proposed in the Natural Environment Bill and any
measures set as part of the climate adaptation system, including managing the risk from natural
hazards.
Between the six-yearly State of the Environment reports, a commentary report must be published
at least once every 12 months. One of the foundational objectives of the bill is to ensure reporting
flexibility. Commentaries report on an issue or topic that sits across one or more of the five
environmental domains. The five domains of air, land, fresh water, marine, and atmosphere and
climate will remain. All must be reported on at least once in the commentary reports between the
State of the Environment reports. However, the amendments recognise that commentary reports
may cut across different domains. This change allows for more flexible reporting, which better
addresses the urgent needs we face.
The bill introduces a new requirement for the Secretary for the Environment. In consultation with the
Government Statistician, the secretary will produce a priorities report within six months of every State
of the Environment report. The report will discuss environmental data, monitoring, and research. It
will also list recommended indicators and priority areas for improving data and evidence.
Several technical advisory groups have provided expert advice on the preparation of synthesis and
domain reports over the years. This bill will, however, amend the Environmental Reporting Act to
require the Secretary for the Environment, in consultation with the Minister for the Environment, to
appoint a strategic evidence panel. The panel will provide independent advice to the Secretary for
the Environment on matters related to environmental data monitoring and reporting. The bill also
clarifies the roles of the Secretary for the Environment and the Government Statistician. The bill
proposes clear roles and also stipulates where consultation between the two organisations is
required, such as setting environmental indicators or producing data and evidence priority reports.
Finally, to bring together all the proposals and drive a cohesive, robust and fit-for-purpose reporting
system, the purpose statement has been extended. The current purpose statement simply stipulates
that the purpose of the Act is to produce national environmental reports. This has been clarified to
align with the underlying policy to inform New Zealanders on the state of the environment and to
support evidence-based decisions. This bill responds directly to a review of New Zealand’s national
reporting regime. It improves efficiency of our reporting regime, making useful improvements to the
frequency of reports, and does so without compromising their timeliness, impact, or independence.
Therefore, I commend the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill to the House.

Legislative Statement
Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction) ( 11:56): Thank you, sir. I
present a legislative statement on the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill.

items.text: That legislative statement is published under the
authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website.
Second Reading
Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction) ( 11:56): I move, That the
Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
The Transport and Infrastructure Committee has considered the bill and recommends that it be
passed with amendments. I’m grateful to the people and organisations who made a submission on
the bill and of course to the select committee itself, who took the time to hear those submitters and
to consider improvements on the bill. Following the Canterbury earthquakes and royal commission
of inquiry, the current earthquake-prone buildings regime was introduced.
I just want to take a moment to acknowledge, as I’m sure all in this House would, the considerable
tragedy, the loss of human life, that was entailed by those tragic events. And I don’t wish to bring you
into the debate, Mr Speaker, but I will acknowledge that you more than most were familiar with the
nature of the tragedy, and of course I commend and salute you for your work following that, of course,
to bring that beloved region of yours back to more normal circumstances.
All that said, of course, I think it’s fairly acknowledged that the introduced legislation at that time—
albeit, of course, in good faith and balancing all the relevant considerations—has not worked entirely
as intended. It has inadvertently imposed large costs on building owners and communities, including
throughout New Zealand, without focusing enough on the buildings that present the greatest risk to
people’s lives.
This cannot continue, and so, even with the recent earthquakes in Venezuela providing a salutary
reminder that we do need to prepare further for such events in New Zealand, nevertheless, we have
decided that it is important to reform the earthquake-prone building regime to target or refocus on
those buildings most likely to cause fatalities in an earthquake.
The changes will remove barriers to strengthening high-risk buildings, making retrofits more
affordable for their owners and better protecting people in and around them. Focusing effort and
investment on the highest-risk buildings will ultimately save more lives than the current one-size-fits-
all approach.
Today I will briefly reiterate the bill’s key elements and summarise the key changes recommended
by the select committee. As I say, we have decided to accept those changes.
First, the bill narrows the systems scope so that it targets only high-risk buildings in medium and
high-risk seismic zones. It introduces tiered remediation requirements, amends the definition of
priority building, and provides greater flexibility through deadline extensions and lower-cost pathways
for alterations and change of use.
Only two types of buildings will remain designated as earthquake-prone buildings (EPBs):
unreinforced masonry buildings and tall heavy material buildings. These are the buildings most likely
to cause harm in an earthquake, and these will be only those located in medium- or high-risk seismic
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 416 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
zones. Territorial authorities must identify and remove other building types from the EPB register in
the three months from 1 July 2027.
Meanwhile, buildings in Auckland, Northland, and the Chatham Islands will be out of scope. These
areas have a scientifically determined lower seismic hazard than other parts of New Zealand. On
Royal assent, therefore, earthquake-prone buildings in these areas will have that designation
removed.
At the same time, other provisions of the bill go through coastal Otago, including Dunedin and
Oamaru and Stewart Island, will shift from a low to medium seismic zone to reflect the latest scientific
understanding of seismic hazard in those places. Current earthquake-prone buildings (EPBs) there
will retain their existing remediation deadlines and territorial authorities will have until 1 July 2032 to
identify potential EPBs there.
The bill also narrows the so-called identify at any time pathway for designating buildings as EPBs.
Too many low-risk buildings have been designated as earthquake-prone using this pathway. So the
bill, as introduced, narrows the pathway to cover only the post-1976, tall, heavy-material buildings
that were constructed before 2027. This includes buildings akin to the CTV building in Christchurch.
For buildings that remain EPBs, territorial authorities will determine their required remediation
measures in accordance with the updated EPB methodology, issue EPB notices, and keep the EPB
register up to date.
The bill narrows the definition of “priority building”. Under the bill, only buildings that could fall on to
a busy street or block a strategic transport route will qualify. Buildings that were priority simply
because of their usage, such as hospitals or fire stations, will lose that status. Together, these
changes provide clearer rules and a stronger focus on the buildings that matter most for public safety.
The bill also introduces a tiered approach to remediation, replacing the current requirement to
strengthen all buildings to 34 percent of the new building standard, commonly known as NBS. There
will be two principal forms of remediation measure. Most unreinforced masonry buildings will need
to mitigate their risk of facades falling on to people below. Multi-storey concrete buildings and large
unreinforced masonry buildings will need targeted work to prevent those buildings collapsing. For
unreinforced masonry buildings then that are one or two storeys high and located outside urban
centres, no remediation will be required by a set deadline. But, at the same time, I note that owners
will need to mitigate the risk of façade collapse if they want the building to be taken off the EPB
register.
EPB owners will be able to apply to territorial authorities for deadline extensions of up to 15 years,
even if the original deadline expired before commencement. This will replace the current “up to 10
year” extension, open only to heritage EPB owners.
The bill also supports lower-cost compliance pathways for owners carrying out seismic work or
changing the use of a building. If the work only involves seismic remediation, no fire or accessibility
upgrades will be required. Similarly, if an owner wants to change an EPB’s use, it would only need
to meet its remediation requirement, rather than anything higher. Together, these changes provide
more practical and cost-effective solutions, more time to comply, and fewer barriers for owners
committed to making their buildings safer.
The Transport and Infrastructure Committee has unanimously recommended amendments to
address issues identified by submitters, officials, and the select committee itself. I welcome these
improvements and again place on the record my thanks to the committee for their detailed
examination of the bill. I note the chair, Mr Andy Foster and I thank him and his colleagues who did
such a careful and coherent job of understanding and in turn explaining the changes that have
ultimately been made.
In response to feedback from submitters, the committee clarified what areas are in “urban centres”,
which helps to determine the remediation requirement of an unreinforced masonry EPB. For
example, Wellington and Porirua are urban centres, whereas Featherston and Greytown are not. To
acknowledge the unique barriers to remediation faced by various buildings, the committee added
heritage status to the list of matters that territorial authorities must have regard to when determining
whether or not to grant a deadline extension. Some submitters were concerned that the alternation
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 417
provisions may allow for reduced building code compliance. For example, drilling stabilising rods
through walls can increase the risk of fire spreading in one room to the next. The committee
introduced a backstop into the bill to ensure that seismic work needs to be done in a way that doesn’t
increase the risk of fire spreading or reduce disabled peoples’ access.
The committee also amended the bill so that warning signs must be displayed on all earthquake-
prone buildings, including those that are only recorded on the register or have a seismic work
exemption. The committee updated the terms for the required remediation measures to façade risk
mitigation and targeted retrofit. This will ensure that approaches to remediation mitigate risk but do
not necessarily involve securing a façade or a full retrofit of the building can be used. This bill now
also includes high-level descriptions of these measures.
Some submitters were unsure how buildings with unusually tall storeys or part storeys will be
treated—a fair question. The committee clarified that the thresholds for determining how many
storeys high an EPB will be will be set out in the EPB methodology. One way that a building can be
a priority building with half the remediation time frame is if it may impede a strategic transport route
if it were to collapse during an earthquake. Submitters recommended that territorial authorities be
allowed to revisit their strategic transport route—again, I think, a very sensible recommendation. The
committee therefore amended the bill to empower territorial authorities—councils, in other words—
to revise and remove strategic transport routes up to 1 July 2027. No new strategic transport routes
may be added, ensuring that no building owners will be worse off.
Last, in my remaining minute, the committee clarified the meaning of a building within scope. This
makes it clearer which buildings are within scope of the system before the reader then looks to the
EPB methodology for further technical detail. An unreinforced masonry building must have an
exterior masonry wall and satisfy other criteria in the methodology to be within scope. A tall, heavy
material building must have one or more significant elements, such as a roof or a floor, built using
concrete or other heavy materials and satisfy any other criteria in the EPB methodology.
Overall, in summary, the bill creates a more focused and workable earthquake-prone buildings
system by targeting the buildings that present the greatest risk, introducing tiered and more cost-
effective remediation requirements, and reducing barriers to remediation for building owners. For all
those reasons, I commend this bill to the House.

ARENA WILLIAMS (Labour—Manurewa) ( 12:06): Thank you, Mr Speaker. This is an
important bill and an important piece of reform that Labour continues to support, with specific
reservations. I’m going to use this speech to set out what those things are. They will be parts that we
consider are the most sensitive and are the least well-supported around the House. It is important
that we come to consensus on these rules which impact on the long-term viability of buildings and
not only those that are being built now but in expensive and costly remediations that are to come in
the next five to 10 years. So it is important to flag where we have bipartisan support which is for a
sensible set of rules for remediation of the highest-risk buildings, but to indicate that we do have
reservations around how some of the exclusions have been applied, particularly around Auckland.
Maintaining affordability has been our concern here. We want a building system and a built
environment which is affordable, where remediations happen from either existing owners or there is
an incentive for buildings to be sold to people who can remediate them. Because you do not want a
situation like Wellington is experiencing now where some important civic sites and main streets have
buildings which have not been remediated because the cost is very high and that continues to pose
a risk to neighbours and to people on the street who walk past them. We want a system which
incentivises that kind of remediation and where it is affordable in the public interest. So that is why
we need some updates to these rules.
We have vociferously opposed at every opportunity the exclusion of Auckland from the rules for
remediation of risky buildings. Colleagues, let me explain what has occurred here. Cabinet has set
out to create a set of rules where the highest-risk buildings around the country are the ones that get
fixed. That makes sense. We shouldn’t fix buildings which are not posing a risk to peoples’ lives and
are not posing a risk to the neighbouring buildings around them. Those rules require expensive fixes
and so they should be something which is sensible. There is also a category of buildings under that

that require being fixed—they need to be fixed. There shouldn’t be rules which force people to adhere
to a certain time line. Building owners in that category should be able to make their own decisions
about what kind of risk they will put up with and what kind of risk the building’s users will put up with.
When I’m talking about these highest-risk buildings, some of those have been excluded from this bill.
The way that these rules have been drawn is that if you have a very high-risk building in Auckland
which is on the main street, it does not need to be remediated any more. The House must understand
that by excluding Auckland, we have drawn lines on a map which mean that those remediations do
not need to occur.
Yes, you could have designed a system where the highest seismic risk regions were the way that we
decided what sorts of buildings would be remediated. But that’s actually not what we’ve done. If you
drew lines on a map, you might use, say, faults, and areas where say, an eruption around the Alpine
Fault was going to cause regional risk and regional land movement. You might have drawn lines
around volcanic movements in our shaky isles.
But that is not the system we have used. We’ve used a system, which is perfectly sensible, whereby
you identify the buildings which are at risk of movement in any kind of event like that and how much
they are used. So a building that might move the same amount and might have the same kind of risk
on the main street in Auckland is a different sort of risk to the one that’s on the West Coast and has
two users a year for family weddings. That’s sensible.
But addition, at the last minute, of an exclusion for Auckland does not fit with the uncontentious and
unpolitical way of identifying risk here. It has overlaid a set of judgements that are, simply put,
relatively political about whether Auckland should be included or excluded from the rules.
I think that is the wrong decision. I think we will be back here in this House debating whether that has
worked, because it is not a system that the public can have faith in, and it will test confidence and
trust in our built environment system and whether central government stands behind the risk that we
are asking Aucklanders to take on, not only as a community, but as individual business owners who,
say, have buildings next to highly risky buildings and people who maintain other parts of built
environment around them that are at risk because of this decision.
This is not also a minor issue for Auckland. The majority of earthquake-prone buildings are in
Auckland, despite many people’s assumptions about the earthquake-prone buildings being in
Christchurch; that is a largely an area which has been through a pretty painful process of having to
come up to speed with the rules that we required of them. People in Canterbury have done what they
have been asked. They have fixed buildings; they have remediated buildings. For some people, have
that has been at personal cost, huge personal investment of family savings. For many businesses, it
has meant years of having to forward-fund capital investment in their buildings, but they have done
that.
This is an exclusion, now, of another region, in fact, where there are 1,400 earthquake-prone
buildings, which was in the queue, and this Government has made a decision to exclude them. That
decision will have lasting consequences for generations to come and is, frankly, being made at a
time where that is possible for the Government to do it because it’s not in people’s minds.
The deadline extensions powers in the bill have also been something that the committee worked
very closely with, and, ultimately, that is something we do not support. There are shifting goal posts
now in the bill, where deadline extensions of up to 15 years don’t come back to this Parliament. They
are made away from public scrutiny. What does that mean? It means that building owners don’t have
a clear indication of the time that they will need to make remediations in the rest of the country.
For Wellington apartment owners, who are an important constituency when Governments of both
stripes have considered this bill, they now do not have certainty of investment decisions. Little old
ladies who live in apartments, and that’s their entire life savings, will be hugely impacted by this bill,
and that is a very hard case.
Labour’s answer to this was not one that National politics supported. It was to use public money to
assist those private owners with their private property because we recognise that there is a no-fault
element of this and that it would be inequitable to treat this in any different way.

But the exclusion of Auckland wholesale should not have been part of the planning of that pipeline.
If we’re serious about an infrastructure pipeline which works for people, we also need to consider the

So when we’re accountable to the people in our electorate who are looking at this Parliament and

One change the committee has also made is around the definition of an urban centre. This bill will

What has been brought to light, however, is that some authorities have perhaps been a little bit more

items.speaker: GEORGIE DANSEY
items.text: Tēnā koe e te Māngai o te Whare. Mr Speaker, firstly,
it’s very good to see you in the Chair. I think the last time I spoke with you in the Chair was at my
maiden speech, so let’s hope this speech is as heartfelt and good as that one.
This is a very important bill that we’re speaking to today, the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings)
Amendment Bill. I want to acknowledge the effects of earthquakes and the importance of getting this
legislation right, as other speakers have spoken to.
We are in a very earthquake-prone country, and we need to do really good and ongoing work on
protecting people who deal with the repercussions of earthquakes across the motu and good work
that’s going to protect the lives of people and our communities.
We’ve all been affected by earthquakes. I acknowledge those living in cities who have been hugely
affected by earthquakes. We all know the huge impact it has on communities, financially and
otherwise, particularly the Christchurch earthquakes, which I know triggered a lot of work in this
space. My colleagues have spoken of the impacts of that and I’m pleased to support this bill in order
to get that legislation right so that we can protect our lives and our communities.
We need to keep safety at the centre of our system when we are considering this bill. Reforms should
focus on genuine risks and public safety must remain the overriding principle. So Labour supports
targeting regulatory efforts at buildings that present the greatest risks to life, safety. As I mentioned,
we have learnt considerable lessons from Canterbury, and other speakers have spoken to the
Kaikōura earthquakes. Governments have a responsibility to protect people from avoidable harm.
As other speakers have mentioned, although Labour supports this bill, we do not support the
exclusion of Auckland, Northland, and the Chatham Islands from these reforms. Even though they
have a low seismic hazard, Auckland doesn’t have a zero risk. We risk building a two-tiered system
in our country by excluding Auckland. A low risk does not mean no risk. We need to ensure that we
are protecting everybody. As other speakers have spoken to, Auckland contains approximately 1,400
earthquake-prone buildings—the majority of identified earthquake-prone buildings nationally.
Excluding our largest population I don’t think is a smart move.
I come from the sunny place of Hamilton. Hamilton and the Waikato also has a low seismic hazard
risk. However, I wouldn’t want the Waikato and the place that I live to be excluded from these
regulations, because, as I said, a low risk doesn’t mean no risk. In fact, Hamilton, as reported, is the
largest urban centre with the lowest natural hazard risk. So a little plug there for the great city but
also let’s not exclude areas. We need to make sure that we are protecting all our people and
communities across the board in this legislation.
The other point I wanted to quickly touch on was balancing affordability with long-term responsibility.
As natural hazards increase, or natural disasters increase, in our country due to climate change, this
is something we need to think about more and more in regard to earthquakes and personal liability
but also in other natural hazards. I don’t think it’s something that gets enough attention—is how are

people going to manage the personal, financial burden on them when a natural disaster affects them?
I think that’s a missed opportunity, and I would have liked to see more support for our public in that
space.
Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam) ( 12:54): Thank you, Mr Speaker. It is a great
honour to stand up and speak on the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill. A lot
of previous speakers have, Mr Speaker, flattered you with many great compliments, but I just want
to acknowledge all the work that you did do for Christchurch after the earthquakes.
This bill would make more pragmatic, tiered system, intended to better reflect the actual risk posed
by individual buildings here in New Zealand. It would focus on mitigating the risk to life. Therefore, I
commend this bill to the House.
Dr TRACEY McLELLAN (Labour) ( 12:54): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I was a bit surprised
that the previous speaker didn’t look at the clock and maybe think to speak for a little bit longer and
we may have been able to go for lunch, but, nevertheless, here I am, on my feet, and I’ve got quite
a lot to say. So I make no apologies for that snafu.
The Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill—where do we start? Well, let’s start at
point one. Labour supports the overall direction of this bill. Obviously, it’s been argued that the current
earthquake-prone building system has imposed substantial and, in some cases, disproportionate
costs on building owners and on councils and on regional communities. That is something worthy of
some reconsideration. So this more targeted system, which focuses on the buildings themselves,
the earthquake risk, and the locations that present the greatest risk and threat to life, we do believe
is sensible.
It’s not a perfect system. There are, as has been discussed, at least two or three major—well, when
I say “major”, two or three very specific concerns that we certainly don’t agree with. That’s not what
we would have done given the opportunity to do so. But a risk-based system that assesses genuine
risk is something that we’re happy to support in this instance.
But we simply don’t think that we can draw a line around Auckland and pretend that every vulnerable
building—of which there were, I believe, 1,400, at least—on one side of a line are no longer a
concern, because it doesn’t take away the concern, it just takes them off a statutory list of concern.
So the central purpose, as has been said by almost everybody on this side of the House, who are,
pretty much, the only people—apart from Andy Foster, who made a very interesting contribution—to
have commented on what is a really important bill and we should have more to say about it. The
most important principle that does have to be underpinning this legislation is that earthquake-prone
buildings regulation exists primarily to protect people’s lives.
As has also been noted, those of us from Canterbury certainly don’t need a reminder that
earthquakes don’t just affect buildings; they affect people and they change lives. Within an instant,
lives can be changed—and lost. Many Cantabrians, as I’m sure yourself, Mr Speaker, will remember
walking past buildings that they had entered hundreds of times or driving pasts buildings, as I did
just before the earthquake, paused at a set of lights because the lights were red—a very frequent
place for me to be paused. Two hours later, that building was down and the person that was
unfortunately paused at those lights on that occasion lost their life.
So buildings that seem like innocuous bricks and mortar that serve the function of housing work, of
housing people, conducting business, and all of those other activities that they afford us the
opportunity to do aren’t just buildings if they are not designed in a way or if legislation and regulation
don’t ensure that aspects of buildings aren’t a little bit more safer for the reality that they involve
housing people and accommodating people who are not nearly as indestructible as we might
somehow like to think we are.
Labour, therefore, supports a greater focus that is in this bill on unenforced masonry buildings. That
was certainly a big lesson from Canterbury—vulnerable concrete buildings, falling facades, and other
known life-safety hazards.
A more proportionate system, however, is, we do believe, a little bit more fairer for regional
communities. The existing system tended to treat every building as if the community that it was
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 428 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
functioning within presented the same level of risk. A small building in a low-risk town shouldn’t
necessarily face the same obligations as a large, vulnerable, concrete building on a busy pedestrian
route.
I know that through the select committee process, that formula, those calculations have been taken
into account to get to where we agree here: there were some aspects of that that Labour were in 100
percent in agreement with when it came to assessing that risk, but some of that was debatable and
we put forward some alternatives. We don’t think that our position was necessarily the perfect one
either, so we were happy to contend with this—acknowledging that the cost of strengthening has
exceeded, for some people, the value of the building itself, and also acknowledging the stress and
the uncertainty that lots of people have faced, wondering how they would be able to now making
those buildings compliant under the previous regime.
However, proportionality must not become an excuse for an indefinite inaction. That is a huge
problem. Extensions should be available where owners are making genuine progress, and we
absolutely believe that, but not simply to push difficult decisions another 10 or 15 years further into
the future.
Ultimately, we actually do want to be able to take this opportunity to say we live in an earthquake-
prone country; there are certain well-known risks; given our recent history, we have been afforded
the opportunity to look into and to research and to have experts and engineers on this, that, and
whatever, design and innovate some possible solutions to make our lived environment a lot safer.
So we should be moving with a certain pace to be able to afford our own selves the opportunity for
that.
As has been mentioned, excluding Auckland, we think, is entirely the wrong approach. I do
understand the rationale behind it, and we listened intently to various people raising their
methodology behind how they came to that decision or how they came to provide us with that advice.
I still don’t think it’s the right thing to do. I think even if we think about the situation where we’re
discussing Auckland as if it’s one homogenous area, just by virtue of the fact that it has some
boundaries and we’ve created a made-up, essentially, boundary—and that’s what we call Auckland.
But even within Auckland itself, there are different geological considerations, and we just think that
with a little bit more time we may have been able to work with the Government to maybe reach a
compromise on how we could have got the best of both worlds.
But we accept that Auckland does have a lower seismic risk, we acknowledge that seismic hazard
is not the only part of risk calculation, however, and a light-tough framework could have been
retained, we think, which would have left highly vulnerable buildings—lots and lots of highly
vulnerable buildings still could have been identified, recorded, and subject to some targeted
obligations, which I think was probably the place that we should have ended up.
I also do want to acknowledge the earthquake notices. I think both Andy Foster and my colleague
Tangi Utikere mentioned these, in so far as it’s one of the things I remember the most from select
committee. Sometimes it’s the little details. The earthquake notices that you put on a building—just
because there’s no remediation required for that building, we didn’t think that that should remove the
need to have a properly displayed notice. People should still know that, yes, the building’s got some
issues; no, not enough to have required the full suite of treatment in terms of remediation—I still want
to know what those issues are and then I can make my own informed choice about how much time
I may choose to spend in that building.
In closing, Labour supports this bill because it is targeted and more proportionate in a genuinely risk-
based system. We do think that we probably do need this now as a pragmatic step forward. We
support this bill at second reading while continuing, obviously, to argue for a more consistent national
safety framework and better support for those people that are expected to carry out some of the
costs to their own homes, including the apartment dwellers. Ultimately, we all want safer
communities.

Second Reading
Hon MARK MITCHELL (Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery)
(14:07): I move, That the Emergency Management Bill (No 2) be now read a second time.
Mr Speaker, while you’re in the seat, I just wanted to acknowledge you. As a member of the National
Party backbench when we were hit by the awful Christchurch earthquakes, I got to observe your
tireless work as emergency management Minister leading the recovery for Christchurch. I just want
to think, reflect, and mourn on those that were lost, but also now recognise that Christchurch is a
thriving city that is a joy to visit and to see how far they’ve come since that event. I want to
acknowledge you, because I got a front-row seat that helped inform me in terms of what I needed to
do when I took on the role of emergency management Minister. So thank you for that work.
I’d like to thank the Governance and Administration Committee for its work to consider this important
piece of legislation. I’m pleased to see the select committee was unanimous in its recommendations.
This reflects the collaborative cross-party approach that we need to strengthen our emergency
management system. In my view, like national security, emergency management should be
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 431
bipartisan. I want to thank all of the parties that have worked hard and had input into the development
of this bill.
I also want to acknowledge the submitters on the bill. Their input has improved the bill and will also
feed into its implementation and other operational improvements. Emergency management is
relevant to every person in New Zealand. Submitters’ insights are important to supporting the whole-
of-society approach to emergency management we need to adopt as a country.
The Government’s objectives for reform are to strengthen the role of communities and iwi Māori in
emergency management; provide for clear responsibilities and accountabilities at the national,
regional, and local levels; enable a higher minimum standard of emergency management; minimise
disruption to essential services; and ensure agencies have the tools to do their jobs effectively when
an emergency happens.
The majority of submitters supported this intent. Where submitters sought changes, it’s clear the
select committee has given those views careful consideration, and, in many cases, has
recommended changes to the bill as a result. These amendments have strengthened the bill, and
the Government will be taking them forward. There are some changes I want to highlight, because I
see them as particularly helpful in supporting improvements on the ground.
The bill as reported back extends civil liability protections to official responders when they’re taking
precautionary actions immediately before an emergency. These protections will also cover the likes
of volunteers and civil contractors when they’re acting under official direction. Concern about civil
liability before a state of emergency is declared should not create hesitation to act, because hesitation
can result in avoidable damage. At worst, it may cost lives. I welcome the select committee’s
recommended changes on this issue, and I thank the submitters who raised it. The committee has
also recommended creating a formal link between regional emergency management plans and the
long-term planning process under the Local Government Act. Good planning is fundamental to
driving action on the ground across the four Rs of risk reduction, readiness, response, and recovery.
While there was already an expectation that local authorities would implement their emergency
management responsibilities through long-term plans, making this link explicit and clarifying how a
multi-council planning process should flow into individual councils and their long-term plans was
important. Emergency management committees are intended to achieve economies of scale and
integrated management of hazards and risks, but they can only be successful if all councils play their
part. Linking regional emergency management plans and long-term plans will ensure that
committees’ decisions translate into action.
This change reinforces a key shift the bill is making to put more emphasis on the emergency
management role of individual councils. Related changes include creating specific roles for regional
emergency management committees and their local authority members, making mayors primarily
responsible for declaring states of local emergency and recovery transition periods within their own
districts, requiring every territorial authority to have a district controller and district recovery manager
with a clear line of accountability to the council’s chief executive, and giving territorial authority chief
executives an explicit mandate to coordinate resources provided by other agencies in the lead-up to
and during an emergency over that longer-term recovery. In late October last year, severe weather
events coincided with the local body elections. Because new mayors had not yet been sworn in, I
needed to declare states of local emergency over Southland and Canterbury.
The committee has recommended a sensible change to address this gap, enabling mayors to be
sworn in early on a temporary basis to declare a state of emergency or transition period. This will
enable local declarations to continue to be made locally and avoid potential delays in the emergency
disruption communications if the emergency is disrupted because of communications between the
affected council and the Minister.
When it comes to improving our resilience to emergencies, this bill is only part of the picture. Councils
also hold many tools to address specific hazards under the planning, building, and biosecurity
legislation. To name just a few: like under the current Act, emergency management committees are
expected to use these tools to support their emergency management responsibilities. I’m pleased to
see that the select committee has recommended making the connection between these
responsibilities clearer by creating a requirement for emergency management committees and
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 432 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
councils to consider whether functions, duties, and powers in other relevant legislation would help
meet their emergency management responsibilities.
New Zealand is one of the most exposed countries to natural hazard risk in the world. I’m sure I don’t
need to convince the House about the need for a strong emergency management system. This need
is reinforced by every severe weather event, let alone when we consider our most serious risks, like
the Alpine Fault. It’s critical we have legislation that sets us up to manage these risks. At its core,
New Zealand’s approach to emergency management is based on three key principles: (1) we
consider all hazards, natural and man-made; (2) we manage the risk from these hazards by taking
action across the four Rs: risk reduction, readiness, response, and recovery; and (3) all parts of
society have a role to play in emergency management: central government, local government,
communities and businesses, iwi and hapū, and individual households.
Overall, this bill will better enable our emergency management system to achieve this intent, and
deliver the improvements identified through past inquiries and reviews. For that reason, I want to
thank, again, the select committee and all of the submitters for the critical role you have played in
improving this bill.
The Emergency Management Bill (No 2) will provide stronger foundations for New Zealand to meet
the growing risk we face as a country, and I commend it to the House.

items.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU-NAN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. As we heard from both
of the previous speakers, this is a bill that is important and very much needed, and the Green Party
also supports this bill. I want to first acknowledge the Governance and Administration Committee for
considering this bill and all of the members on that committee for doing a very thorough job of it. I
also do want to acknowledge the Minister for Emergency Management and Recovery for the role
that the Minister has played in managing some of the emergency responses I’ve seen. I’ve seen the
Minister firsthand going out to those affected areas, so I do want to thank the Minister for that.
Like the previous speaker said, this is something that is facing Aotearoa New Zealand broadly, and
it’s really good to see that this bill has, broadly, the support of this House, and definitely the support
of the Green Party. As mentioned before, the bill would replace the existing Civil Defence Emergency
Management Act and then build this new legislative framework by this bill in terms of the 2023
Government inquiry into the response to the North Island severe weather events. In terms of the
2023 events, what we have seen from that, both in terms of the Auckland anniversary floods that
affected areas such as Auckland Central, Epsom, and Mount Albert more severely, as well as areas
over the shore, and the responses that MPs have had on that, but also personally having relatives
on the East Coast and in Napier, Tokomaru Bay, Tolaga Bay, was going to those areas and seeing
the ongoing impact, even to this day, that Cyclone Gabrielle had in those kinds of areas. This is
something that very much is facing Aotearoa New Zealand on the whole.
I think, with that, it’s really important for us to address the first major issue that we have in this House,
which is around climate change and how we are responding to both climate mitigation and also
climate adaptation. Of course, this is something that the Green Party in particular is very interested
in and would like to follow through in having this conversation, with any Government, and on this bill
and during the committee stage in particular. Now, the reason for that is because what we have seen
is an increase. What we normally have seen to be once-every-hundred-year events are now
annually, and our local authority simply—our people, our communities, our society—is not at this
stage prepared to handle that kind of level of frequency. Right now, we’re seeing more extreme
weather patterns all around the world, most recently with the heat waves in France hitting record
highs again. We’re seeing that happening every year. We just declared that El Nino is here in
Aotearoa and the impact that that, potentially, will have in the coming months.
So climate change is absolutely an important focus when we’re looking at the way we look at
emergency management, of course, with all of the other natural disasters on the bill we have just
spoken on, the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill, on other forms of natural
disasters like earthquakes. With that kind of setting the scene, it’s important then to ask: it’s very well
to have a bill such as this, but what is the level of resourcing that is needed to be able to undertake
and actually do what is set out as a legislative framework to its full effect and give credit to what we’re
trying to do here today?
For example, one of the things we have raised and we are concerned about is that in Budget 2024
we did see that ring-fencing for the Climate Emergency Response Fund has been taken back and
nearly $1 billion has been wiped from that fund to subsidise other parts of that Budget. What we have
seen is that the marae resilience fund is drying up, even though marae play such an important role
in an emergency response. I want to give a specific shout out to the marae that supported the local
communities, our tourists, our visitors—not just Māori but everyone who was in the communities in
the climate-charged extreme weather we saw in the Bay of Plenty earlier in the year. All of these are
important considerations as we progress this bill further through the House.
What we have also seen is that the Government has given record investment and record funding to
Defence but, proportionately, we have not seen the personnel, particularly when it comes to civil
defence, receiving a proportion of that record increase in Defence. Again, we feel like, if we’re really
talking about emergency management and emergency response, there is a little bit of an imbalance
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 435
in terms of what we see as a legislative framework and what we’re seeing in action from a resourcing
perspective. Another important aspect of that resourcing is what we have seen most recently here in
Te Whanga-nui-a-Tara, in terms of the sudden flood that we saw only a few months ago, which has
also left many, many of our families here in Wellington in hardship. I do want to give a special
acknowledgment to our local Green MPs, Julie Anne Genter and Tamatha Paul, for the role that they
played—as all electorate MPs do in the event of an emergency, when it comes to the emergency
response.
One of the things we did see, through a series of these emergency events that we’ve seen since the
beginning of this year, was a record number of local states of emergency being triggered; yet what
we don’t see is the corresponding response from, for example, the Minister of Social Development
(MSD) when it comes to the civil defence payment. There has to be constantly this battle with MSD
to trigger the civil defence payment, because, if a local authority doesn’t ask for it, it’s not triggered—
whereas, when people are in hardship, particularly when we were looking at a local state of
emergency or national state of emergency, those civil defence payments should be automatically
triggered rather than people having to ask for that. That all comes down to the package of what the
Greens would really like to see when it comes to resourcing.
Another area that I want to touch on is the disproportionate effect that this will have on certain
communities. Two communities that come to mind in particular are our disabled communities and
our seniors communities, as we saw when it came to Cyclone Gabrielle a few years ago. We noticed
that when it comes to seniors, when it comes to the disabled, there was no really good record—
particularly for civil defence personnel, for firefighters, for those who were on the front line—to know
if a particular family or people that they were evacuating actually required those kinds of additional
specialised support. It’s really good to see this particular bill having a specific mentioning and
acknowledgment of the importance of those disproportionately affected communities.
With that kind of legislative framework—towards the policy framework, again—it comes down to what
sort of resourcing we need. What kind of collaboration with hapū, with iwi, with disabled communities,
with seniors, and with our elders are we expecting to see, to ensure that these sorts of things are
being addressed, so that we are not in a position where older people are left stranded at home
because those people who are on the front line don’t know that they require additional support—
wheelchair access and all of those things?
Finally, I think another important area when it comes to the idea of emergency management is that
the idea of schools and also communities being local hubs in the event of emergency management
is absolutely crucial. From the perspective of schools, we have seen that schools have also recorded
an incredible rate of needing additional support from the Ministry of Education as a result of school
property damage, which has also meant that our schools couldn’t open as well. This is, again,
something that we’d really like to see: how can we build up schools’ resilience as a local hub? We’re
looking at even more than what the Government has put in this year’s Budget when it comes to solar
panels on schools, as well as the ability for schools to have things like industrial grade kitchens and
the broader school lunch availability that’s done locally. That way, in the event of an emergency, the
schools can also be a source or hub for the local communities as well.
Finally, I think it’s important for me to actually acknowledge all of our electorate MPs here in this
House and every single one of you for the role that you play in response to any form of extreme
climate-charged weather events, whether you are Grant McCallum from Northland to Ingrid Leary
from Taieri, from David MacLeod in the west to Dana Kirkpatrick in the east, in East Coast.
