This amendment bill is an omnibus bill that amends legislation administered by the Ministry of Social
Development and the New Zealand Defence Force. Specifically, the bill makes a number of minor
policy and technical changes to the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001,
the Social Security Act 2018, and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, and repeals the Family Benefits
(Home Ownership) Act 1964. This bill is intended to improve the provision of social welfare benefits.
The amendments in the bill will update statutory provisions, address regulatory duplication gaps and
errors, and bring legislation up to date with public expectations. The bill will reduce the chance of
regulatory failure and unintended consequences that harm the wellbeing of New Zealanders. The
changes are small and do not warrant stand-alone bills, but together the changes will ensure greater
effectiveness and efficiency of the social welfare system.
The first minor policy change is to extend the sustainable employment trial for supported living
payment recipients from 26 weeks to a maximum period of 104 weeks. The supported living payment
is a benefit payable to people who are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work
because of a health condition, injury, disability, or because they are totally blind. The purpose of the
sustainable employment trial is to encourage and support supported living payment recipients who
want to move into employment or increase their hours of work to establish whether they can sustain
that employment and cease receiving the benefit.
Feedback from health and disability stakeholders and international evidence indicates that the fear
of losing the supported living payment entitlement can be a significant barrier to work and that 26
weeks is not long enough for some recipients to test their ability to work. Furthermore, increasing
hours of work incrementally over a longer period better supports people to sustain employment and
become independent. Extending the sustainable employment trial to two years will therefore improve
incentives for supported living payment recipients to work as much as they can, leading to a better
financial position and improved wellbeing outcomes for those who can participate.
The second policy change is to ensure that residents of the Realm countries of Niue, Cook Islands,
and Tokelau cannot use social security agreements to meet the residence requirements for New
Zealand superannuation and veterans’ pension. Social security agreements are bilateral treaties
between Governments that provide for the reciprocal payment of social security benefits and
pensions. These agreements are intended to apply to the residence of the two agreement partner
countries. However, the Ministry of Social Development has advised that a court would likely find
that some of New Zealand’s social security agreements could apply to people applying for New
Zealand superannuation or veterans’ pension while resident in the Realm countries.
Social security agreements are not intended to apply to residents of the Realm countries. Realm
countries do not have the resources to participate in the cost-sharing aspects of social security
agreements. Instead, New Zealand superannuation special portability provisions are extended to the
residents of the Realm. Therefore, the bill will amend the New Zealand Superannuation and
Retirement Income Act 2001 and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014 to exclude the application of social
security agreements to Realm country residents.
The third minor policy change will enable people who are live organ donors to be eligible for an
emergency benefit payment equivalent to the rate of the supported living payment. Currently, a
supported living payment recipient who is caring for a person who would otherwise require hospital
or residential care is not eligible to receive supported living payments should they be recovering from
surgery for a live organ donation. This is because they are not caring for someone while they are
recovering from surgery, which is a criterion to receive the supported living payment—caring.
Instead, they are transferred on to the emergency benefit while they are in their recovery period and
can only receive the rate of the equivalent main benefit that they would be entitled to, which is either
the jobseeker support or sole parent support. This anomaly in the supported living payment does not
align with the Compensation for Live Organ Donors Act 2016, which is designed to remove financial
deterrents to the donation of organs by live donors. Therefore, the bill will establish explicit legal
authority to pay emergency benefit to clients at the same rate that they were receiving on the
supported living payment on the ground of caring for another person for a period of up to 12 weeks
after the donation.
As I noted earlier, the bill also contains minor technical amendments. These minor amendments are
mostly related to the Social Security Act 2018 and the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement

Income Act 2001. Rather than go through each technical amendment, let me highlight the common
themes behind the changes. The majority of the proposed amendments will address errors or
omissions found following the rewrite of the Social Security Act 1964 to the Social Security Act 2018.
Other changes are aimed to improve the provision of social welfare benefits and strengthen the
performance of the social security system. There are also changes which will repeal redundant

In conclusion, it can be difficult to find time on the parliamentary calendar for repairs and maintenance

items.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
items.text: I move, That the Regulatory Systems
(Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation)
Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
I am pleased to speak to these bills in the House again today. As I noted in my first reading speech,
the regulatory system amendment bills are one of the ways that this Government maintains and
repairs existing legislation and ensures that our regulatory systems deliver for New Zealanders. At a
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 450 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
high level, these two bills reflect the Government’s commitment to delivering fit for purpose regulation
and to improving access to justice. They will have a significant impact on the regulatory regimes that
govern tribunals and occupational regulation, enhancing their effectiveness and efficiency while
improving consumer protection and the quality of justice legislation.
The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill makes practical improvements to tribunals and
quasi-judicial bodies. It removes barriers to justice by allowing successful applicants in the disputes
tribunal to recover their filing fee from the respondent where it is appropriate. It strengthens the
regulation of the private security industry by providing more effective information-gathering powers
to investigate breaches. It also streamlines appointments and employment arrangements for tribunal
members to ensure these bodies operate efficiently.
The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill strengthens protections for both
consumers and regulated professionals while reducing unnecessary compliance costs. One
important change allows conveyancers’ professional undertakings to be enforced in the High Court,
just as lawyers’ undertakings already are. This promotes competition in the conveyancing market
and benefits consumers.
The bill also removes a disproportionately harsh penalty that automatically disqualifies real estate
agents from practising for five years simply because they failed to complete continuing professional
development or pay fees on time. That issue has been recognised by the profession for many years,
and this bill delivers a more proportionate response. At the same time, the bill strengthens the Real
Estate Authority’s ability to investigate unlicensed trading and ensure licensee’s meet their
obligations, improving consumer confidence in the industry.
Both bills have benefited from the select committee process, and I would like to thank the Justice
Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee for their careful consideration, along with
everyone who made submissions. Their constructive feedback has resulted in sensible
improvements.
The Justice Committee has clarified the role of the Complaints, Investigations and Prosecution Unit
when dealing with complaints about unlicensed private security operators. The Education and
Workforce Committee has recommended that the Real Estate Authority’s new powers be exercised
on a reasonable basis and clarified that provisions relating to unsatisfactory conduct apply only where
behaviour is connected to a licensee’s professional role and affects public confidence in the
profession. These are practical improvements that make already sensible bills even stronger.
I also thank officials and the Parliamentary Counsel Office for their work in developing these bills.
Whether someone is taking a claim to the Disputes Tribunal, buying a home through a conveyancer,
or working as a real estate agent, these reforms will make our regulatory systems fairer, more
efficient, and easier to navigate. They demonstrate this Government’s commitment to good
regulatory stewardship, maintaining the laws we already have, reducing unnecessary compliance,
and improving access to justice and ensuring regulations work for the people they are meant to serve.
I commend these bills to the House.

items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I’d to rise and take a call on
the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational
Regulation) Amendment Bill and just echo my colleague’s sentiment around how exciting these bills
are. The Hon Dr Duncan Webb’s contribution was exceptionally exciting. For those members of the
public that have just tuned in to watch these bills progress, I will attempt to cover off some of the key
points with this legislation.
These bills focus on improving systems that people interact with every day. They make changes to
tribunal processes, occupational regulation, complaints procedures, and licensing arrangements, so
that those systems operate more effectively and efficiently. Both bills have now completed the select
committee process. The Justice Committee considered submissions on the tribunals bill and heard
oral evidence from submitters. The Education and Workforce Committee received a larger number
of submissions on the occupational regulation bill and heard evidence from a range of interested
parties as well. The committees received advice from officials, support from the Office of the Clerk,
and assistance from the Parliamentary Counsel Office as they worked through the details of both
pieces of legislation.
Labour supports the changes that have emerged from that process, and these bills are part of a wider
programme of regulatory systems legislation administrated by the Ministry of Justice. The purpose
of that work is not to revisit major policy decisions that Parliament has already made. The purpose
is to identify parts of the legislation that can be improved through experience and feedback from
regulators and professional bodies, and people like tribunal users and those responsible for
administrating these systems on a daily basis, and it’s an important part of Parliament’s role. No
regulatory framework stays perfect for ever. Over time, gaps emerge, inconsistencies develop,
language becomes dated, and administrative processes no longer reflect how a sector actually
operates. So, periodically, Parliament needs to revisit these settings and make improvements, and
this bill does just that.
The committee process demonstrated that point. Submitters raised practical issues, officials provided
advice, and members tested the provisions that are before us, and the result is legislation that is
stronger than what it was when it was first introduced. One of the themes running through both bills
is public confidence. Whether somebody is dealing with a lawyer, engaging with a real estate
professional, lodging a complaint with a regulator, or appearing before a tribunal, they need
confidence that the rules are clear and that institutions involved have the ability to carry out their
responsibilities properly. Confidence is built in different ways. Sometimes it comes through strong
professional standards, sometimes it comes from effective complaint systems, sometimes it comes
through regulators having access to information that they need to investigate concerns, and
sometimes it comes through accessible dispute resolution processes that ordinary New Zealanders
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 458 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
can use without excessive cost or complexity. Across these two bills, we see examples of all those
things.
The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill focuses on three key areas:
lawyers and conveyancers, the real estate sector, and provisions within the Prostitution Reform Act.
Its purpose is to strengthen consumer protection, improve efficiency, remove inconsistencies, and
reduce those unnecessary compliance costs across all of those systems.
One of those significant changes concerns the Lawyers Complaints Service. Under this bill,
complaints can be made subject to an initial assessment process before being referred to the lawyers
standards committee. The legislation identifies circumstances where no further action may be
appropriate, including where complaints are trivial, frivolous, or, as the Hon Dr Duncan Webb
mentioned in his contribution, vexatious, made in bad faith, or excessively delayed, or where another
remedy might very well exist. That intention is pretty straightforward. Complaints systems work best
when resources are focused on matters that require investigation and resolution. Every profession
depends on public confidence, and maintaining that confidence requires complaints processes that
are both robust and efficient.
The bill also contains significant reforms relating to the Real Estate Authority. The real estate sector
plays a major role in the lives of New Zealanders; everyone knows that. For many families,
purchasing a home is the largest financial commitment they will ever make, and there’s an
expectation that professional standards will be maintained and that regulators will have the ability to
investigate concerns where those standards may not have been met. The legislation strengthens the
authority’s ability to obtain documents relevant to investigations. During select committee
considerations, amendments were recommended to ensure that the authority must have reasonable
grounds before exercising those powers and to clarify the circumstances in which relevant
documents may be sought from those parties holding information relevant to an investigation. The
bill also updates a number of licensing provisions. It allows licences to be renewed up to 12 months,
I think it was, after expiring. It provides mechanisms that recognise the experience and knowledge
of practitioners returning to the profession. These are practical changes that simplify administration
while maintaining the expectations around competence and professional standards.
There are also a number of amendments, as mentioned earlier, to the Prostitution Reform Act. Those
changes update the references to criminal offences so that legislation continues to reflect the
developments elsewhere in criminal law while preserving the existing policy intent around
disqualification from holding a certificate, essentially.
Taken together, the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill strengthens
consumer protections. It improves the operation of complaints systems and provides regulators with
clear tools to fulfil those responsibilities.
Now, turning to the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill, the purpose of that bill is to
improve the operation and efficiency of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies, remove barriers to
accessing justice, and address legislative inconsistencies to better support statutory authorities in
carrying out their functions. One amendment relates to the Disputes Tribunal. As has already been
traversed in the House today, the bill allows the tribunal to order reimbursement of filing fees where
an applicant succeeds wholly or partly in their claim. For many New Zealanders, the Disputes
Tribunal is the most accessible way to resolve disagreements without entering the formal court. The
system was designed to provide a relatively low-cost and straightforward avenue for dispute
resolution. The ability to reimburse filing fees recognises that, where somebody has pursued a
legitimate claim successfully, there may be circumstances where reimbursement is appropriate. The
legislation also preserves incentives for parties to reach settlement, recognising the value of
resolving disputes before they require a formal determination.
The bill also includes amendments relating to the appointment of referees. Those provisions
formalise the assessment process used for appointments and reappointments, providing a more
consistent mechanism for selecting people to carry out those very important roles. The quality of

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Members, the House is in committee on the Regulatory
Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation)
Amendment Bill.
We come first to the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill, and we begin with the debate
on Part 1.
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts) ( 16:39): Thank you, Madam Chair, for the
opportunity to open the committee stage of the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill. I’m
pleased to say that there was broad support across the House for this bill at its second reading, and
I look forward to hearing the views of the other parties as we debate this bill.
The bill amends five Acts to improve the effectiveness and the efficiency of tribunals and quasi-
judicial bodies by reducing barriers to accessing justice and better enabling statutory authorities to
investigate and regulate the industry. The amendments will, among other things, give disputes
tribunal referees the ability to order a respondent to pay the filing fee to a successful applicant, to
simplify the appointment process for disputes tribunal referees and Motor Vehicle Disputes Tribunal
adjudicators, and provide a new information-gathering power to the unit responsible for private
security investigations and prosecutions. These improvements will support the maintenance and
continuous improvement of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies, and this will help to ensure that the
tribunal system is accessible and fit for purpose.
I also wish to draw my Amendment Paper 353 to the attention of the House for consideration during
this committee stage. This Amendment Paper is straightforward. It only makes some minor technical
changes to ensure the provisions read as intended. I’m happy to take questions on the bill as we go
through the committee.

Amendment Bill. I’m pleased to say that there was broad support across the House for this bill at

This bill amends the Lawyers and Conveyancers Act, the Prostitution Reform Act, the Real Estate
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed

Agents Act, to increase protections for regulated professionals, such as real estate agents, and for
consumers of those regulated services. The amendments will, among other things, enable the
undertakings or professional commitments of conveyances to be enforced in the High Court in the
same way that lawyers’ undertakings are; to remove a disproportionately harsh punishment for real

items.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
items.text: Thank you, Madam Speaker. I move,
That the Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill and the Regulatory Systems
(Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill be now read a third time.
I’m pleased to take this final call on two practical bills that improve the way parts of our justice and
regulatory systems operate. These bills are not about creating unnecessary new layers of regulation,
they’re about maintaining the laws we already have, fixing known problems, removing
disproportionate penalties, and making sure our regulatory systems work better for the people who
use them.
The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill improves access to justice and supports the
effective operation of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies. It allows successful applicants in the
disputes tribunal to recover their filing fee from the respondent where it is appropriate.

items.speaker: DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: You can get another Minister to read it out for you.

items.speaker: Hon NICOLE McKEE
items.text: Yes, if you wouldn’t mind.

items.speaker: Hon LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: That is a sensible change. People who have had to enforce their legal
rights should not be left bearing unnecessary costs when they have been successful.
The bill also strengthens oversight of the private security industry by improving information gathering
powers. This will help detect and deter people operating outside the rules. It also makes practical
changes to appointments and employment arrangements for tribunal members so these bodies can
operate more consistently and efficiently.
The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill improves the occupational
regulation system for both professionals and consumers. It allows conveyancers’ professional
undertakings to be enforced in the High Court, as lawyers’ undertakings already are. That will support
competition in the conveyancing market and give consumers more confidence in the services they
use.
It also removes an overly harsh penalty that disqualified real estate agents from practising for five
years for failing to complete continuing professional development or pay fees on time. That kind of
penalty is out of proportion to the breach. This bill replaces it with a more sensible and balanced
approach. At the same time, the bill strengthens the real estate authority’s ability to investigate
unlicensed trading and ensure licensees are meeting their obligations.

Second Reading
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health) ( 21:01): I move, That the Mental
Health Bill be now read a second time.
It’s a privilege to be standing here today for the second reading of the Mental Health Bill. I’d like firstly
to start by thanking the Health Committee for all their hard work—ably led by the chair, Sam
Uffindell—in examining this bill. Can I say, from the start, that I think it’s vitally important for tangata
whaiora that this bill comes back with full cross-party support. I’d also like to thank the people who
took the time to make a submission and engage with the select committee process—particularly
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 498 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
those who shared their personal experience. It is a deeply personal thing to share your own
experience, so thank you for your bravery. I do want to acknowledge all those with lived experience.
The committee considered submissions from 358 individuals and groups. Those submitters brought
a range of perspectives, including those who have experience of compulsory treatment, those with
family with lived experience, clinicians, academics, and mental health organisations. I’d also like to
thank the 89 people who spoke directly to the Health Committee to share their views. I’d also like to
acknowledge those who bravely came forward to share their stories in the Royal Commission of
Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and in the Care of Faith-based Institutions. It is important
that we carry their voices, not only tonight but through any work looking into how the State cares for
people when they need it the most.
I want to reiterate that this bill will demonstrate meaningful and significant progress by contributing
towards at least 10 of the abuse in care recommendations, relating primarily to care safety and
monitoring. All of you have helped shape a Mental Health Bill that goes beyond compulsory
treatment, as we know it today, and that, instead, firmly places a person at the centre of their care
and empowers people to make decisions about their own care.
While most in New Zealand who access specialist mental health and addiction services are not
subject to the Mental Health Act, over the course of a year, around 11,000 people receive compulsory
care. In an ideal world, we would not need compulsory mental health care; however, we need a
system in place for New Zealanders experiencing mental distress at a level that does require
intervention to support their recovery. This bill strikes a balance of a future focus on safe and effective
mental health care for people who require that State intervention, while having the right safeguards
in place to ensure people’s rights are upheld and protected. This bill will be a critical safety net for
those experiencing severe mental distress who are unable to make decisions about their own mental
health care. I do want to reiterate tonight that it is intended to be used as a last resort only.
The submissions received on this bill represented a variety of views. This is an important piece of
legislation, and I expected there to be views across the board on key areas in the bill to assist the
Health Committee’s consideration. It has been heartening to see that, of the individuals and groups
that commented on the general policy intent of the bill, the majority were supportive. People
recognise that we need compulsory care in some form; however, there were divergent views on what
people felt this should look like.
I’m also encouraged by the support from submitters for the introduction of compulsory care principles,
the supported decision-making provisions, and establishment of new roles and processes to
safeguard those under compulsory care. This includes independent support persons and advocates,
nominated persons, and collaborative care teams. These are integral to the shifts I want to see under
this new legislation.
There were some key changes made through the select committee process. These include
introducing a “dignity of risk” principle. This aligns with the legislation’s purpose of promoting
decision-making capacity. I believe it’s critical that the legislation recognises a person’s right to take
reasonable risks to achieve personal growth, self-esteem, and overall quality of life.
Terminology is really important to how people see themselves and how people are treated. I’m
pleased to see the Health Committee has made changes to the term “patient” to instead be “person
under compulsory care”. This change responds to submitters who said the term “patient” is
stigmatising and can reinforce power imbalances between someone seeking support and
professionals. Submitters also said it reinforces a paternalistic approach to care, which we want to
move away from.
Offences and penalties are important enforcement tools in the legislation. The royal commission of
inquiry raised the need for appropriate and significant penalties for failures to comply with standards
of care. I’m very pleased to see that the select committee has made changes to modernise the
offences and penalties in this legislation, with a more structured regime as well as more tools for the
regulator to use to support greater compliance with the Act.
However, I also recognise that many people who submitted on the bill had concerns about specific
areas—in particular, the use of restrictive practices such as seclusion and the use of
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 499
electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT. People also want strong safeguards for care of those under 18.
As I spoke about in the first reading on this bill, these practices have a history of inappropriate use,
abuse, and overuse.
I want to be very clear that I remain committed to seeing the reduction and elimination of seclusion.
However, it is critical that this is done in a way that minimises the risk of unintended consequences.
In particular, I would not want to see an increase in other inappropriate practices such as chemical
or physical restraint. The bill strengthens requirements on the use of seclusion to drive the change
needed to reduce and eliminate seclusion. The bill prohibits seclusion for children and young people.
This is an incremental but significant step towards elimination that I am proud of, but I’m aware that
there’s going to be a big shift for mental health workers, and it is important that we manage this
change safely for both children and young people as well as staff.
I do want to acknowledge that the Health Committee has made a number of improvements to further
strengthen provisions relating to seclusion to ensure there are stronger protections and greater
monitoring of progress. The committee received a wide range of views about ECT, from being an
effective, life-saving treatment in modern clinical practice through to wanting it banned. The
committee has also recommended a range of improvements to make sure there are greater
safeguards on the use of ECT, including for people under 18.
From the submissions received, the Health Committee has recommended changes that will improve
clarity and ensure greater safeguards for those subject to the Act. The word I want to emphasise
here is “balance”; the bill aims to strike a balance between placing limits on people’s rights when
there is a need to intervene to provide care and ensuring that this intervention is only done when
absolutely necessary and in a way that protects and upholds an individual’s rights.
In closing, I acknowledge that there are diverse views on this piece of legislation, which were heard
through the select committee process. Developing this bill has involved careful balancing of all of
those views.  I believe the bill represents a meaningful step forward, and I’m pleased to present it to
you today. The bill will enable supported decision making, safer practice through stronger protections
for people subject to legislation, and care that is provided in the least coercive way—that is
therapeutic and responsive to a person’s needs. I hope to see continued cross-party support on this
important bill. I commend this bill to the House.

Dr HAMISH CAMPBELL (National—Ilam) ( 21:41): It’s an honour to rise and speak on the
second reading of the Mental Health Bill. I do just want to acknowledge New Zealand’s first Minister

Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour) ( 21:42): Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a privilege to
rise to take a call on this bill, which has been a long time coming following on from the He Ara Oranga
review, and then work by successive Ministers in the Labour Government, and now the National
Government. It’s great to see it in the House.
I do have to admit that the select committee hearings feel like quite some time ago now, and it is a
shame that such a landmark piece of legislation is being debated under urgency, meaning that we’re
not hearing full calls from the other side. This is really important, and I can’t think of much other
legislation that has the same human rights impact in the health sector. It was with that lens that I
went into the select committee hearings, from which I had my involvement when I was briefly the
Minister— well, my engagement with the bill as Minister was brief compared to the other Ministers
who have shepherded this bill.
The 1992 Act I would characterise as having the test of who could be placed under compulsory care
in the Act, and then the main defence of the person’s human rights under the existing Act is largely
through processes of review that are structured throughout the course of the person’s treatment and
the time periods at which they must occur. This Act takes a very different approach to upholding the
rights of people who are subject to the compulsory treatment clauses of the Act. So, for a start,
compulsory treatment should only be used to improve the person’s mental health. So it’s not an
opportunity to improve other elements of the person’s health—t hey still have to consent for that—or
their social circumstances. I think that’s important to remember because sometimes some mental
health conditions do mean that people’s living circumstances can deteriorate.
The bill requires that the least restrictive option be used. Voluntary care options should be always
preferred to compulsory care, and compulsory care should only be used for as short a period as
possible. There’s also the reassessments of whether compulsory treatment can be used. Those are
positive developments.
In addition, there are some new and innovative concepts that clearly can be done, but it’ll be
interesting to see how these practices interact with the law and how, ultimately, people’s care and
human rights are affected. This includes the creation of mental health advance directives. That is
something viewed favourably in many of the submissions that we received on the committee. But
advance directives of all sorts have limitations, and I hope they are not too easily set aside by busy
care teams who wonder if the circumstances in which the advance directives were set are no longer
in place. There can be good reasons why they’re not followed, and so I hope that we are able to live
up to the aspiration in the bill in terms of how we implement those.
I think the appointment of nominated persons to stand up for the rights of the person in compulsory
care is as important, as well as the practice of wellbeing meetings. These are practices that may well
be being used across the health system already, but they are not mandated. Overall, I think those
would be good things.
I think one of the things about the involvement of family and whānau in someone’s care is that, at
times, and I guess under the current Act, treatment teams can confuse , and we all as a society can
confuse—w ell, excessive concern about respecting someone’s privacy might lead to the non-
inclusion of family members, in some situations. So I think the bill’s presumption is that family
member involvement is a good thing and will mean that people have greater access to the supports
that they will depend on when they are no longer in compulsory care, and also during the time that
they are in compulsory care. So I think that’s positive.
The requirement for independent support people to advocate for the person under the Act and assist
them with participating in decision making and exercising their rights is another really, really positive

There are some areas where rights have been strengthened as well. People have to be able to

I was pleased my colleague Ingrid Leary and I were able to lead a discussion on the committee about

So, all in all, there is a lot to be positive about in this bill.
I do want to mention our concern about the continued use of seclusion. Seclusion has been
eliminated in some parts of our health system in New Zealand, and good on the teams who have

Resourcing and workforce are always challenges in the health system, and there are always difficult

the hands of people who were meant to be caring for her. For that reason, that is my one reservation
about this bill, but there are a lot of other positive developments in it, and I commend it to the House.
Dr CARLOS CHEUNG (National—Mt Roskill) ( 21:52): This bill is a significant step forward

items.speaker: Dr TRACEY McLELLAN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. I, too, rise to take a call
on the Mental Health Bill at this second reading. It’s very appropriate that Labour supports this bill
because it is essentially updating—well, it is replacing a very outdated law that we simply can’t
continue to operate under: the Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992. A
lot has changed since 1992. Certainly, the way that society as a whole conceptualises the difference
between mental illness, mental health, and mental wellbeing, and a lot of improvement in our
understanding—and in our expectations—of what people care could and should expect from their
mental health system.
As has been noted, the law was written more than three decades ago. It no longer reflects the modern
understanding of human rights, of supported decision-making and how that can be possible, not just
in an idealistic way but in a therapeutic way, and something not just to strive towards but something
that can be inculcated into something even as complicated and as important as treating mental illness
and mental wellbeing.
It also no longer reflects our modern understanding of disability rights and cultural safety, or the
importance of involving whānau in care, and all of those other things that, since 1992, we have prided
ourselves in this country of improving. So we do think this bill was a substantial improvement.
I’d like to acknowledge the Minister for his work. I’d like to acknowledge the Health Committee for all
of the work that they have done. I wasn’t on that committee, but even just listening tonight, you can
see the nature of the robust questioning that would have happened, the nature of the genuine and
inquisitive inquiries that would have been offered only with the absolute intentionality to do the very
best by this bill and the very best by the people who would be most impacted by this bill. I’d also like
to acknowledge, no doubt, all of the officials and the people with expertise who submitted, people
with lived experience, because only with that breadth of input could we make necessary
improvements.
Whilst I say that the bill has made substantial improvements—as we’ve heard, it follows the He Ara
Oranga and the royal commission into abuse in care—I do agree also with my colleagues that it does
also feel somewhat of a missed opportunity. I understand the tension between fixing something that
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 508 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
needs to be fixed because it is outdated and no longer reflects society’s expectations, and the tension
between doing something that is much more transformative. That has been the decision that has
been made. Would we have made, potentially, a different decision? Yes, probably so, but we do
respect where we’ve landed, but it is incumbent upon us to make those notes.
The bill introduces, as I said, a more modern rights-based framework and places a greater emphasis
on participation, which we know, therapeutically, is actually a really important factor in the efficacy of
any kind of treatment regime, particularly when people are under all sorts of stressors, as is often
the case in this domain, but ultimately, always need to be treated with dignity, and voluntary care
should always be the goal, so that direction is welcome. We fundamentally believe that compulsion
should never be the default simply because there is a lack of time, staffing, or resources.
It’s on that point that I do just want to take a moment because that, for as long as I can remember,
has always been a justification, an excuse, a perfectly decent and reasonable explanation—however
we want to term it—but for as long as I can remember, a lack of time, staffing, and resources has
always held up a different way of doing things in mental health. I’ve worked with many nurses in
particular who have worked in mental health, and my goodness, they really do an amazing job. I
have worked with nurses who work in all sorts of health sectors. Whilst some people, for instance,
might assume that some aspects of nursing are harder than others, I can absolutely tell you that the
people that work in mental health have a very unique perspective, and they work incredibly hard
under very difficult circumstances, and often face quite personal issues in terms of their own safety
in those areas. We shouldn’t be allowed to use a lack of staffing as a means by which to have lower
expectations of what the system could look like.
A right written into legislation, ultimately, is only as meaningful when a person can actually exercise
it. We do implore, along with our support of this bill, much more focus on increased staffing and even
things like increased capital spend, because I’ve seen several facilities that just simply are not
designed for what they’re being utilised for, and even just basic layout can pose really, really
significant risks to people’s safety, including staff. Without those foundations, there is a risk that the
language of this law changes—which it will through the passage of this bill—but people’s experience
of the system doesn’t necessarily change if it’s not resourced properly.
We have also touched on tonight, and both of my colleagues on this side of the House have, I think,
spoken quite eloquently about the need to have a genuine plan to end seclusion, and Labour
supports New Zealand’s commitment to eliminate seclusion. This bill doesn’t go that far. It doesn’t
turn that commitment into a credible plan. We acknowledge that annual reporting is important, that
the five-year legislative review is better than no review at all, but neither of those things actually
amount to a commitment to end seclusion in practice. I acknowledge that that’s a resourcing issue
as much as it is an educative and a legislative process, but Labour certainly does believe that the
legislation should set a goal of ending seclusion. Even within five years would be a reasonable goal
to require a proper systems phase-out plan. That matters because ending seclusion can’t simply be
directed from Parliament. It requires, as I’ve said, the investment in workforce capacity first and
foremost, therapeutic environments as I’ve mentioned, and appropriate building designs, specialist
training, and alternative models of care. All of those things are possible. All of those things are well-
advanced in terms of knowledge. There are just some pieces missing to the puzzle, and that is
appropriate resource.
With regards to electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), I’d like to echo my colleagues’ reservations and
their comments that they made about the process and about making the Health Committee’s ability
to be able to make some leeway on what the bill as drafted had in it. I would also like to note that
ECT can be a really emotive topic, and it’s one of those things that we’ve heard, quite rightly so, a
lot of horror stories over the years. It absolutely is something that has been used abusively over
many, many years. It is an area that I’ve had a little bit to do with through my personal background,
and I have seen it also be put to incredibly good therapeutic use. When it’s considered as a treatment
of last resort, it actually can save lives. I think that this bill does strike a right balance between
acknowledging the therapeutic qualities and the necessities that still exist for ECT, but also having
much more robust safeguards around when it should be used and on who that should be used too.
Labour will support this bill. We absolutely acknowledge the fact that the 1992 Act is old and not fit
for purpose. The bill moves us closer to the goals that I think many of us, regardless of what side of

the House we sit on, would agree is an ultimate outcome and an ultimate goal of a much, much better
mental health system, and we are therefore happy to commend it to the House.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Members, the House is in committee on the Mental Health
Bill. Before we begin debating this bill, I will note that Government Amendment Paper 648 on this bill
was released at 12.45 p.m. today. I remind members of Speaker Brownlee’s ruling earlier in the
sitting that committee stages are always going to proceed slowly when substantive Government
amendments are released on the day that the bill is in committee. While I am satisfied that the
majority of the amendments in this Amendment Paper are minor and technical, there are some that,
on the face of it, appear to be more than minor. The committee stage is always an opportunity to
correct matters in a bill, but it is not good practice to release a Government Amendment Paper so

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Members, we come now to Part 2. This is the debate on
clauses 12 to 40, “Tāngata whaiora rights and support”. The question is that Part 2 stand part.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri) ( 23:47): Thank you, Mr Chair. I don’t have a huge number
of suggestions or questions on this part, but I do want to go into the community care orders, because
what we currently have is a situation in New Zealand where we use a significant number of these
orders, compared with countries that we compare ourselves to. They have a disproportionate effect
on Māori in particular, and yet we have before us a bill that purports to strengthen the human rights
of tāngata whaiora.
There is international research-based consensus that compulsory community treatment is not
effective in achieving its stated aims of reducing hospital readmission and improving mental health
outcomes. Given that—and given that it is a significant breach of human rights—we’d expect a
substantial amount of evidence of the benefit needed to justify these orders, but that evidence doesn’t
seem to exist. In fact, in their submission, the FACTORS team, which included Professor Anthony
O’Brien, concluded that, if the bill were to pass in its current form, it would be unlikely to have a
significant impact on the current practice or on reducing the use of compulsory community care.

items.speaker: My questions to the Minister are
items.text: does he know roughly how many people are currently on
compulsory care orders? What evidence does he have that they actually work? Why is he so
resistant, and why are his officials so resistant, to making community care orders voluntary? Is it do
with a sense of moral panic or the assumptions from medical practitioners, who maybe haven’t seen
the evidence, of wanting to do something that looks like they are being accountable and responsible
for patients yet doesn’t seem to have the evidence to back up that they actually work? And is he
aware of evidence that participation by patients in their own care in the community actually has a
better chance of getting people on to the road to recovery? That is my first tranche of questions. I’ll
continue so we can move through the bill.
In section 13, there were submissions around the advance mental health directives and the status
that they have, where there seems to be—again, I hate to use the words “lip service” because they
do have some waiting, so that would be too cynical. What are his reasons for saying that section 13
can be overridden when the advance directive was made by the person when they had capacity?
There may be good reasons, but it would be good to understand what they are because I think there
is a sense that these community care orders provide a lot more human rights protection than what
they actually do in practice. I’ll stop my questions there, and I’ll go into clause 17 later. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Look, I
think it’s well traversed with this bill that before it was introduced to the House, there was significant
public consultation. On top of that, it had its own expert advisory group. It had a full select committee
process. We’re here at 10 minutes to 12, so it would be good to get some questions specific to the
clauses, not just general questions that, quite frankly, could have been answered—and probably
were—several times with officials in the select committee. We are talking about community care. By
definition, if you are not providing that, what sort of level of care are you providing some of the most
vulnerable New Zealanders in a time of need? Now, if the member’s advocating that every person
needs to then go into inpatient hospital care because there is no community care, then that’s an
interesting proposition, because she’s just been going on for the last few days about Wakari and the
issues we’ve got in there. The whole principle of this bill is to ensure that we have compassionate
care for people at some of the most vulnerable times of their life, and it just, quite frankly, beggars
belief that we are now still questioning whether we should have community care in New Zealand.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri) ( 23:52): Thank you. The Minister has said that we
traversed this in select committee. In fact, we didn’t really get much time to look at it. Just for clarity,
we’re not suggesting that there wouldn’t be community care. The suggestion is that there would be
assertive outreach with statutory resourcing and people being able to participate in their own level of
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed

care and that there would be a small number of cases of people who might need to be under
compulsory care.
The Minister didn’t answer any of my questions regarding evidence, but the numbers of people under
compulsory care at any one time in New Zealand is around 6,000. The researchers who have done
this— well-respected university researchers—have shown that around 50 people might need to be
held under compulsory care. So the question is not whether to remove community care but whether
to remove the presumption of having it be compulsory and, instead, to legislate and resource the
care that would be needed for assertive outreach, to make sure that people could participate in their
own wellbeing. I did say that very directly in relation to clause 12.
I do have an amendment. I’m not going to read it out, but if the Minister was minded to read it, it is
around giving effect to valid advance community care orders. I also have some other amendments,
which I may as well go through now, since it is late. Another one is making sure that if somebody’s
advance mental health directive is not used, then they would be able to get something in writing
around that. I’ve got an amendment to clause 17 around attendance at hui by order, where people
should be able to request that somebody else could come along, and there are insertions there in
clause 17(4)(a) and (ca).
I have an amendment around clause 23, “Independent supported person”, to make sure that when
there are independent supported persons under the bill, they can’t be people working for Health New
Zealand, the Ministry of Health, or their agencies. That is just, really, to reflect some of the
arrangements that happen because there are so many organisations that have formal relationships
through legal relationships that may not necessarily be seen as being independent.
In clause 24, I’ve got an amendment around independent advocates—that we amend clause 24(2)(c)
so that they will represent “the views, will, and preferences of persons under compulsory care”. That
is to make sure that that person does have a distinct role, compared to a legal advocate, because
we didn’t get any clarity from the Minister about what the different roles were in the definition section.
I’ve also got another amendment under clause 24 around what those advocates could do—
particularly in relation to electroconvulsive therapy and also seclusion—to strengthen safeguards
there, because, as we’ve said, we don’t believe that there are enough safeguards in the bill as it is
currently worded. Also, it is making sure, in clause 37, that a responsible practitioner must take all
reasonable steps to ensure that a person is able to access independent advice as soon as
practicable. That is something that was said to us at select committee would be good, and I don’t
believe it was given due regard.
Then we have some other amendments around the rights of children and young persons. A great
deal of the evidence that we heard at select committee was around the fact that children and young
people are, unfortunately, going into adult institutions. It’s happened under successive Governments.
There isn’t any statutory resourcing requirement under this bill, and there is a requirement for children
to be put into appropriate care where it’s available, but where it’s not available, there aren’t additional
safeguards for them. We heard that there’s nothing to safeguard their educational development, their
outdoor living space, the things that would make them feel nurtured and protected. The most we
were able to get was the ability for them to be accompanied when they were being transported
between facilities. So this amendment in clause 38—[ Bell rings]

Hon Dr AYESHA VERRALL (Labour) ( 09:07): If the Minister’s referring to the point in the

What I guess is uncomfortable, currently, about the Minister’s amendment is that it does seem like

outweighs this.

items.text: Given the number of clauses in this rather large bill, we have been running

us, because it currently seems to extend powers to non-medical people to be able to make decisions
around compulsory care. The questions I have are, really: what has been the basis of this, and has
the ministry somehow included in its thinking whether it’s primarily intended to address workforce
shortages rather than improve clinical care? I won’t go back into the questions that were raised in

items.speaker: My specific questions are
items.text: why does clause 41(2) allow any mental health practitioner to be appointed
as a responsible practitioner rather than requiring a medical practitioner or a psychiatrist? What
clinical decisions are they expected to make under the bill, and are those decisions appropriate to
be exercised by someone who is not medically qualified? If they’re not a psychiatrist, who, ultimately,
carries responsibility for the diagnosis, the treatment decisions, and the compulsory care reviews?
What safeguards are there for the postcode lottery across different districts, where one director may
appoint nurses or psychologists in one area, while, in a different area, somebody else might only
appoint psychiatrists? If the Government intends psychiatrists ordinarily to perform this role, why is

the role beyond medical practitioners improves patient outcomes?
We do know that we have a shortage of psychiatrists, and that’s, indeed, across the mental health
services. The Minister himself alluded to the associate psychologist role and the fact that they do not
have clinical competence as currently assessed under the Act. We need to be really clear who is
expected to be authorised under this provision and who will be accountable under this provision.
Would the Minister look at my amendment 19A, which would tidy this up for him?

are a few other bits to it on later parts. But I want to speak to her amendment for clause 49. This is

items.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
items.text: Thank you, Madam Chair, and
thanks to that member for those questions. The first two questions were more around, I suppose,
how we operationalise the Act, which I think is a fair question. There’s one around the ratio and the
access. This being an operational matter, the guidelines and secondary legislation will guide that
practice. And also there was the question around size of the team and, I suppose, multi-disciplinary
care planning teams. The size and make-up of a team is expected to reflect the needs of the person.
To the more substantive question around seclusion, I think we’ve heard loud and clear that, as a
direction of the country, we need to look towards removing seclusion in our mental health services.
The first point I’d raise is it’s not necessarily a question of money. If you look at, potentially, some of
the announcements of the last Government around funding into mental health, the data shows
seclusion rates actually went up. The conclusion I’ve drawn from being Minister is not only is it about
adequate resourcing—I’m not disagreeing with that—there is a particular focus needed on training
and the workforce. I would like to share a reflection where I visited an inpatient facility, not far from
here, that had actually reached zero seclusion because of a decision made by the clinical leadership
team around the culture of the organisation. I think it’s incumbent on us, when we are aware that no
comparable countries have achieved the removal of seclusion, that as we move towards potentially
being the first country in the world, we ensure that we have the right plan.
I’m comfortable that the regulations in the bill allow for ending seclusion. That’s why I do not believe
there needs to be a sunset clause. What I’m also encouraged by is the Mental Health and Wellbeing
Commission’s recommendation around New Zealand’s first seclusion plan that Health New Zealand
has accepted to be published in 2027. My expectation, with that plan, is that it would set out a road
map of how we would achieve that and that it would then be incumbent on any Government of the
day to ensure that we follow the road map.
The final point I’d make is that the regulations allow for that and actually could be brought well forward
from the five-year review and a lot earlier within the regulatory framework that this bill sets up.
INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri) ( 09:47): Thank you, Madam Chair. I’m sure we’ll have a
number of questions around the Minister’s response to that question on seclusion. I just want to tidy

The Minister himself, last night, raised the relationship between the compulsory care order and the
person’s care plan under clause 43. It’s important because the compulsory care order authorises
compulsory care but the advance directive or the care plan arrangement records a person’s wishes,
preferences, and treatments. Understanding what parts of those will be given weight and when is
really important.

items.speaker: My questions are
items.text: does a compulsory care order compel treatment generally, or does it only authorise
the compulsory care that is subject to the treatment safeguards elsewhere in the bill? If a person has
an advance mental health directive refusing a particular treatment, how is that reflected under the
care plan required under clause 43, and, if they do refuse, what legal effect will that refusal have?
Where there is an inconsistency between a care plan and an advance mental health directive, which
one of those prevails? And shouldn’t there be a requirement under clause 43 to distinguish between
treatment that the person consents to, treatment authorised despite lack of consent under the Act,
and treatment that has been expressly refused in an advance mental health directive?
The reason I raise that is because we did hear evidence from people who had been subject to
different treatments under the Act—some of them restraint treatments; some of them seclusion.
Almost all of them universally talked about the increased trauma and the impact it had on their
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed

items.speaker: Hon MATT DOOCEY
items.text: I thank that member for those
questions. I think that the bill, quite rightly, as a part of some of the 10 recommendations, achieves

There was a question around involvement of the family, and I think a good example of that is around
the new advance mental health directives, where a hui whaiora must be convened if a person under
compulsory care does not have an advance mental health directive to assist with decisions about

INGRID LEARY (Labour—Taieri) ( 09:52): Turning to seclusion. We did have multiple
submissions, including really strong submissions from the Mental Health Commission, page 10,
clauses 47 to 50, and also the Ombudsman, pages 18, 19, 20—particularly point 88.
The question that we have is it feels like there is a practicality kind of “we don’t have the resourcing
to do this, but we might be able to one day”, and when I heard the Minister talk about a plan being
ready in 2027, that sounds like we are inching at a snail’s pace to something that both the Minister
has experienced and also we, on the select committee, had heard, has been able to be achieved in
this country through planning, culture change, training and so on. So my questions are: if he’s saying
that seclusion is an objective of the bill, why is he still declining to set an end date? Doesn’t he accept

and so on. And, particularly, if there had been a workforce training and resourcing statutory
requirement, which is in my amendment, which I think the Minister is probably going to decline, in
the workforce capability, then that would be really helpful, because it would set the Minister’s
expectation. He’s said it’s his expectation, but there’s nothing in the legislation that reflects that
expectation of the Minister. This would strengthen the expectation and make it very clear to the
institutions what they need to do and there would be the requirement for there to be adequate
funding.
What evidence does he have that five years is the right amount of time to transition away from
seclusion? The Minister will be aware of my tabled amendment that says, “at least have two yearly
reviews”, so that we can put some kind of pressure on the system to show the direction of travel.
What message does retaining an indefinite statutory power to seclusion send to those services who

I’m curious to know if it’s the Government’s position that seclusion will always remain necessary
somewhere in the system. I know there are different clinical and professional views on this, and I’d
like to have on the Hansard what the Minister’s view is on that. I don’t have a position for or against

to end seclusion, but, equally, there are force and search powers, in and clause 204, that also relate
to those limitations on human rights. That worries us because we all know that any limitation on
human rights should be in primary legislation. Wouldn’t it be better to lift and drop both of those
elements into the bill? The sunsetting of seclusion as well as the limitations on people through force
and search powers—once again, it is feeling like bad law making to be relegating that to regulation.
I agree seclusion could be done through that, which is less problematic, but if we’re going to do that,
we should have everything in primarily legislation, so we avoid the issues caused by clause 204.

something we absolutely welcome. The reason that we’re given also for the non-ending of seclusion
is that other restrictive practices that could be harmful, as harmful, or even more harmful to adults
will occur as a result. Now, the Minister can’t have it both ways. If that is the logic relating to adults,
surely that is the logic relating to young people—many of whom, we have established, are also in
these adult secure mental health facilities. Against the backdrop of what we were discussing in the
committee last night and with Waikari Hospital and the Otago Daily Times story this morning, I
think it’s important, particularly, to hear the Minister’s view about whether there could be an
unintended consequence in the way the bill divides up the rights of under-18-year-olds with adults
as we discussed seclusion.
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health) ( 09:57): There’s a bit in there, so I’ll
step through it. I suppose we are slightly returning to Part 1. If I remind members that one of the
principles in this bill is the principle of the least restrictive practice, the second is that this bill brings
in quite significant safeguards. I’m confident that we are heading in the right direction as a country.
When we came into office, seclusion rates had significantly increased, and the data shows that they
have now significantly reduced. So we are on a direction as a country.
As previously said, I’m confident that we’ve got the right regulatory framework to ensure that we
continue that direction as we work with the mental health system. I’m acutely aware, as that member
is, there is actually a wide-ranging number of views within the existing workforce, and other
advocates within the system, that I think we need to bring along in that journey as well.
There is a concern by some of the workforce around the risk of removing seclusion, and I think that
does need to be acknowledged; and others, as was well-canvassed during the select committee
stage, are concerned about the unintended consequences of seeing a reduction in seclusion but,
actually, then seeing an increase in chemical and physical restraint as well.
There was a question about why we are confident we can remove seclusion or prohibit seclusion in
under-18s but not apply the same measure in over-18s. Well, the advice around under-18s is that it
is a very small number of young people that are secluded. I’ve just got the number here: 32 young
people across all inpatient services in 2023-24, compared to 561 adults.
The point I’d make there is that it’s very emblematic of past Governments that think they can put an
end date somewhere and it will just happen. I think what we’ve shown around the reduction and the
prohibition of seclusion for young people in this bill is that if we take a targeted approach, we can
continue to reduce the numbers. That’s why the regulatory framework allows for that and also New
Zealand’s first seclusion plan.

Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health) ( 12:16): I present a legislative

Third Reading
Hon MATT DOOCEY (Minister for Mental Health) ( 12:16): I move, That the Mental
Health Bill be now read a third time.
It is a privilege to stand here as New Zealand’s first mental health Minister, today, at the final stage
of this bill. This legislation represents a significant step forward, modernising a system that is more
than 30 years old, and bringing it up to date with how we expect mental health care to be to be
delivered in this country.
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Page 568 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026
The bill sits within the Government’s broader commitment to improve the effectiveness of mental
health and addiction services. It responds to long-standing calls for reform, and contributes to the
Government’s response to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and
in the Care of Faith-based Institutions, ensuring our system is grounded in human rights, safety, and
effective care. It also builds on the work already under way to strengthen our mental health system:
improving access, growing the workforce, and strengthening crisis support by helping ensure people
receive effective recovery-focused care when they need it.
At its core, this bill shifts us towards a more right space and recovery-focused approach, placing
people at the centre of their care and supporting them to make decisions about their own support
and recovery wherever possible. It provides a modern legislative framework for when compulsory
care is needed as a last resort, while protecting the rights of people under compulsory care and
ensuring care is therapeutic, delivered in the least restrictive way, and responsive to individual needs.
I want to acknowledge two areas where the bill introduces particularly important changes. First, on
seclusion, the bill takes a much stronger approach to reducing, and, over time, eliminating the use
of seclusion. It prohibits its use for children and young people, and strengthens safeguards and
oversight to drive its reduction across the system as we work collectively towards eliminating this
practice.
Second, on the use of electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT, I want to be clear that while ECT remains
an important treatment option for some people, the bill lifts the threshold for its use and puts stronger
safeguards in place to ensure it is only used in tightly controlled circumstances in line with best
practice.
The bill has been the subject of extensive scrutiny by the Health Committee, which received hundreds
of submissions and heard directly from people with lived experience: families, clinicians, advocates,
and community organisations. As I’ve said before, I want to acknowledge those who shared their
experiences. Your input has directly strengthened this legislation.
Through the committee stage, a number of targeted amendments have been made to ensure the
legislation is clear, workable, and provides strong safeguards in practice. These include clarifications
to ensure powers and rights are clear for those working under the legislation, such as clarifying when
police detention powers begin and end, strengthening requirements for recording and oversight, and
refining provisions to ensure they are workable in practice, including those relating to the care of
birthing parents and their newborns.
The changes also ensure that the Ministry of Health can require Health New Zealand to provide the
information needed to support the ministry’s regulatory monitoring and assurance role. These
changes matter and ensure that the intent of the legislation can be delivered effectively on the
ground. Ultimately, this will mean people receive care that is more respectful, more responsive, and
more focused on supporting their recovery. It ensures people can access care when they need it,
while putting stronger protections around how that care is delivered.
While the passing of this bill is a major milestone, I also want to acknowledge the significant amount
of work that lies ahead for the sector to implement these changes. This is why the commencement
date has been updated to ensure the sector has a full two-year lead-in period following enactment.
This reflects feedback from the sector about the need to prepare for these changes and implement
them safely.
This is now a bill that is fit for purpose, well scrutinised, and ready to become law. The process has
had integrity. People have been heard, concerns have been addressed, and the legislation has been
improved as a result. The Mental Health Bill represents a modern, balanced, and more effective
approach to compulsory mental health care in New Zealand. Today marks a significant milestone for
our mental health system.
To close, I want to acknowledge the many people that have contributed to the development of this
legislation, particularly those with lived experience. I want to thank them and their families for helping
to improve the system for others in the future. I commend this bill to the House.

mental health laws when the front page of the Otago Daily Times has shone a light on the

example of why our laws need reforming but also why the legislative safeguards need to be in the

We hear that too often in this House. We have the abuse in State care, the abuse in faith-based care,
the abuse in Wakari. We have this bill before us, which is certainly an improvement on the current
mental health Act, but I know for many tāngata whaiora and people working in the sector, it does not
go far enough, and it really does feel like a missed opportunity for us, given that it is unlikely to come
back before this House, as the Minister has said, for a decade or perhaps 20 or 30 years. The reason
I say that is because we still have the binary definitions of mental health competence in this bill that
fly in the face of best practice internationally, which would suggest that better outcomes are reached
if people are assessed on their competence on a decision-by-decision basis. Mental competence is
a fluctuating experience. It is not a state or a label to be put on to a person. The application of the
law as it will currently happen under this bill doesn’t allow us to get up to speed with that international
thinking.
The other element is around the participation of tāngata whaiora. A lot of noise has been made in
the House about their increased participation, and, indeed, there are some avenues now for them to
have more of a voice. But if we were really going to look at the evidence and take an evidence-based
approach, I think it ’s worth putting on the record that the Health Committee saw no evidence that
compulsory care orders work for the 6,000 people in our communities who currently live under them,
and yet there is good evidence from other jurisdictions and studies conducted by people in New
Zealand to show that those who participate voluntarily in their own mental health journey are far more
likely to achieve states of wellbeing and to be in recovery. If we really wanted to make this a mental
health bill, we missed the opportunity to think through how we could reduce the number of people on
compulsory care orders and how we could skill up the sector and resource the sector to really be
able to walk alongside our tāngata whaiora and their families to enable wellbeing.
Instead, what we are often seeing is people cycling in and out of the system—feeling well enough to
be out in the community, sometimes well enough to work; an event happens or a crisis point is
reached, for whatever reason, in their mental health, and they ’re back into the hospital system and
back under the Act. We need to be more aspirational than that. We need to be looking at the evidence
that tells us how people can achieve recovery longer. I fear that in looking and focusing our efforts
on the compulsion elements of this bill, we missed the opportunity to look at recovery through
participation.

items.text: Thank you. It’s good to take a call on the third reading
of the Mental Health Bill. It was really interesting to hear through the committee of the whole House
process the questions raised and the answers from the Minister for Mental Health. I wanted to speak

The first one I wanted to mention was clause 42 on the decision making for compulsory care. There

was made by medically qualified professionals, and I really wanted to emphasise the importance of
having qualified professionals in this space dealing with some—sorry, “dealing” is not a good word;
supporting—of our most vulnerable people in New Zealand.
Last night, when I took a call on this bill, I spoke about my brother-in-law Nicky, who passed away
11 years ago while he was in compulsory care. The coroner found that Nicky’s death was avoidable
due to a number of mishaps which led to him taking his own life. The reason this is so important to
me is to honour Nicky’s life and our whānau who still deal with that loss every single day; my kids,
who will never meet their uncle. For him, when he was at the compulsory care facility, he left the
facility on unescorted leave, and that was part of what led to him eventually taking his own life. The
key thing there, where things fell apart, was that there weren’t medical professionals in place to

constituent in my electorate of Nelson, and we’re working very closely with the mother of this

Labour’s alternative view, which is outlined in the select committee report and through speeches

strengthened by giving effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi—including explicit recognition of tikanga, hapū
and iwi—by strengthening decision-making processes for people to make supported decisions; by
moving even further towards voluntary participation wherever possible, where the therapeutic
evidence supports this; by improving the treatment of advance mental health directives; by
strengthening protections for disabled people, children, and young people, and other vulnerable
groups; by requiring legislated implementation planning and workforce training; and by strengthening
accountability and public reporting.
In particular, the bill has some changes around seclusion, and we are concerned around the fact that
there’s still retention of seclusion in limited circumstances. We support New Zealand’s commitment
to eliminate seclusion, but, as my colleague Ingrid Leary pointed out in an earlier contribution today,
the Ombudsman continues to make scathing recommendations around the practice of seclusion and

opportunities.
I mentioned the use of electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) earlier, in the beginning of my speech. What
is good is that the bill provides some additional safeguards for adults, including specialist oversight
where statutory authorisation is required. It also provides some additional safeguards for people
under 18, so it may only be used in rare and exceptional circumstances where two independent

advanced mental health directive must also be considered.

Second Reading
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) ( 14:17): I move, That the Constitution
Amendment Bill be now read a second time.
This bill makes a small but important change to the Constitution Act to ensure that the post-election
process is run smoothly. After the election, there’s a small period of time where there are no members
of Parliament, which continues until election results are finalised and the new MPs take up office.
During this time, the Constitution Act provides an exception to the rule that Ministers must always be
an MP, to ensure the caretaker executive Government can continue to act during the post-election
period. This is critical to our constitutional arrangements and the smooth transition of power.
Currently, this exception is limited to 28 days.
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 579
There are a few circumstances where the conclusion of an election will be delayed—for example, an
extreme weather event or a judicial recount. In these cases, the 28-day rule can expire before the
new MPs formally take office, meaning Ministers can no longer hold their ministerial office, which can
result in a constitutionally untenable position of the Governor-General being left without advisers.
This happened in 2023, and while party leaders worked to find a stop-gap solution, I consider a
constitutional setting should have clear and fit for purpose rules. Therefore, this bill removes the 28-
day rule and replaces it with one that does not give rise to the possibility that ministerial tenure will
expire before the post-election period.
The new rule will allow Ministers to continue to hold office until the election writ is returned with the
names of the successful electorate MPs and list MPs who have been declared. It means that if there’s
a delay to the official vote count, incumbent Ministers remain in office until new MPs are appointed.
I want to thank the Justice Committee for all their hard work on this, and I commend this bill to the
House.
