potentially. That’s sort of how things are looking. So I think they’re going to pinch some off National
and ACT, potentially, at this election. So we’ll see, we’ll see. “Minister Arbuckle”, that could be a—
Minister Arbuckle could get sworn in for a few days. There we go.
This is an important bill though, because the continuity of Government is important. It’s important
that the bills are paid. It’s important that if there is some type of emergency like a pandemic, like a
war, that we end up entering into—any of these types of things—that we actually do have a
Government that’s able to provide that stability when a change of Government is happening. We look
forward to the change of Government on 7 November, and Labour commends this bill to the House.
TOM RUTHERFORD (National—Bay of Plenty) ( 14:51): I commend the bill to the House.
GLEN BENNETT (Labour) ( 14:51): Kia ora, Mr Speaker. Thank you for this opportunity. In
reflecting and listening to the contributions this afternoon, I looked at the two pieces of legislation
that are being discussed. One is the Constitution Act of 1986, and the other is the Electoral Act of
1993. Both the pieces of legislation are Acts that predate MMP, which is 30-years-old this year. Was
it 13 October, I think, 1996 was the first MMP election? And so things have changed since then. It is
a different time, and in terms of the process of election night and the process of course of counting
the votes, and then of course the party vote and trying to figure out and understand what the make
up of the new Parliament looks like, it is quite different to what it was in 1986 or what it was in 1993,
when it was a far simpler but, I think, a less diverse political system. Therefore, it is good that we
bring this piece of legislation to the House this afternoon, to look at what we do and if it is fit for
purpose, and we’ll be discussing it in the committee of the whole House stage.
As I was thinking about why we need to do this, one: of course MMP has changed the landscape of
what the Parliament looks like, and how long it takes to form a Government or a coalition
Government. The second part for me was around looking at models around the world and how
different it is. Of course, the Westminster system is very binary, and many of us—well, probably all
of us in this House—might remember the morning after the night before of an election. You get that
phone call from some random number saying, “Hello, congratulations, you’ve been elected. We’ve
just booked a flight for you at 6.30 tomorrow morning. Please be ready to fly to Wellington.” So
suddenly you’re on this flight the next day to Wellington and it’s all sort of a, you know, possum in
the headlights kind of thing.
Whereas, you look at jurisdictions around the world—an example would be the United States, where
they have their elections generally, or depending what cycle it is, but an example is the start of
November. So an election is held for a member of Congress at the start of November, but then they
don’t actually get sworn in. There’s not actually the transition until the start of January of the next
year. So it makes it clearer, and there’s obviously time to make those changes, to put those things
in place. We don’t have that here. It is, as I say, one night you win and then 48 hours later, or less,
you’re actually down here in Parliament preparing to be sworn in and take up your office. What your
area of the office may be.
We look forward to the committee stage and having some good robust discussion, making sure that
this is small and simple and it is the right thing to do. But obviously, as members of the Opposition,
our job is to scrutinise and to ensure that the public feel confident that we have done due process to
make sure that when it comes out the other end, this piece of legislation, when it’s enacted, is
effective and will do what it says on the biscuit tin.
Motion agreed to.
Bill read a second time.

Third Reading
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) ( 15:19): I move, That the Constitution
Amendment Bill be now read a third time.
I want to acknowledge the support across the House for this legislation after a long period of urgency
where Parliament has been very busy for a very extended period of time until late in the evening,
with the support of many people across this building. I want to acknowledge the hard efforts of
everybody across the House and in the various rooms and back rooms and corridors and all over
the place, including security—thank you very much for this extended period, which we’re now coming
to the end of.
This bill, as we’ve just heard, is a simple bill that addresses a little issue that has come up in previous
elections whereby—after we’ve had an election, and we’re waiting for the final results and what’s
called the writ being declared, which has the final results of who are the new MPs in the new
Government or the new Parliament—there is a period of time, after 28 days, where MPs are no
longer MPs. If you can’t be a Minister or if you’re not an MP, we’ve got a problem, and so this
legislation does away with that 28-day rule and has as a trigger point the declaration of the writ. It’s
something that everybody across the Parliament agrees with; it changes our settings, and it is just a
small detail that we decided is worth getting corrected.
It sits within the context of a parliamentary system that has, throughout its history, managed the
transition of power between Governments in our democracy very effectively. This is a small way in
which this Government is fixing the basics when it comes to our democratic system so that we can
build a future together.
CAMILLA BELICH (Labour) ( 15:22): Thank you, Mr Speaker. It’s a pleasure to take a call
on this Constitution Amendment Bill—as the Minister said, the last bill that we’re debating now in this
rather long period of urgency, but an important bill. Any amendments to our constitution are
important. Of course, in New Zealand, we have the Constitution Act, but we also have an unwritten
constitution, so anything that stipulates how our constitutional conventions are to occur is of probably
increased importance, because this bill will form a part of our constitution as it stands, as an unwritten
constitution.
I think any bill that challenges our democracy does deserve scrutiny. I do know that there are checks
and balances in place to ensure that when you have bad faith actors in Government—which hopefully
we never will have—these types of provisions aren’t utilised in a way that would seek to defeat the
purposes of our democracy. I’m sure that will never happen in New Zealand, but certainly when we
are considering these bills, it’s important to scrutinise them and to ensure that those kinds of things
wouldn’t happen.
This bill does do an important thing; it does change the 28-day rule for members of the executive—
so Ministers and MPs, and in fact the Prime Minister, the leader of our country. Instead of that ending
28 days after an election, it ends with the return of the writ. I think a check and balance on that, which
would have been good to hear articulated by the Minister, is that this will only come into effect when
there is an election, because the writ will only be able to be returned when there is an election. We
would hope that this doesn’t impact—and I’m sure that it won’t—the regularity of our elections, and
the good faith, as I mentioned earlier, that we have generally had in New Zealand in relation to the
caretaker provisions when there has been an election to ensure the smooth transition of Government,
and also the utmost respect that the democratic vote is given to determine the executive.
Of course, that’s not as clear-cut as it is in some jurisdictions, because we have an election and then
it’s up to those of us lucky enough to be in a position to earn a seat in this House to try to negotiate

the confidence of the House. That confidence of the House can take a period of time, and that does

time I need to get up during this urgency. I have lost track of how many—I have genuinely lost track.
I hope that members of this House also take comfort in knowing that this is the last time that they
hear my voice for at least two weeks.
We are kind of on the final stretch of this particular urgency by the Government. I do want to
express—because the Minister has sort of opened the scope into just having a broader expression
of thanks to everyone who works in Parliament, as well as all of our officials during this period, for
providing advice and continuously providing services. That includes, obviously, the Chamber
Officers, the Office of the Clerk, those at Copperfield’s, security, officials who have to work very late
into the night, and also translators who are, unfortunately, a very small team who may not have the
same flexibility as some of the others to be able to do things in shifts. Indeed, even MPs have that
flexibility and ability. We do want to thank all of you for this period.
If you’ll indulge me, Mr Speaker, I do want to reiterate the fact that during this urgency period, we
have seen 21 bills being discussed in various forms across 34 stages—which some would some is
an achievement, and some would say, is it really the best use of Parliament time, but also is this the
most democratic? But, you know what, if the Government have KPIs they want to tick off, then KPIs
are KPIs.
Just on this bill—as we have mentioned in the second reading—

In terms of the Constitution Amendment Bill here—

items.text: —I do want to say that, with this bill, it is an important change, as
we have discussed both in the second reading but also in the committee stage. I think the first thing
is to highlight that, as we’re discussing this reasonably short five-clause bill and we go through clause
by clause as opposed to part by part, that it is good to hear from the Minister of Justice the
reassurance that, despite the fact that this bill was supposed to come back into the House at end of
last year, that we are seeing that even though after Royal assent that the nature of this bill does lend
itself to be implemented quite quickly. Also, it’s very assuring to hear from the Minister that as well
that the title of this bill will be updated to 2026 to reflect the fact that we’re no longer in 2025.
Once we get into the substance of our clause 4 and 5 of the bill, it is worth noting that the previous
speaker, Camilla Belich, has already mentioned the constitutional importance of this. We would have
liked to see a little bit more engagement from the Minister, in terms of some of the questions and
also some of the context that this could come up. Again, even if you look at the departmental report,
it’s a very short departmental report, and there is not a lot of information in there. So if a constitutional
situation or issue does come up, Hansard then becomes the default of how we are able to have that
clarity from the ministerial statement.
There are a few things that I think it’s important for us to address on some of the conversations that
we did have here. I think the first one is around the 28 days and the important part around the removal
of that—we have discussed the event of force majeure, which, potentially, would affect the way that
elections could be conducted. I do want to correct something I said in the second reading, which is
around, I guess, Government arrangement, which is more to do with election and the return of the
writs. In those cases, the way that the existing legislation in section 6 of the Constitution Act is really
triggered around the day after the 28th day, whereas now it could be actually earlier than that because
it has now opened this ability to be a little bit more flexible. So the clarification that I was trying to
seek from the Minister is around what then happens between when the Electoral Commission
declares and the day after, and how would that interact with this new change.
I think, more importantly, one of the things that I asked the Minister, and this is a genuine concern
was raised by the submitters, was around what kind of decision-making powers would those
caretaker roles and caretaker Ministers would have during this. As we see in the department report,
it just simply says, “Look, Cabinet Manual does address this.” But then, when we asked the Minister
to potentially elucidate some of that, we didn’t actually get a clarification. I did have a look at the
Cabinet Manual on this. This is to do with particularly paragraph 6.31 onwards of the Cabinet
Manual, around some of the expectations for the Ministers during this caretaker process. It’s
important to note that in the earlier section of the Cabinet Manual it does say that the Ministers
have the full power of the Minister—I believe that is around paragraph 6.21, which where it says “the
incumbent government is still the lawful executive authority, with all the powers and responsibilities
that go with executive office.”
I think one of the things that is worth mentioning—I think this is something that my colleague Camilla
Belich alluded to in the committee stage—is while the Ministers do have the executive power, without
a Parliament, without a Speaker, that we may not see potentially bills being introduced as a part of
that caretaker arrangement. I think that’s an important reminder for people and for those who had
concerns on this section, that while they have all of the powers, the ability to make law falls on this
House here, as opposed to the Ministers and the executive. So that interaction between the executive
and the legislature remain. I think that’s an important reminder.
Some of the other things that we did ask as a part of this is how would that list be finalised, and I
think that’s something that, again, this side of the House has asked the Minister around that kind of
clarity during the committee stage. It’s unfortunate that I didn’t get a response from the Minister. I’m
hoping that presumably that means it’s not applicable, which is fine, or potentially outside the scope.
But what would happen if we see—we talked about the fact that other disruptions we see could be a
recount or a judicial review, etc., but what happens in the event of a by-election; would that be
captured under this scenario as well, or is that something that is completely different?

Question No. 2 
LAURA McCLURE (ACT) ( 14:10) to the Associate Minister of Education: What recent 
reports has he seen on school attendance? 
Hon DAVID SEYMOUR (Associate Minister of Education) ( 14:10): A wonderful report, 
from these numbers: since this Government’s been in place, we have been, actually, reporting, every 
day, the number of children that went to school. This stands in stark contrast to earlier times, when 
a Minister of Education was actually hauled before the Privileges Committee for not revealing that 
information, and, in the end, was actually let off on the grounds that the Minister didn’t actually know 
what the facts were. We are now, every day, reporting the number of students that show up. Members 
might be interested to know that, this term—term 2, 2026—so far, on every day bar two, which were

pattern where every term bar one since this Government has been in place, we have had better 
attendance than the term before. This is for a number of reasons, but, more than anything, it is about

AMENDMENTS IN COMMITTEE OF THE WHOLE HOUSE 
SPEAKER ( 15:08): Before we proceed further, I want to raise the issue of amendments in 
committee of the whole House. At present, members are free to lodge as many amendments as they 
wish. Presiding officers rule on whether they are relevant, serious, in the proper form of legislation, 
and on their relationship to previously-agreed positions. 
Recently, we have seen numerous amendments on some bills, which has led to hours of voting. 
Parliament’s time is limited and best spent on debate, rather than voting. We already have a very 
fast party-voting system, but hundreds of amendments take hours to deal with. They place 
considerable pressure on the presiding officers and clerks to check they are in order. I would 
encourage members to produce amendments that propose important amendments that they wish to 
see in legislation. If the House is overwhelmed by amendments, it is likely that we will see some 
Standing Order changes, and I would not like to see undoubted right of members to propose 
amendments curtailed. 
Having said that, committee stages are always going to proceed slowly when substantive 
Government amendments are released on the day that the bill is in committee. Members need time 
to analyse the proposed changes and, when they wish to move amendments, are likely to present 
them clause by clause. They do not have time do anything else.  
I encourage Governments to release amendments as soon as they are drafted. That is likely to lead 
to more constructive engagement in the committee of the whole House process.  
Substantive amendments late in the legislative process, where there is no select committee scrutiny 
of them, is not desirable. It suggests the policy process was not completed before the bill was 
introduced or the select committee was not given sufficient time to consider the bill. To be clear, 
these types of amendments will always lead to longer committee stages as members deal with new 
material they’ve only just seen. 
I occasionally hear members discussing notional time limits for committee stages. That has never 
been a rule or practice of this House. The size and content of a part, the willing engagement of 
Ministers in answering questions, and the factors I’ve mentioned previously determine how much 
time will be spent on a part. 
I encourage all members to take a reasonable approach in committee of the whole House, with a 
view to focusing on the bill and serious amendments to it in a way that gives all members time to 
consider the legislation in front of them.

Hon MARK MITCHELL (Minister of Police) ( 15:18): I move, That the House take note 
of the declarations of inconsistency: Extended Supervision Orders under the Parole Act 
2002 and Public Protection Orders under the Public Safety (Public Protection Orders) Act 
2014. 
We are here to debate the declarations of inconsistency relating to the extended supervision order 
(ESO) and public protection order (PPO), as well as the Justice Committee report on the declarations 
and the Government’s response. 
It is important for us to recognise the critical public safety role that these regimes have. Both PPO 
and ESO are preventative measures designed to manage the risk of reoffending from serious sexual 
or violent offenders when they reside in the community. The orders are put in place once the offender 
finishes a prison sentence or returns from overseas. They are only applied to offenders with a high 
or very high risk of serious reoffending. An ESO can be similar to parole conditions, and ESO can 
restrict where the offender lives or require that they are monitored in person 24/7. A PPO is more 
restrictive; it authorises detention in a secure facility on prison grounds, potentially for life. 
Right now, officials are reviewing the legislation in response to multiple reviews of it, not just the 
Supreme Court’s declarations, but also, in September last year, the Government tabled its response 
to a Law Commission review on ESO and PPO. That review proposed fundamental reform, including 
repeal and replacement of the current measures because they do not capture all the public safety 
risks that these offenders pose and do not fully address rehabilitative and other rights. 
The two declarations that we’re debating here today were also issued by the Supreme Court in 
September last year. In its first declaration, the Supreme Court found that PPOs are inconsistent with 
the freedom from a second penalty for the same crime, which is enshrined in the New Zealand Bill 
of Rights Act. In its second declaration, the Supreme Court found that the parts of an ESO that 
amount to detention, such as restrictions on living conditions, are also inconsistent with the right to 
freedom from a second penalty. 
The court also said that if either orders applied based on offences committed before the orders 
existed—in other words, retrospectively—the inconsistency could never be justified. A declaration of 
inconsistency is a formal statement by the court that an act is inconsistent with the New Zealand Bill 
of Rights Act. It does not affect the validity of an Act. What it does is signal that the court considers 
the Act infringes on fundamental human rights in a way that is not justified in a free and democratic 
society. 
I would like to thank the Justice Committee for its report on the declarations, and members of the 
public who made submissions during the process. The committee recommends repeal and 
replacement of ESOs and PPOs with a single-tiered preventative regime. This was based on the

Colleagues, today is a great day for communities up and down New Zealand. People have had 
enough of the chaos, the fleeing police, illegal street racing, burnouts, disorderly dirt bike gatherings, 
intimidating vehicle convoys, and siren battles. These activities are not harmless thrills. They are 
disruptive, they’re dangerous, and they’re deeply damaging to the sense of safety that people 
deserve in their own neighbourhoods. This bill is about restoring order, restoring confidence, and 
restoring the basic right of people to feel safe in their own streets. Throughout the legislative process, 
the purpose of this bill has remained very clear—to ensure that Police and the courts have the right 
tools and penalties to deter antisocial road use and to protect the public. After select committee 
scrutiny and very robust debate at committee of the whole House, I’m confident that we have a bill 
that does just that. The bill hasn’t materially changed since it was first introduced into the House in 
July 2025. I think that reflects the mandate that there is for these changes both from communities 
and from this House, as well as the well-crafted nature of the legislation, of course. 
None the less , I will celebrate some of the key features one last time. First of all, presumptive 
sentences. At the heart of this bill is the establishment of presumptive sentences of vehicle forfeiture 
or of forfeiture and destruction. This applies to first and subsequent offences of illegal street racing 
or burnouts. This presumptive sentence will also apply to the new offence for individuals participating 
in an intimidating convoy and the extended offence for failing to provide Police with information that 
will help them to identify drivers. Let’s be clear what this means under the new legislation: if anyone 
out there commits any one of these offences, their vehicle will likely be forfeited or crushed. 
In the House, today, we tabled a minor and technical Amendment Paper in advance of the committee 
of the whole House debate to carry over the Police’s existing power to prevent the sale or disposal 
of a motor vehicle following impoundment, and this helps to ensure offenders’ vehicles are forfeited 
or destroyed. Another thing this bill does is it gives Police stronger powers. We are giving Police the 
ability to temporarily close a larger range of areas, notably those areas that are used for antisocial 
road use events and behaviours, such as beaches and car parks. The bill also creates a new $1,000 
infringement fine for anyone who fails to leave a temporarily closed area when directed to by Police. 
These powers will help Police to prevent and manage unruly antisocial road use events, which can 
attract hundreds of participants and bystanders. 
It’s not always safe for police to respond at the time of the event. Much of this dangerous behaviour 
occurs at night, which poses some enforcement challenges for our police. This bill will strengthen 
the existing powers that police have to help them identify a broad range of offenders and will penalise 
vehicle owners who then withhold that identifying information.  
Finally, to the issue of siren battles, and we all know what these are and we all know what we’re 
talking about. This bill will increase the penalty for excessive noise coming from within or on a vehicle 
to $300—no more $50 slaps on the wrist. This is primarily to target and deter what’s known as siren 
battle behaviour, where people compete with each other to make the loudest noise. It reminds me a 
lot of Parliament sometimes, and maybe we need some siren battle prohibitions here in Parliament.  
Submitters and other members of the public have spoken or have written to our offices to remind us 
how distressing this is. It’s distressing due to nights of having no or disrupted sleep because of this 
totally inconsiderate behaviour.

courts maintain discretion as to whether or not offenders are allowed to purchase new vehicles, the 
new offence for participating in an intimidating convoy applies to individual drivers rather than a whole 
convoy, and—let me repeat what has been said many times—this bill does not target car enthusiasts 
or legal car meetings. It targets illegal, antisocial behaviour.

Hon BROOKE VAN VELDEN: Thank you. This bill is about restoring clarity, common sense, 
and focus to New Zealand’s work health and safety system. At its core, this Government has taken 
a straightforward approach. Laws should work in practice, not just in theory. They should support 
safer workplaces without creating unnecessary confusion, duplication, or cost. This bill reflects that 
approach. It maintains the core purpose of the Health and Safety at Work Act, which is preventing

harm, but it improves how the system works on the ground. It sharpens the focus on what matters 
most: reducing deaths, serious injury, and illness. 
Importantly, this is a Government that has listened. We have heard consistent feedback from across 
New Zealand from workers, from small business owners, and from large employers that the system 
has become harder to navigate than it needs to be. Too much effort can go into compliance for its 
own sake, rather than improving actual safety outcomes.  
We have taken that feedback seriously. Through consultation, engagement, and roadshows, we 
have spoken directly with people who live and breathe health and safety every day—not just those 
who advise on it, but those who rely on it to keep their workplaces running and their people safe—
and what we heard was clear: New Zealanders want a system that is practical, proportionate, and 
focused on managing real risk; they want clarity about what is expected of them; and they want to 
be able to focus their time and resources on keeping people safe, not on navigating unnecessary 
complexity. This is exactly what this bill delivers. 
First, it strengthens the system’s focus on critical risk. It makes clear that attention should be directed 
towards the hazards that can kill or seriously injure people or that could cause serious illnesses—
the risks that seriously change lives. By sharpening this focus, businesses can concentrate their 
efforts where it has the greatest impact, and regulators can target their activity more effectively.  
Second, it improves clarity and certainty about what is required. Having clear expectations make it 
easier for both businesses and workers to understand their responsibilities and apply them in day-
to-day settings. This supports better decision-making on the ground and greater confidence about 
what good practice looks like.  
Third, it supports a more proportionate approach across the system. What is appropriate for a large, 
complex operation will not always be appropriate for a small business. This bill recognises that, while 
maintaining the same underlying objective—preventing harm. It ensures that expectations are 
practical and workable in different contexts.  
Fourth, it reduces unnecessary complexity and duplication. By improving how the frameworks fit 
together, businesses can focus on managing risks, rather than navigating overlapping or unclear 
requirements. This makes the system easier to use and more effective in practice. 
Taken together, these changes make the work health and safety system easier to understand, easier 
to apply, and better focused on what matters most. This bill also reflects the priorities of this coalition 
Government. It delivers on a clear commitment in the ACT-National coalition agreement to reform 
health and safety law and regulations, and I’m pleased to have delivered on that commitment.  
We are committed to restoring confidence in New Zealand’s regulatory systems, including the work 
health and safety framework. That means ensuring protections remain strong while also ensuring 
obligations are clear, proportionate, and focused on managing the risks that cause the most harm. 
When systems become overly complex or unclear, that doesn’t help workers, and it doesn’t help 
businesses. It can undermine confidence, create unnecessary cost, and distract from what actually 
keeps people safe. 
This Government is taking a different approach. We are focused on outcomes. We are focused on 
enabling businesses to operate with confidence, to invest, and to create jobs. We are focused on 
ensuring workers have clear, effective protections that are understood and applied in practice. This 
bill strikes that balance. It supports businesses and workers to do the right thing, it provides greater 
certainty about what is expected, and it strengthens a system that is fundamental to the wellbeing of 
New Zealanders. 
Finally, I want to acknowledge the many New Zealanders who have engaged constructively with this 
process. Your feedback has directly informed these changes, and that is what good lawmaking looks 
like. It’s listening, responding, and delivering practical improvements that work in the real world.  
This is a forward-looking reform. It is about making our work health and safety system clearer, more 
effective, and better aligned with the needs of modern workplaces, and, ultimately, it is about keeping 
New Zealanders safe. I commend this bill to the House.

Hon SIMEON BROWN (Minister of Health) ( 23:28): I move, That the Healthy Futures 
(Pae Ora) Amendment Bill be now read a third time. 
It is a privilege to rise for the third reading of the Healthy Futures (Pae Ora) Amendment Bill. This is 
a bill New Zealand’s health system needs to bring clarity to its purpose under this Government. It is 
a key step in delivering the Government’s promise to put patients first and to ensure that every New 
Zealander can access timely, quality healthcare when and where they need it, from a health system 
that is accountable for its results. 
New Zealanders might think this is not a controversial idea. The bill is, after all, only asking the health 
system to do what New Zealanders would reasonably expect it to do. However, when this 
Government came into office, we inherited an under-performing health system, long wait times, 
delayed infrastructure projects, distraction, and a clear lack of accountability in our health system. 
Our Government has been focused on fixing the basics and building the future, and this bill is one 
part of moving from a system focused on processes, bureaucracy, and a system which would have 
simply been restructured during the middle of a pandemic, the very worst time to have thought about 
restructuring a system, to one focused on delivery, clarity, and accountability. 
Before I get into what the bill does, I want to thank the people who have made it possible. I want to 
acknowledge the Health Committee and particularly chair Sam Uffindell for his guidance of the 
committee, and also the many stakeholders, health professionals, and members of the public who 
made submissions on this important topic.

There are a number of key changes that this bill does. It focuses the health system on what should 
be its main purpose: patients receiving timely and quality care. The bill introduces a new statutory 
purpose for the Act to guarantee that all patients have access to effective and timely health services. 
Every decision Health New Zealand makes will now be anchored in this purpose. The bill also repeals 
the health sector principles and charter. New Zealanders do not need a 16-page charter that omits 
the word “patients” but mentions “unions” 11 times. All I can say about that charter is that I hope the 
previous Government did not spend too much money developing it. The Government requires the 
health system to put its efforts into better experiences for patients, shorter wait times for cancer 
treatment, and of course, meeting our elective surgical wait times. More kids being immunised, 
shorter wait times in our emergency departments—that is how to make a difference in our health 
system. 
Of course, when this Government came to office, we had had a previous Government in which its 
first action, when it came to office after the 2017 election, was to remove the health targets, and for 
the following six years, we saw performance in our health system decline. The number of people 
waiting for elective surgery ballooned; the number of children fully immunised, absolutely falling 
down; and of course, the number of Māori children, that went backwards significantly from about 90 
percent down to around 67 percent of two-year-old Māori children. For all of the arguments from the 
other side of the House when it comes to equity and Māori healthcare, they have that responsibility, 
which they need to be remembered for.  
Ultimately, we are seeing improvements against all of our health targets. We’re seeing year-on-year 
improvement after years of decline under the previous Government. This bill helps to reinforce that 
and provide clarity by putting those targets into legislation and removing the lack of accountability, 
the pieces of the documents which were causing confusion and simply duplication, and refocusing 
the health system back on what matters. The health sector principles, for example, had been a recipe 
for confusion, outlining 21 different considerations for every decision maker needing to make a 
decision—21 different considerations that every decision maker at Health New Zealand needed to 
make. Instead, this bill legislates health targets focused on things that matter to patients. The targets 
also include a new target around primary care, which, of course, also substantially went backwards—
access to primary care—under the previous Government.  
The bill says Health New Zealand must deliver services efficiently, and also partner with private 
providers where appropriate to clear backlogs and increase access to services. A clear example of 
what this Government is doing is, when it comes to elective surgeries, partnering with our private 
hospitals to get more patients being seen in a faster manner so we can get through the wait-lists, get 
patients being seen, and actually mean that fewer patients are waiting in pain, and more patients are 
getting the care that they need. As I have said, no one lies on the operating table angsting about 
whether Government funding or private capital paid for the ceiling which they are looking at. They 
want to get fixed, they want to get on with their lives, and that’s what this Government wants for them 
too.  
The bill also strengthens Health New Zealand’s focus on infrastructure, creates a permanent 
infrastructure committee appointed by the Minister so that health facilities are planned and delivered 
on time and within budget. I just saw some pictures from Health New Zealand today with cranes in 
the sky at the new Dunedin in-patients building; cranes in the sky because after six years under the 
previous Government of talk, talk, talk, we’ve signed a contract, we have construction under way, 
and cranes in the sky getting things done. We are building the future of our health infrastructure 
under this Government. Under that Government, all there was talk, talk, and talk.  
This bill strengthens governance and accountability, and accountability will no longer be optional but 
embedded in the legislation. The changes also strengthen the role of the Hauora Māori Advisory

board of Health New Zealand must take into account. That advice will have a national perspective

is not about organisational charts, it’s about making sure that we get the health services that New 
Zealanders need. This Government’s focus on healthcare is clear and straightforward. The 
Government sets the priorities, Health New Zealand delivers the care, patients feel the benefits, the 
public sees the results. This is a Government focused on fixing the basics, which Labour broke, and

Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction) ( 15:34): I present a

Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction) ( 15:35): Thank you, Mr 
Speaker. I move, That the Building Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the 
Transport and Infrastructure Committee to consider the bill. 
Building in New Zealand has become more complex with risk averse practices, limited accountability, 
and slow, costly consenting processes holding the sector back. This bill supports the Government’s 
objective to promote and enable a more efficient and productive building system—one where it is 
more quick and affordable for Kiwis to build. It delivers major systems reform, including a fundamental 
change to liability settings, removing barriers to building consent authority (BCA) consolidation and 
modernising the building research funding system. It also includes two targeted measures: a fast-
track consent pathway for homes with solar generation and other sustainable features, and an 
amendment to support the uptake of offsite buildings for consent-exempt small, stand-alone 
dwellings, popularly known as granny flats.  
A central feature of the bill is the shift for building and construction from joint and several liability, 
which prioritises full recovery of the claimant, to proportionate liability—a fairer system where each 
party can only be held responsible for their contribution to defective building work. Of course, the 
purpose is to prevent work from being defective in the first place.  
The joint and several setting has held back the sector’s performance for decades. It creates an 
imbalance where parties with deeper pockets, such as building consent authorities—typically 
councils, and therefore their ratepayers—can be held responsible for the full cost of defects, even 
where their contribution is relatively minor, at least in some situations, exposing ratepayers to those 
costs and making BCAs disproportionately risk averse. This has slowed building progress across 
New Zealand. 
This is not a new issue. The Law Commission carried out reviews of joint and several in 1998 and 
2014 and the inefficiencies it causes and considered whether it’s the right system for New Zealand. 
This has been raised in the office of various Ministers of building and construction since long before 
my time, yet nothing has changed, and the issues persist. In that sense, it’s been a team effort, and 
I’m glad that we are in the process of being able to bring it to a conclusion together. 
Australian states, by contrast, have been operating proportionate liability models for some 30 years. 
We’ve taken lessons from our counterparts across the Tasman and engaged directly with them as 
well as local stakeholders, of course, and legal experts in the development of the bill. In April 2025, 
I attended a roundtable hosted by the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment. I give a 
particular shout out to Dr Michael Warren. The roundtable brought together leading Australian liability 
experts and key stakeholders from New Zealand’s building, legal, and insurance sectors. Their 
message was loud and clear: it’s time to move from joint and several liability to a proportionate model, 
with appropriate measures in place to protect consumers.

While fairer at a system level, some building owners risk being left out of pocket when building work 
goes wrong and liable parties are absent or insolvent. To mitigate this, and to help protect the so-
called mum and dad homeowners in particular, we are introducing mandatory home warranties for 
most residential building work and higher value renovations. This requirement will also make it harder 
for cowboys to operate—yee-ha. Without a track record of quality and accountability, it will be difficult 
to obtain warranty backing, and that’s a good thing because these measures are about better 
protecting homeowners taking on significant risk.  
We’re also making professional indemnity insurance compulsory for design professionals, such as 
engineers, architects, designers, and surveyors. These changes formalise existing good practice and 
have been welcomed by industry. As a precaution, to avoid disruption in the construction sector, we 
have enabled targeted, temporary suspension of home warranty and insurance requirements should 
this become necessary in the future. It’s not a signal of concern but a forward-looking safeguard 
developed alongside the sector. These requirements can be paused in the event of significant 
disruptions and global market shifts, with home warranties and insurance remaining available on a 
voluntary basis, if that should come to pass, just as they are now. Taken together, these reforms 
rebalance the system, moving to fairer allocation of liability while ensuring that homeowners are 
supported by stronger, more reliable consumer protections. 
Another change introduced by the bill, which is again being welcomed by councils and industry alike, 
is the removal of legislative barriers that have hampered the consolidation and collaboration of 
building consent authorities. When the current framework was introduced in 2004, it was expected 
that smaller building consent authorities would consolidate over time to achieve greater scale, 
resilience, and consistency.  
In practice, though, this has been limited. Some building consent authorities process up to 3,000 
building consents per year, while the smallest handle only a handful.  Many lower-volume building 
consent authorities rely on rates to subsidise their consenting functions. There are also 
inconsistencies in how consenting requirements under the Building Code are interpreted and applied, 
contributing to delays in efficiencies, including across different council borders. The bill enables 
greater flexibility in how building consent functions are delivered. It removes requirements that 
currently constrain how territorial authorities arrange their consenting services, including enabling 
functions to be transferred to another council or a stand-alone BCA, improving competition and giving 
councils more options. 
Alongside these changes, statutory processing times for councils to provide project information 
memoranda, or PIMs, are being reduced from 20 working days to 10 working days. This will support 
more timely delivery of consent-related services by stand-alone BCAs. BCA consolidation is 
voluntary, I emphasise to fellow members of the House; the changes do not force building consent 
authorities to change how they operate, but they remove unnecessary barriers for those that wish to 
do so, supporting a more consistent, efficient, and competitive consenting system. At the same time, 
the bill modernises the way that building research is funded, improving parliamentary oversight and 
accountability and alignment with sector priorities. 
The current Building Research Levy - funded system, established back in 1969, is no longer fit for 
purpose. To better support housing and infrastructure development heading into the future, we need 
to enable greater innovation, promote value for money, and open opportunities beyond the single 
current provider. The bill repeals the Building Research Levy Act and gives the Ministry for Business, 
Innovation and Employment (MBIE) chief executive a new role in funding building research, with 
funding ring-fenced and collected through a single building levy. The research levy has historically 
been paid only to BRANZ, the Building Research Association of New Zealand, which has received 
more than $260 million in levy revenue over the last 12 years. Amalgamating the two levies creates 
a more coherent and streamlined funding framework, improves oversight and accountability, and 
introduces new mechanisms to support contestable funding processes and a clearer link between 
research, investment, and sector needs. A more coherent system and a more coherent Minister for 
Building and Construction would also be helpful, Mr Speaker! 
In addition to the system-level reforms, the bill includes two more targeted changes to support faster, 
more efficient, and sustainable building. It introduces a fast-track building consent pathway for new 
residential buildings with solar generation and sustainable attributes, requiring eligible building

Legislative Statement 
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (16:14): I present a legislative statement on 
the Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill. 
ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh):  That legislative statement is published under the 
authority of the House and can be found on the parliamentary website. 
First Reading 
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (16:15): I move, That the Climate Change 
Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Justice 
Committee to consider the bill. At the appropriate time I intend to move that the bill be reported to 
the House by 30 July 2026 and that the committee have authority to meet at any time while the House 
is sitting (except during oral questions), during any evening on a day on which there has been a 
sitting of the House, on a Friday in a week in which there has been a sitting in the House, and outside 
the Wellington area, despite Standing Orders 193,195, and 196.  
This bill clarifies climate change laws to provide businesses and New Zealanders with certainty 
around their obligations. Ongoing litigation in the High Court, where civil claims have been made, is 
creating uncertainty in business confidence and investment. It risks the development of a new regime 
that runs in parallel and it may contradict the framework that Parliament has already enacted to 
respond to climate change. Ultimately, if there is legal uncertainty, there is less investment over time, 
and that affects us all by making our country less competitive. Therefore, the Government will amend

Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 307 
the Climate Change Response Act 2002 to prevent findings of tort liability for activities that cause or 
contribute to the emissions of greenhouse gas and, through those emissions, may cause or 
contribute to climate change harm.  
A tort is a civil claim brought in private law in situations where the conduct of one person causes 
harm or invades the interests of another person. Tort law has primarily been developed through the 
common law, which arises from decisions made by judges in court, rather than by legislation that has 
developed in Parliament.  
In the Smith v Fonterra case, the defendant is asking the court to develop a regime to control and 
reduce the emissions of six of this country’s largest businesses. This would be potentially contrary 
to the regulatory response set by Parliament under the Climate Change Response Act 2002, which 
sets out our legal framework for New Zealand’s regulatory response to climate change. This 
framework includes a 2050 target for emissions reduction and a regime for setting and meeting 
successive emissions budgets with a view to achieving that target.  
The Government’s view is that greenhouse gas emissions and climate change harm are best 
regulated by Parliament and the executive, who take a whole-of-economy approach that carefully 
considers environmental, economic, and social implications, rather than having that done on a case 
by case basis through litigation in the courts. A statutory bar prevents courts from issuing a certain 
type of finding or considering a particular issue. In this case, the bill will prevent a person or entity 
from being liable in tort law for climate change or harm caused by greenhouse gas emissions. This 
will apply to all activities contributing to greenhouse gas emissions directly and indirectly, regardless 
of when or where they occur.  
However, the bill is targeted and will only affect tort claims relating to climate change damage or 
harm arising from greenhouse gas emissions. It will not affect traditional environmental torts—for 
example, where a factory burning fossil fuels causes harm through odour or ash residue. This may 
still be covered under the tort of nuisance.  
The bill will also apply to the proceedings of Smith v Fonterra. I acknowledge that care is needed 
when deciding whether legislation should apply to existing court proceedings. However, these 
proceedings are still at the procedural stage, and the substantive proceedings have yet to start.  
Currently, there is no tort liability for climate change damage caused by greenhouse gas emissions, 
but this is what Mr Smith is asking to be developed. I therefore consider that the application of the 
bar to existing proceedings that have not been finally determined is necessary. This will ensure that 
there’s no risk of a parallel regulatory regime being developed in future which applies to some of 
emitters and is inconsistent with the Government’s regulatory response. As no rights have yet been 
identified in the existing case, this legislation will not deprive the litigants of the fruit of litigation.  
The bill clarifies the regulatory framework in which we are operating as a country with regard to 
climate change. The bill doesn’t change New Zealand’s climate targets or the approach that the 
Government has taken. Businesses with obligations under the emissions trading scheme will still be 
required to meet them. We have a good regime in the Climate Change Response Act and the 
emissions trading scheme, and we’re seeking to make sure this regime is clearly in place without 
confusion.  
The bill makes it clear that the response to climate change sits squarely with the elected Parliament 
and the executive. The bill clarifies the law to ensure that there is certainty around climate change 
obligations of New Zealand businesses. It also ensures our response to climate change is managed 
by Parliament and the executive at a national level, rather than on a case by case basis through the 
courts. On that basis, I commend this bill to the House.

Legislative Statement 
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (20:56): I present a legislative statement on 
the Crimes Amendment Bill. 
ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Greg O'Connor): That legislative statement is published under the

Second Reading 
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) ( 20:57): I move, That the Crimes 
Amendment Bill be now read a second time. 
One of the core pledges of this Government when we came into office 2½ years ago was to restore 
law and order. That is the work of generations and is certainly the work of all New Zealanders—to fix 
the basics and build a future where people feel safe in their communities. That has been an unerring 
focus of this Government for the last 2½, years, and this bill, the Crimes Amendment Bill, is about 
putting victims at the heart of our justice system, and it strengthens consequences for crime. It builds 
on work that we’ve done bringing back real consequences for crime through changes to the 
Sentencing Act and three strikes, but it also moves its focus to dealing with matters around retail 
crime. 
I want to thank the Justice Committee for its careful consideration of the bill—very hard-working 
committee—and extend my hand across the aisle to work and contributions on the other side. The 
committee received 233 submissions on the bill, and I want to thank all the submitters and the time 
that they put into it. 
So what does it cover? Coward punch—what it does there is it recognises the horrendous nature of 
these so-called coward punches, where people come and attack somebody from behind, with no 
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed 
Tuesday, 30 June 2026 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Page 349 
warning, to the head and can turn a life upside down. The bill targets perpetrators of these attacks 
by adding three coward punch offences to the mandatory sentencing framework of three strikes and 
maximum penalties for coward punches causing grievous bodily harm increasing to eight and 15 
years depending on the intent. The coward punch manslaughter offence defines this category of 
violent offending and responds to the need for greater denunciation. 
The Act will be another tool for police in their response to violent crime. While I’m sympathetic to 
calls for even tougher responses around, say, minimum sentences, that can’t be accommodated 
within the confines of this crimes bill, but it’s something that people can give consideration to over 
time. 
Now, the committee also notes that the Government’s capping of sentence discounts is already 
increasing sentences for coward punch offenders and will make it more likely that fewer of such 
offenders would be eligible for home detention, for example. I’ll continue to monitor the impact of the 
recent sentencing reforms on penalties imposed for coward punch cases. I also intend to put an 
Amendment Paper to better address this issue at the committee stage. 
The second area is around citizen’s arrest. There has been a lot of discussion around that matter. 
We are recognising that we’ve had provisions in place for a long time for things happening at night 
after 9 p.m., but during the day it’s been a different regime. We were concerned about instances, 
particularly in the retail crime sector, of people walking off with trolleys full of food, not paying, people 
seeing that, and undermining public confidence in law and order in our community. We wanted to 
make it clear that people, security workers for example, can grab hold of somebody and hang on to 
them, with very clear instructions that they need to immediately call the police and follow the 
instructions of the police. 
There have been a lot of comments about this, and I just want to make the point, of course, that 
nobody is compelled to do anything. Everybody will make a judgment based on the circumstances 
of the time, and whether they think it’s safe to get involved or not. Businesses can decide whether 
they’ll have protocols around this, or not, but we heard a very strong call, particularly from small, 
family-owned dairies and retailers who wanted to have another tool available to them to deal with 
what continues to be a real problem in the retail crime sector. 
Another one is shoplifting. This bill brings in an infringement regime for shoplifting. At the moment, if 
you steal a small amount of goods from a shop, the only option is to arrest that person and send 
them off to court. That’s quite a high threshold. Our concern was, well, the outcome of that is that a 
lot of people tend to, in practice, get away with it and face no real consequences. An infringement 
regime provides an opportunity for a police officer to bring an instant consequence such as a fine, 
such as a speeding ticket situation, so that there are immediate consequences. It doesn’t replace 
our theft offences, but it’s another tool for police to use. 
Finally, our human trafficking offences are strengthened by this bill. As one submitter noted, these 
reforms are long overdue and warmly welcome. They’ll help close loopholes and better equip law 
enforcement to hold traffickers accountable, and that’s what we’re prepared to do there. As a result 
of consultation with agencies, I intend to take a step further with an Amendment Paper which will 
remove requirements around the Attorney-General’s consent for cross-border trafficking offences. 
Finally, the bill brings in tougher consequences for people who attack first responders, those Kiwis 
who go racing into danger—our prison officers, constables, ambulance staff, firefighters—and with 
intent-to-injure offences added to the mandatory sentencing framework for three strikes. All of these, 
collectively, bring a continuation of this Government’s effort to restore real consequences for crime 
and to push back against the tide of retail crime that we saw when we came into power 2½ years 
ago. We’ve made great progress as a country. People do feel safer in this country, but we’re very 
conscious that there is much, much more to do, and this legislation will continue that effort.

Mr Speaker, colleagues, this bill is yet another step in the evolution of our land transport funding 
system and it meets our changing circumstances and upholds one of the fundamental principles of 
how we fund land transport in New Zealand. That principle is that vehicle users should contribute 
fairly in proportion to the use that they undertake on our roads. Since we centralised our roading 
system in the 1920s—planning came a bit later—this principle has continued to underpin how we 
fund and pay for our roading network. However, the system is now under increasing pressure. As 
our vehicles have become more fuel efficient, and we start to drive more and more electric vehicles, 
the traditional method of collecting revenue from our petrol excise duties and our fuel taxes has 
dropped while our transport investment demands have continued to grow.  
To better support sustainable transport investment, we must ensure that the tools we collect for 
revenue are sustainable, fair, and fit for purpose. To achieve this, the bill advances the Government’s 
revenue action plan by proposing amendments that reform the tolling network and modernising the 
road user charges system. This bill does two key things: it looks at how we toll in a modern day and 
age, and it reforms our road user system. 
First, to tolling. We’ve actually got a long history of tolling in New Zealand. We’ve been doing it for 
over 100 years. The Auckland Harbour Bridge was built by tolls. The Lyttleton Tunnel was built by 
tolls. Tauranga have a few, so there are some people here who are familiar with how they work. 
What tolling does is it helps us to bring forward investment and build the roads and infrastructure that 
New Zealand needs sooner. It means the users who benefit most from new roads contribute most to 
those roads. We currently have toll roads in New Zealand, as I mentioned before, and we now want 
Subject to Revision—Not to be Quoted or Distributed

to progress our roading system plan, so we need to make sure we have the revenue to match those 
ambitions. It is about fixing the basics of our transport system so we can build a future where New 
Zealanders can get around our routing network in a quick and efficient manner.  
The bill does a number of things around tolls. It has gone through the select committee process, and 
I’ll outline a few of the changes that have come through in a moment. It does allow for the tolling of 
existing roads where the users benefit from new roads on the same corridor, so that we can take a 
revenue approach across an entire tolling scheme rather than just on new sections of the road. Road 
users out there should be aware that the requirement for a feasible, untolled, or free route will remain. 
Of course, nothing is free in life. Those so-called free roads are still paid for by our road users. 
However, there will be an untolled alternative to all of our tolled roads. The bill will also enable heavy 
vehicles to be restricted from using unsuitable alternative routes, but only in specified circumstances.  
Finally, we’re also updating the rules to toll concessions to make it easier to partner with the private 
sector to deliver the infrastructure we need. Taken together, these changes will ensure tolling is a 
more effective tool to help fund new roads, including our roads of national significance, those that 
deliver the infrastructure that New Zealand needs.  
The second key thing this bill does is it looks at the road user charge system that we deal with in our 
modern day State, and it recognises that some changes are needed to be made. We need to 
modernise the system. We need to keep the system fair. We must ensure it’s ready to go for a shift 
in the future of all light-petrol vehicles onto the road user charge system. Our current system was 
designed in the 1970s. It is admittedly a bit clunky. It’s a manual process that relies on us to monitor 
our own odometers, pre-purchase road-user charges (RUC) in thousand kilometre blocks, and 
display teeny tiny little paper licences on our windows.  
I’ve already said many times in this House how annoying those little bits of paper are, particularly 
when they fall down the dash, and a zealous parking officer comes along and gives you a nice wee 
donation to make to the local council or to the local NZTA because you haven’t put the right sticker 
in the right place. This bill does away with those stickers around road user charges. It removes the 
requirement to display, carry, or produce a RUC licence. In an electronic age, a paper licence should 
not be a strict requirement where people are paying bills, not to put paper in the front of the 
windscreens. The bill updates the definition of an electronic distance recorder to address some 
current restrictions and allow for more flexible, cost-effective approaches to recording distance. 
In a bold modern move, it allows us to have more flexible regular payment systems, so that, instead 
of that thrill we get when we’re driving along the road and we realise we might be running out of road 
user charges soon, and we’d better pull over to the side of the road, jump on the NZTA website, and 
buy another thousand blocks to get us around the countryside a bit more, we’re going to be able to 
create some new options for some more regular payments to make it a little bit easier to deal with 
that. Yes, we will no longer get that thrill of driving and seeing the odometer tick over and wonder 
when that next thousand block will kick in. But maybe—just maybe—it might make it more helpful 
and easy for us to run our lives as we’re going around the countryside.  
We are also aiming to change the road user charge retail landscape in general. We’re going to make 
it easier for other providers to help manage the road user charge system, particularly as we move to 
a system where all petrol vehicles will be on it at some point. Of course, that makes sense, because 
as our fuel efficiency increases in our petrol vehicles, we’re going to be using less fuel on the road. 
That is good, obviously, for our emissions, but it does impact our revenue streams. We’ve got to 
make sure that those vehicles still have an impact on the road. We’ve still got to make sure they still 
contribute to the impact on the road that they make, and we’ll be doing that in the future through road 
user charges rather than fuel tax.

Legislative Statement

I’d like to start this contribution by thanking all of those involved in getting this bill to the second 
reading. To the members of the Finance and Expenditure Committee for their careful consideration 
of this bill, to the members of the public who took the time to provide both oral and written 
submissions: thank you to you all. Your input has helped to strengthen and improve this bill and it is 
greatly appreciated. 
The rationale for this bill is as follows: we need to increase the effectiveness of the Infrastructure 
Funding and Financing Act. That is a key component of pillar two of the Government’s Going for 
Housing Growth programme, which is focused on making improvements to infrastructure funding—
you might say fixing our infrastructure funding network—and making improvements to the financing 
tools to help get more housing and the future of New Zealand’s housing built. 
Under the status quo, councils and developers do face significant challenges to fund and finance the 
enabling infrastructure for housing. This Government and hopefully this House wants to move to a 
future state where funding and financing tools will enable a responsive supply of infrastructure where 
it is commercially viable to build new houses. This will shift market expectations of future scarcity, 
bring down the cost of land for new housing, and improve incentives to develop land sooner instead 
of holding it for land banking. This is a necessary step to help fix our housing crisis. 
First, some background. The Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act was first established in 2020 
as an alternative means to fund and finance infrastructure needed to support urban growth. It was a 
good idea and it had good intentions. However, the Act has fallen short of delivering additional 
infrastructure needed to respond to growth. To date, only three levies have been authorised. So this 
bill has the purpose of removing unnecessary barriers to using the Act to improve its viability for a 
range of infrastructure projects and to make the levy development and approvals process simpler 
and more streamlined. 
The bill makes changes to streamline that levy approvals process. Currently, there’s an extensive 
process required for applicants to have a levy approved, and that can be a barrier when trying to use 
the Act. This bill will streamline the process and improve certainty for developers by simplifying 
requirements for levy proposals and recommendation reports, simplifying the mandatory 
considerations that the Minister of Housing must take into account when assessing the levy and 
improving certainty for developer-led proposals.

The bill also broadens the scope of the Act to improve its flexibility and viability for a range of 
infrastructure projects. This will better reflect the developer-led use of the tool and enable the Act to 
be used for transport projects delivered by agencies—for example, the New Zealand Transport 
Agency and KiwiRail—as part of a funding stack for transport infrastructure investment where it 
benefits property owners. 
The bill also makes changes to enable the Act to be used for water infrastructure investments 
delivered by new water organisations established through the Local Government (Water Services) 
Act 2025 and allows for those water organisations to act as the responsible levy authority. In addition, 
the bill replaces the definition of community infrastructure so it is not required to be owned or 
controlled by a territorial authority. This broadens the potential use of the Act to therefore include 
community infrastructure that is owned or controlled by a third party, rather than that vested in a 
territorial authority. There are a number of other changes that the bill makes that are very, very 
important, but they are the key ones outlined so far. 
In December last year, the bill was referred to the Finance and Expenditure Committee, so it’s been 
a while to get to this stage, and we’re hoping that it’ll progress with pace tonight. The bill received 
submissions from 60 interested groups and individuals and the select committee heard oral evidence 
from six submitters at hearings in Wellington and some via video conference. The select committee 
examined the bill and recommended that it be passed with amendments to a number of clauses, 
which the Government supports in full. 
To strengthen consideration of affordability, the select committee proposed a change so that when 
the relevant Minister is assessing the affordability of a levy, they will also need to consider the 
cumulative affordability of the levy when combined with existing levies, rates, and water services 
charges. That’s sensible change, and I’m glad the select committee offered it forward. 
In respond to feedback from iwi and Māori, an amendment is proposed to require levy proposals to 
include details of any consultation undertaken, including with affected landowners, iwi, or hapū. This 
will enable the recommender—that’s the person who assesses levy proposals and writes the 
recommendation report—and the responsible Minister to consider any consultation that has 
occurred, including any impacts for Māori raised during consultation as part of overall decision-
making on the levy proposal. 
An additional safeguard has also been added to the accelerated recovery mechanism to require a 
special-purpose vehicle to seek a court judgment for Infrastructure Funding and Financing Act (IFF 
Act) funding and financing costs before the special-purpose vehicle may apply to the registrar for the 
sale of undeveloped land. This new step would introduce an independent assessment of the amount 
of IFF Act funding and financing costs the special-purpose vehicle has determined needs to be 
repaid, and ensures that there is a judgment issued before sale proceedings may be commenced. 
A number of further technical amendments have also been proposed by the committee to improve 
the workability of the bill, and, of course, we all agree with them wholeheartedly and look forward to 
their passage and acceptance in the second reading. 
In conclusion, the changes in the bill and the bill itself will make the Act far more viable and flexible 
so that councils, developers, and other infrastructure providers can get on with fixing the basics of 
our housing crisis and building the infrastructure that our growing communities need. I commend it 
to the House.

important time. This Government believes that every child deserves the best-possible start in life. 
That start does not begin weeks or months after birth; it begins immediately, in those first precious 
days, when mothers are recovering from childbirth and families are learning to care for a newborn 
together. This bill responds directly to what women and families have told us about their post-natal 
experiences. They’ve told us that greater certainty and support in the early days following childbirth 
is needed. We know that quality early post-natal care can shape positive long-term outcomes well 
beyond the hospital stay. 
It is for these reasons that this Government is proud to back this bill with significant new funding 
delivered in Budget 2026. We are committed to ensuring that this legislation is matched with the 
investment needed to deliver it. This new funding of $34.4 million over four years increases maternity 
system capacity so mothers can confidently choose up to three days of in-patient post-natal stay 
knowing it will be supported by the beds and the workforce required to do this safely. 
First-time mothers will be the first to benefit. Starting immediately, up to 2,000 new mothers per year 
will be able to access a three-day post-natal stay within the first two years, utilising existing capacity. 
As access is expanded to all mothers after three years, we anticipate that up to 18,000 mothers per 
year will be able to access a 3-day post-natal stay. 
I want to acknowledge the original sponsor of this legislation. How good, Catherine Wedd. This bill 
began its life as a member’s bill grounded in a genuine concern for the post-natal experiences of 
women and families. This Government made the decision to adopt the bill because we agreed with 
the fundamental importance of guaranteeing three days of in-patient post-natal care for all women if

widespread support for the intent of the bill and for the principle that post-natal care should be a

the post-natal period is for families across this country. 
Taking this bill forward with the support of my colleague the Hon Casey Costello also delivers on a 
clear commitment in the National - New Zealand First coalition agreement to strengthen maternity 
services and post-natal support for women. Crucially, it’s a practical and compassionate step that

The bill established a clear entitlement that women can access three days of in-patient post-natal 
care if they choose, rather than leaving that decision uncertain or inconsistently applied. In doing so, 
it supports better outcomes for mothers and babies and reinforces that post-natal care is a valued 
and essential part of that maternity journey. 
It does not mandate that women stay in in-patient care for three days. Many women will continue to 
choose to return home earlier, supported by community-based services and their families, just as 
they do now. What this bill does is ensure that women who would benefit from staying longer have 
that option available to them without ambiguity or inconsistency. 
For some families, particularly first-time parents, the early post-natal period can feel overwhelming. 
There is a great deal to learn in a very short space of time. Having the option of additional support, 
monitoring, and reassurance within an in-patient setting can make a meaningful difference to 
confidence and wellbeing. Some women have told us they would have welcomed more time in in-
patient care—more time to recover physically, more time to establish breastfeeding, more time to 
receive advice, and reassurance before returning home. Others have reported leaving hospital within 
48 hours, even though they did not feel ready because they were unsure whether staying longer was 
an option. This uncertainty adds pressure at a time when families already have a great deal to 
manage. The bill removes the uncertainty and replaces it with clarity and confidence. This bill 
respects that different families will make different choices about what is right for them, and it ensures 
the system is better equipped to support those choices. 
This legislation is not the only change. The Government has a broader programme of work to 
strengthen the maternity system and ensure it can deliver high-quality post-natal care in a 
sustainable way. Health New Zealand is already taking action to build and support the maternity 
workforce needed to deliver the strengthened post-natal care set out in this bill. This includes targeted 
recruitment initiatives, including international recruitment where appropriate, as well as return-to-
practice support to help experienced midwives and clinicians re-enter the workforce safely and 
confidently. 
I also understand that retention matters just as much as recruitment, particularly in districts facing 
ongoing workforce pressures. Supporting and retaining skilled staff is essential to maintaining safe 
services, continuity of care, and good outcomes for mothers and babies. That is why I’m focused on 
backing the maternity workforce and ensuring they’re supported to do their jobs well. 
The community sector will have an important part to play in the implementation of this bill. Primary 
maternity units run by both the public and community providers, including the private sector, will 
expand the range of in-patient post-natal care options available to mothers, including care that is 
closer to home. Mothers may remain in hospital, where hospital level care is required, or transfer to 
a primary maternity unit once that level of care is no longer needed, depending on their preferences 
and clinical need. Having a broader range of options, both public and private, reduces pressure on 
hospital facilities while continuing to deliver safe and appropriate post-natal care to woman and 
babies. 
Taken together, this work underpins the delivery of this bill and will support its long-term success. It 
reflects my commitment to ensuring women and their babies receive safe, timely, and appropriate 
care when they need it. I want to acknowledge the midwives and other health professionals who care 
for women and babies every day. Their experience and advice has been central to shaping the 
approach set out in this bill. They understand better than anyone the importance of post-natal support 
and the need for careful, well planned implementation. I thank them for their professionalism, 
dedication, and ongoing commitment to high-quality care. In closing, this bill delivers three important 
outcomes: it provides greater certainty for women and families about post-natal care; it supports 
choice at a critical moment in family life; and it strengthens our maternity system in a practical and 
responsible way. I commend this bill to the House.

Legislative Statement 
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts) (10:54): I present a legislative statement on the 
Community Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill. 
ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Maureen Pugh):  That legislative statement is published under the 
authority of the House and can be found on the Parliament website. 
First Reading 
Hon NICOLE McKEE (Minister for Courts) ( 10:55): I move, That the Community 
Magistrates Legislation Amendment Bill be now read a first time. I nominate the Justice 
Committee to consider the bill. 
Too many New Zealanders are spending too long caught in the court system. For victims, delays 
mean waiting a year or more for a case to be resolved. For witnesses, it means uncertainty and 
repeated disruption. For defendants, it means cases hanging over their lives. For families, employers,
