Page 404 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026 
and communities, it means the justice system is not working as quickly as it should. Timely justice 
matters, because justice delayed is justice denied. 
This Government is focused on practical changes that make the courts work better. This bill is a 
practical reform that improves access to justice, reduces delays, and makes better use of the 
resources that we already have. This bill expands the role of community magistrates so that they can 
deal with more straightforward matters from start to finish. It will reduce unnecessary adjournments, 
free up District Court judges to focus on more serious and complex cases, and will improve the 
public’s confidence that the justice system can deliver. 
Community magistrates are not new. The role was introduced in the late 1990s to increase judicial 
capacity to take pressure off the District Court judges. They were intended to deal with lower-level 
criminal matters, represent the communities that they serve, and help the courts to operates more 
efficiently. Community magistrates generally sit part time. They preside over certain lower-level 
matters in the District Court’s criminal jurisdiction. They are not required to hold a legal qualification, 
although many of them do. They bring practical experience, judgment, and community knowledge to 
the court system. 
But at the moment, they are not being used to their full potential. Too often, if a case reaches a point 
where a decision is needed outside of a community magistrate’s jurisdiction, it has to be adjourned 
and transferred to a judge. That means another court event, another delay, another day off work, 
another round of uncertainty for victims and other court users. It also means some cases are never 
scheduled before a community magistrate in the first place, because everyone knows that they might 
have to be transferred again later on. That’s not efficient, nor is it fair on court users, and it certainly 
is not the best use of judicial time and resource. 
This bill changes that. It will enable community magistrates to take guilty pleas for all cases except 
those tried in the High Court—that means murder, manslaughter—to preside over trials and 
determine guilt for offences with a maximum penalty of a fine, community-based sentence, or up to 
three months imprisonment; to order pre-sentencing reports for offences being referred to a District 
Court judge for sentencing; to make a greater range of bail decisions, where the defendant has 
pleaded guilty before a community magistrate; and make a greater range of administrative decisions, 
including transferring proceedings from one District Court to another and hearing unopposed limited 
driver licence applications. 
These are sensible, practical changes. They do not ask community magistrates to replace judges; 
they allow community magistrates to do more of the work that they were created to do so that judges 
can spend more time on cases that genuinely require a judge. It is expected that these changes will 
free up a net 5.2 District Court judge full-time equivalents. Put simply, this bill is, effectively, five 
judges for the price of none. This is good value for taxpayers, good for court timeliness, and good for 
victims who have waited too long for justice. The benefits will be felt across the justice system. When 
cases move faster victims get answers sooner. Witnesses are not left waiting indefinitely.  
Defendants are not held in limbo longer than necessary. Remand pressure can reduce as cases 
progress more quickly. Judges can focus on the work only they are able to do.  
Expanding the role of community magistrates is sensible, but it must be done carefully. The public 
needs confidence that the cases will continue to be dealt with appropriately and consistently. This 
bill does not change the sentencing jurisdiction of community magistrates. Community magistrates 
will still not be able to impose imprisonment or home detention. Where a community magistrate 
considers that either of those sentences may be appropriate, the case must be transferred to a 
District Court judge, and that is an important safeguard. 
The bill also supports stronger leadership and oversight of community magistrates. Judge Moses

Legislative Statement 
Hon SCOTT SIMPSON (Minister of Statistics) (11:24): on behalf of the Minister for the 
Environment: I present a legislative statement on the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill. 
ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono): That legislative statement is published under the

First Reading 
Hon SCOTT SIMPSON (Minister of Statistics) (11:24): on behalf of the Minister for the 
Environment: I move, That the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill be now read a 
first time. I nominate the Environment Committee to consider the bill. 
New Zealand is undertaking significant transformations regarding how we protect, conserve, and 
restore our natural environment, how we sustainably use our resources, and how we mitigate and 
adapt to climate change. However, to understand the impacts that our activities have on the 
environment and to respond accordingly, we need a comprehensive, reliable, consistent data and 
information base. 
In 2015, the Environmental Reporting Act was enacted to do exactly that : to establish a trusted, 
reliable, and independent environmental reporting regime. Since then, we have completed four 
cycles of environmental reports. The Act has made significant improvements to the previously ad 
hoc way New Zealand reported on the environment; however, we need to extend its functionality and 
flexibility so that trustworthy data and information is at the heart of decision making. 
In 2019, the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment released a report raising concerns 
about gaps and inconsistencies in environmental data. The commissioner noted a reliance on 
passively harvested data and information collected under other pieces of legislation and a lack of a 
coordinated environmental monitoring and reporting system. The high frequency of report production 
placed the Ministry for the Environment and Stats NZ on a never-ending treadmill of report-making. 
These often recycle old, patchy, and inconsistent data collected using a myriad of disparate 
monitoring practices. We have a significant opportunity now to address the Parliamentary 
Commissioner’s concerns, so in this piece of legislation a number of changes are being put forward. 
The Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill before the House represents a commitment by the 
Government to quality environmental data and information. The bill will refocus reporting content and 
time frames. It aligns roles and responsibilities, and a more active collection of environmental data 
and knowledge. The bill ensures improvements to environmental reporting are safeguarded for the 
future. These include making data available to the public and decision makers when it is ready, rather 
than when a report is merely published. It also means expanding the reporting and setting up an 
interim strategic, in-evidence panel. 
The bill will require the Secretary for the Environment to publish a State of the Environment report 
every six years, independent from political interference. This will achieve a more appropriate balance 
between reporting timeliness and the rates of change in our environment. The bill stipulates that the 
first State of the Environment report must be published in 2031.

Page 410 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026 
The Pressure-State-Impact framework embedded into the Environmental Reporting Act has been 
expanded to include drivers and outlooks. Drivers describe the long-term social, demographic, 
economic, and environmental factors that cause pressure on the environment. Outlooks describe 
how the environment may change in the future based on projections and trends. Their ongoing 
inclusion will render a more complete picture and bring New Zealand more in line with international 
best practice. 
The report must continue to describe changes to the state of the environment over time and how it 
measures against national and international standards. In addition, they can now report on progress 
towards Government priorities and limits, goals, and policy outcomes set in other legislation. This 
could include, for example, reporting on limits as proposed in the Natural Environment Bill and any 
measures set as part of the climate adaptation system, including managing the risk from natural 
hazards. 
Between the six-yearly State of the Environment reports, a commentary report must be published 
at least once every 12 months. One of the foundational objectives of the bill is to ensure reporting 
flexibility. Commentaries report on an issue or topic that sits across one or more of the five 
environmental domains. The five domains of air, land, fresh water, marine, and atmosphere and 
climate will remain. All must be reported on at least once in the commentary reports between the 
State of the Environment reports. However, the amendments recognise that commentary reports 
may cut across different domains. This change allows for more flexible reporting, which better 
addresses the urgent needs we face. 
The bill introduces a new requirement for the Secretary for the Environment. In consultation with the 
Government Statistician, the secretary will produce a priorities report within six months of every State 
of the Environment report. The report will discuss environmental data, monitoring, and research. It 
will also list recommended indicators and priority areas for improving data and evidence. 
Several technical advisory groups have provided expert advice on the preparation of synthesis and 
domain reports over the years. This bill will, however, amend the Environmental Reporting Act to 
require the Secretary for the Environment, in consultation with the Minister for the Environment, to 
appoint a strategic evidence panel. The panel will provide independent advice to the Secretary for 
the Environment on matters related to environmental data monitoring and reporting. The bill also 
clarifies the roles of the Secretary for the Environment and the Government Statistician. The bill 
proposes clear roles and also stipulates where consultation between the two organisations is 
required, such as setting environmental indicators or producing data and evidence priority reports. 
Finally, to bring together all the proposals and drive a cohesive, robust and fit-for-purpose reporting 
system, the purpose statement has been extended. The current purpose statement simply stipulates 
that the purpose of the Act is to produce national environmental reports. This has been clarified to 
align with the underlying policy to inform New Zealanders on the state of the environment and to 
support evidence-based decisions. This bill responds directly to a review of New Zealand’s national 
reporting regime. It improves efficiency of our reporting regime, making useful improvements to the 
frequency of reports, and does so without compromising their timeliness, impact, or independence. 
Therefore, I commend the Environmental Reporting Amendment Bill to the House.

Legislative Statement 
Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction) ( 11:56): Thank you, sir. I 
present a legislative statement on the Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill.

Hon CHRIS PENK (Minister for Building and Construction) ( 11:56): I move, That the 
Building (Earthquake-prone Buildings) Amendment Bill be now read a second time. 
The Transport and Infrastructure Committee has considered the bill and recommends that it be 
passed with amendments. I’m grateful to the people and organisations who made a submission on 
the bill and of course to the select committee itself, who took the time to hear those submitters and 
to consider improvements on the bill. Following the Canterbury earthquakes and royal commission 
of inquiry, the current earthquake-prone buildings regime was introduced. 
I just want to take a moment to acknowledge, as I’m sure all in this House would, the considerable 
tragedy, the loss of human life, that was entailed by those tragic events. And I don’t wish to bring you 
into the debate, Mr Speaker, but I will acknowledge that you more than most were familiar with the 
nature of the tragedy, and of course I commend and salute you for your work following that, of course, 
to bring that beloved region of yours back to more normal circumstances. 
All that said, of course, I think it’s fairly acknowledged that the introduced legislation at that time—
albeit, of course, in good faith and balancing all the relevant considerations—has not worked entirely 
as intended. It has inadvertently imposed large costs on building owners and communities, including 
throughout New Zealand, without focusing enough on the buildings that present the greatest risk to 
people’s lives. 
This cannot continue, and so, even with the recent earthquakes in Venezuela providing a salutary 
reminder that we do need to prepare further for such events in New Zealand, nevertheless, we have 
decided that it is important to reform the earthquake-prone building regime to target or refocus on 
those buildings most likely to cause fatalities in an earthquake.  
The changes will remove barriers to strengthening high-risk buildings, making retrofits more 
affordable for their owners and better protecting people in and around them. Focusing effort and 
investment on the highest-risk buildings will ultimately save more lives than the current one-size-fits-
all approach. 
Today I will briefly reiterate the bill’s key elements and summarise the key changes recommended 
by the select committee. As I say, we have decided to accept those changes. 
First, the bill narrows the systems scope so that it targets only high-risk buildings in medium and 
high-risk seismic zones. It introduces tiered remediation requirements, amends the definition of 
priority building, and provides greater flexibility through deadline extensions and lower-cost pathways 
for alterations and change of use. 
Only two types of buildings will remain designated as earthquake-prone buildings (EPBs): 
unreinforced masonry buildings and tall heavy material buildings. These are the buildings most likely 
to cause harm in an earthquake, and these will be only those located in medium- or high-risk seismic

Page 416 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES Tuesday, 30 June 2026 
zones. Territorial authorities must identify and remove other building types from the EPB register in 
the three months from 1 July 2027. 
Meanwhile, buildings in Auckland, Northland, and the Chatham Islands will be out of scope. These 
areas have a scientifically determined lower seismic hazard than other parts of New Zealand. On 
Royal assent, therefore, earthquake-prone buildings in these areas will have that designation 
removed. 
At the same time, other provisions of the bill go through coastal Otago, including Dunedin and 
Oamaru and Stewart Island, will shift from a low to medium seismic zone to reflect the latest scientific 
understanding of seismic hazard in those places. Current earthquake-prone buildings (EPBs) there 
will retain their existing remediation deadlines and territorial authorities will have until 1 July 2032 to 
identify potential EPBs there. 
The bill also narrows the so-called identify at any time pathway for designating buildings as EPBs. 
Too many low-risk buildings have been designated as earthquake-prone using this pathway. So the 
bill, as introduced, narrows the pathway to cover only the post-1976, tall, heavy-material buildings 
that were constructed before 2027. This includes buildings akin to the CTV building in Christchurch. 
For buildings that remain EPBs, territorial authorities will determine their required remediation 
measures in accordance with the updated EPB methodology, issue EPB notices, and keep the EPB 
register up to date. 
The bill narrows the definition of “priority building”. Under the bill, only buildings that could fall on to 
a busy street or block a strategic transport route will qualify. Buildings that were priority simply 
because of their usage, such as hospitals or fire stations, will lose that status. Together, these 
changes provide clearer rules and a stronger focus on the buildings that matter most for public safety. 
The bill also introduces a tiered approach to remediation, replacing the current requirement to 
strengthen all buildings to 34 percent of the new building standard, commonly known as NBS. There 
will be two principal forms of remediation measure. Most unreinforced masonry buildings will need 
to mitigate their risk of facades falling on to people below. Multi-storey concrete buildings and large 
unreinforced masonry buildings will need targeted work to prevent those buildings collapsing. For 
unreinforced masonry buildings then that are one or two storeys high and located outside urban 
centres, no remediation will be required by a set deadline. But, at the same time, I note that owners 
will need to mitigate the risk of façade collapse if they want the building to be taken off the EPB 
register.  
EPB owners will be able to apply to territorial authorities for deadline extensions of up to 15 years, 
even if the original deadline expired before commencement. This will replace the current “up to 10 
year” extension, open only to heritage EPB owners. 
The bill also supports lower-cost compliance pathways for owners carrying out seismic work or 
changing the use of a building. If the work only involves seismic remediation, no fire or accessibility 
upgrades will be required. Similarly, if an owner wants to change an EPB’s use, it would only need 
to meet its remediation requirement, rather than anything higher. Together, these changes provide 
more practical and cost-effective solutions, more time to comply, and fewer barriers for owners 
committed to making their buildings safer. 
The Transport and Infrastructure Committee has unanimously recommended amendments to 
address issues identified by submitters, officials, and the select committee itself. I welcome these 
improvements and again place on the record my thanks to the committee for their detailed 
examination of the bill. I note the chair, Mr Andy Foster and I thank him and his colleagues who did 
such a careful and coherent job of understanding and in turn explaining the changes that have 
ultimately been made. 
In response to feedback from submitters, the committee clarified what areas are in “urban centres”, 
which helps to determine the remediation requirement of an unreinforced masonry EPB. For 
example, Wellington and Porirua are urban centres, whereas Featherston and Greytown are not. To 
acknowledge the unique barriers to remediation faced by various buildings, the committee added 
heritage status to the list of matters that territorial authorities must have regard to when determining 
whether or not to grant a deadline extension. Some submitters were concerned that the alternation

provisions may allow for reduced building code compliance. For example, drilling stabilising rods 
through walls can increase the risk of fire spreading in one room to the next. The committee 
introduced a backstop into the bill to ensure that seismic work needs to be done in a way that doesn’t 
increase the risk of fire spreading or reduce disabled peoples’ access. 
The committee also amended the bill so that warning signs must be displayed on all earthquake-
prone buildings, including those that are only recorded on the register or have a seismic work 
exemption. The committee updated the terms for the required remediation measures to façade risk 
mitigation and targeted retrofit. This will ensure that approaches to remediation mitigate risk but do 
not necessarily involve securing a façade or a full retrofit of the building can be used. This bill now 
also includes high-level descriptions of these measures. 
Some submitters were unsure how buildings with unusually tall storeys or part storeys will be 
treated—a fair question. The committee clarified that the thresholds for determining how many 
storeys high an EPB will be will be set out in the EPB methodology. One way that a building can be 
a priority building with half the remediation time frame is if it may impede a strategic transport route 
if it were to collapse during an earthquake. Submitters recommended that territorial authorities be 
allowed to revisit their strategic transport route—again, I think, a very sensible recommendation. The 
committee therefore amended the bill to empower territorial authorities—councils, in other words—
to revise and remove strategic transport routes up to 1 July 2027. No new strategic transport routes 
may be added, ensuring that no building owners will be worse off. 
Last, in my remaining minute, the committee clarified the meaning of a building within scope. This 
makes it clearer which buildings are within scope of the system before the reader then looks to the 
EPB methodology for further technical detail. An unreinforced masonry building must have an 
exterior masonry wall and satisfy other criteria in the methodology to be within scope. A tall, heavy 
material building must have one or more significant elements, such as a roof or a floor, built using 
concrete or other heavy materials and satisfy any other criteria in the EPB methodology.  
Overall, in summary, the bill creates a more focused and workable earthquake-prone buildings 
system by targeting the buildings that present the greatest risk, introducing tiered and more cost-
effective remediation requirements, and reducing barriers to remediation for building owners. For all 
those reasons, I commend this bill to the House.

This amendment bill is an omnibus bill that amends legislation administered by the Ministry of Social 
Development and the New Zealand Defence Force. Specifically, the bill makes a number of minor 
policy and technical changes to the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement Income Act 2001, 
the Social Security Act 2018, and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014, and repeals the Family Benefits 
(Home Ownership) Act 1964. This bill is intended to improve the provision of social welfare benefits. 
The amendments in the bill will update statutory provisions, address regulatory duplication gaps and 
errors, and bring legislation up to date with public expectations. The bill will reduce the chance of 
regulatory failure and unintended consequences that harm the wellbeing of New Zealanders. The 
changes are small and do not warrant stand-alone bills, but together the changes will ensure greater 
effectiveness and efficiency of the social welfare system. 
The first minor policy change is to extend the sustainable employment trial for supported living 
payment recipients from 26 weeks to a maximum period of 104 weeks. The supported living payment 
is a benefit payable to people who are permanently and severely restricted in their capacity to work 
because of a health condition, injury, disability, or because they are totally blind. The purpose of the 
sustainable employment trial is to encourage and support supported living payment recipients who 
want to move into employment or increase their hours of work to establish whether they can sustain 
that employment and cease receiving the benefit.  
Feedback from health and disability stakeholders and international evidence indicates that the fear 
of losing the supported living payment entitlement can be a significant barrier to work and that 26 
weeks is not long enough for some recipients to test their ability to work. Furthermore, increasing 
hours of work incrementally over a longer period better supports people to sustain employment and 
become independent. Extending the sustainable employment trial to two years will therefore improve 
incentives for supported living payment recipients to work as much as they can, leading to a better 
financial position and improved wellbeing outcomes for those who can participate. 
The second policy change is to ensure that residents of the Realm countries of Niue, Cook Islands, 
and Tokelau cannot use social security agreements to meet the residence requirements for New 
Zealand superannuation and veterans’ pension. Social security agreements are bilateral treaties 
between Governments that provide for the reciprocal payment of social security benefits and 
pensions. These agreements are intended to apply to the residence of the two agreement partner 
countries. However, the Ministry of Social Development has advised that a court would likely find 
that some of New Zealand’s social security agreements could apply to people applying for New 
Zealand superannuation or veterans’ pension while resident in the Realm countries. 
Social security agreements are not intended to apply to residents of the Realm countries. Realm 
countries do not have the resources to participate in the cost-sharing aspects of social security 
agreements. Instead, New Zealand superannuation special portability provisions are extended to the 
residents of the Realm. Therefore, the bill will amend the New Zealand Superannuation and 
Retirement Income Act 2001 and the Veterans’ Support Act 2014 to exclude the application of social 
security agreements to Realm country residents. 
The third minor policy change will enable people who are live organ donors to be eligible for an 
emergency benefit payment equivalent to the rate of the supported living payment. Currently, a 
supported living payment recipient who is caring for a person who would otherwise require hospital 
or residential care is not eligible to receive supported living payments should they be recovering from 
surgery for a live organ donation. This is because they are not caring for someone while they are 
recovering from surgery, which is a criterion to receive the supported living payment—caring. 
Instead, they are transferred on to the emergency benefit while they are in their recovery period and 
can only receive the rate of the equivalent main benefit that they would be entitled to, which is either 
the jobseeker support or sole parent support. This anomaly in the supported living payment does not 
align with the Compensation for Live Organ Donors Act 2016, which is designed to remove financial 
deterrents to the donation of organs by live donors. Therefore, the bill will establish explicit legal 
authority to pay emergency benefit to clients at the same rate that they were receiving on the 
supported living payment on the ground of caring for another person for a period of up to 12 weeks 
after the donation. 
As I noted earlier, the bill also contains minor technical amendments. These minor amendments are 
mostly related to the Social Security Act 2018 and the New Zealand Superannuation and Retirement

I am pleased to speak to these bills in the House again today. As I noted in my first reading speech,

high level, these two bills reflect the Government’s commitment to delivering fit for purpose regulation 
and to improving access to justice. They will have a significant impact on the regulatory regimes that 
govern tribunals and occupational regulation, enhancing their effectiveness and efficiency while 
improving consumer protection and the quality of justice legislation. 
The Regulatory Systems (Tribunals) Amendment Bill makes practical improvements to tribunals and 
quasi-judicial bodies. It removes barriers to justice by allowing successful applicants in the disputes 
tribunal to recover their filing fee from the respondent where it is appropriate. It strengthens the 
regulation of the private security industry by providing more effective information-gathering powers 
to investigate breaches. It also streamlines appointments and employment arrangements for tribunal 
members to ensure these bodies operate efficiently.  
The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill strengthens protections for both 
consumers and regulated professionals while reducing unnecessary compliance costs. One 
important change allows conveyancers’ professional undertakings to be enforced in the High Court, 
just as lawyers’ undertakings already are. This promotes competition in the conveyancing market 
and benefits consumers.  
The bill also removes a disproportionately harsh penalty that automatically disqualifies real estate 
agents from practising for five years simply because they failed to complete continuing professional 
development or pay fees on time. That issue has been recognised by the profession for many years, 
and this bill delivers a more proportionate response. At the same time, the bill strengthens the Real 
Estate Authority’s ability to investigate unlicensed trading and ensure licensee’s meet their 
obligations, improving consumer confidence in the industry. 
Both bills have benefited from the select committee process, and I would like to thank the Justice 
Committee and the Education and Workforce Committee for their careful consideration, along with 
everyone who made submissions. Their constructive feedback has resulted in sensible 
improvements.  
The Justice Committee has clarified the role of the Complaints, Investigations and Prosecution Unit 
when dealing with complaints about unlicensed private security operators. The Education and 
Workforce Committee has recommended that the Real Estate Authority’s new powers be exercised 
on a reasonable basis and clarified that provisions relating to unsatisfactory conduct apply only where 
behaviour is connected to a licensee’s professional role and affects public confidence in the 
profession. These are practical improvements that make already sensible bills even stronger. 
I also thank officials and the Parliamentary Counsel Office for their work in developing these bills. 
Whether someone is taking a claim to the Disputes Tribunal, buying a home through a conveyancer, 
or working as a real estate agent, these reforms will make our regulatory systems fairer, more 
efficient, and easier to navigate. They demonstrate this Government’s commitment to good 
regulatory stewardship, maintaining the laws we already have, reducing unnecessary compliance, 
and improving access to justice and ensuring regulations work for the people they are meant to serve. 
I commend these bills to the House.

disproportionate penalties, and making sure our regulatory systems work better for the people who

effective operation of tribunals and quasi-judicial bodies. It allows successful applicants in the

powers. This will help detect and deter people operating outside the rules. It also makes practical 
changes to appointments and employment arrangements for tribunal members so these bodies can 
operate more consistently and efficiently.  
The Regulatory Systems (Occupational Regulation) Amendment Bill improves the occupational 
regulation system for both professionals and consumers. It allows conveyancers’ professional 
undertakings to be enforced in the High Court, as lawyers’ undertakings already are. That will support 
competition in the conveyancing market and give consumers more confidence in the services they 
use.

years for failing to complete continuing professional development or pay fees on time. That kind of 
penalty is out of proportion to the breach. This bill replaces it with a more sensible and balanced 
approach. At the same time, the bill strengthens the real estate authority’s ability to investigate 
unlicensed trading and ensure licensees are meeting their obligations.

It is a privilege to stand here as New Zealand’s first mental health Minister, today, at the final stage 
of this bill. This legislation represents a significant step forward, modernising a system that is more 
than 30 years old, and bringing it up to date with how we expect mental health care to be to be 
delivered in this country.

The bill sits within the Government’s broader commitment to improve the effectiveness of mental 
health and addiction services. It responds to long-standing calls for reform, and contributes to the 
Government’s response to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Historical Abuse in State Care and 
in the Care of Faith-based Institutions, ensuring our system is grounded in human rights, safety, and 
effective care. It also builds on the work already under way to strengthen our mental health system: 
improving access, growing the workforce, and strengthening crisis support by helping ensure people 
receive effective recovery-focused care when they need it. 
At its core, this bill shifts us towards a more right space and recovery-focused approach, placing 
people at the centre of their care and supporting them to make decisions about their own support 
and recovery wherever possible. It provides a modern legislative framework for when compulsory 
care is needed as a last resort, while protecting the rights of people under compulsory care and 
ensuring care is therapeutic, delivered in the least restrictive way, and responsive to individual needs.  
I want to acknowledge two areas where the bill introduces particularly important changes. First, on 
seclusion, the bill takes a much stronger approach to reducing, and, over time, eliminating the use 
of seclusion. It prohibits its use for children and young people, and strengthens safeguards and 
oversight to drive its reduction across the system as we work collectively towards eliminating this 
practice. 
Second, on the use of electroconvulsive therapy, or ECT, I want to be clear that while ECT remains 
an important treatment option for some people, the bill lifts the threshold for its use and puts stronger 
safeguards in place to ensure it is only used in tightly controlled circumstances in line with best 
practice.  
The bill has been the subject of extensive scrutiny by the Health Committee, which received hundreds 
of submissions and heard directly from people with lived experience: families, clinicians, advocates, 
and community organisations. As I’ve said before, I want to acknowledge those who shared their 
experiences. Your input has directly strengthened this legislation.  
Through the committee stage, a number of targeted amendments have been made to ensure the 
legislation is clear, workable, and provides strong safeguards in practice. These include clarifications 
to ensure powers and rights are clear for those working under the legislation, such as clarifying when 
police detention powers begin and end, strengthening requirements for recording and oversight, and 
refining provisions to ensure they are workable in practice, including those relating to the care of 
birthing parents and their newborns. 
The changes also ensure that the Ministry of Health can require Health New Zealand to provide the 
information needed to support the ministry’s regulatory monitoring and assurance role. These 
changes matter and ensure that the intent of the legislation can be delivered effectively on the 
ground. Ultimately, this will mean people receive care that is more respectful, more responsive, and 
more focused on supporting their recovery. It ensures people can access care when they need it, 
while putting stronger protections around how that care is delivered. 
While the passing of this bill is a major milestone, I also want to acknowledge the significant amount 
of work that lies ahead for the sector to implement these changes. This is why the commencement 
date has been updated to ensure the sector has a full two-year lead-in period following enactment. 
This reflects feedback from the sector about the need to prepare for these changes and implement 
them safely. 
This is now a bill that is fit for purpose, well scrutinised, and ready to become law. The process has 
had integrity. People have been heard, concerns have been addressed, and the legislation has been 
improved as a result. The Mental Health Bill represents a modern, balanced, and more effective 
approach to compulsory mental health care in New Zealand. Today marks a significant milestone for 
our mental health system. 
To close, I want to acknowledge the many people that have contributed to the development of this 
legislation, particularly those with lived experience. I want to thank them and their families for helping 
to improve the system for others in the future. I commend this bill to the House.

CONSTITUTION AMENDMENT BILL 
Legislative Statement 
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) (14:16): I present a legislative statement on 
the Constitution Amendment Bill.  
ASSISTANT SPEAKER (Teanau Tuiono): That legislative statement is published under the

Second Reading 
Hon PAUL GOLDSMITH (Minister of Justice) ( 14:17): I move, That the Constitution 
Amendment Bill be now read a second time. 
This bill makes a small but important change to the Constitution Act to ensure that the post-election 
process is run smoothly. After the election, there’s a small period of time where there are no members 
of Parliament, which continues until election results are finalised and the new MPs take up office. 
During this time, the Constitution Act provides an exception to the rule that Ministers must always be 
an MP, to ensure the caretaker executive Government can continue to act during the post-election 
period. This is critical to our constitutional arrangements and the smooth transition of power. 
Currently, this exception is limited to 28 days.

There are a few circumstances where the conclusion of an election will be delayed—for example, an 
extreme weather event or a judicial recount. In these cases, the 28-day rule can expire before the 
new MPs formally take office, meaning Ministers can no longer hold their ministerial office, which can 
result in a constitutionally untenable position of the Governor-General being left without advisers. 
This happened in 2023, and while party leaders worked to find a stop-gap solution, I consider a 
constitutional setting should have clear and fit for purpose rules. Therefore, this bill removes the 28-
day rule and replaces it with one that does not give rise to the possibility that ministerial tenure will 
expire before the post-election period.  
The new rule will allow Ministers to continue to hold office until the election writ is returned with the 
names of the successful electorate MPs and list MPs who have been declared. It means that if there’s 
a delay to the official vote count, incumbent Ministers remain in office until new MPs are appointed. 
I want to thank the Justice Committee for all their hard work on this, and I commend this bill to the 
House.
